World.title: Ancient Book of Revelation city gives up stunning secret buried for 1,500 years
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An ancient mosaic was recently revealed in a Turkish city long known for being one of the seven churches mentioned in the Book of Revelation.

The artwork was uncovered in the ancient city of Smyrna, an archaeological site in modern-day İzmir, Türkiye, according to Turkish state news outlet Anadolu Agency (AA).

Smyrna — along with Ephesus, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea — is one of the seven churches of Asia Minor addressed by Jesus in the Book of Revelation.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH ANCIENT TREASURE CACHE AT BIBLICAL CITY CONNECTED TO GENESIS

Revelation 2:8 states: "To the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These are the words of him who is the First and the Last, who died and came to life again."

The mosaic was found during infrastructure work at the archaeological site. It dates to between the fourth and sixth centuries A.D., according to officials, and measures roughly 16.4 by 8.2 feet.

Photos show archaeologists brushing away centuries of dirt to reveal the remarkably preserved 1,500-year-old mosaic and its geometric and floral motifs.

Excavation director Akın Ersoy said the mosaic was first found last year, but archaeologists did not fully excavate the artwork until this year, according to AA.

LOST SERMONS FROM ONE OF CHRISTIANITY'S GREATEST SAINTS DISCOVERED AFTER 1,600 YEARS

"In connection with this, we also found traces of the walls that defined the space," said Ersoy.

"We believe that a structure was built over the mosaic during the Ottoman period in the 19th century, and that the new layout was created while avoiding damage to the mosaic floor as much as possible."

The most striking motif is the heart-shaped ivy leaf, which is made of red tesserae, or mosaic tiles.

Though modern people see the heart as a symbol of love, Ersoy said the mosaic was created long before the symbol came to represent romance.

CLICK HERE TO 

"It was not very clear in the early periods that the heart represented affection and love. We see the heart emerge as a symbol of love in paintings during the Renaissance," he said.

Rather, Ersoy said the heart-shaped ivy leaf was intended to symbolize loyalty.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"The ivy leaf clings to trees and walls," he said. "It came to symbolize loyalty and has been used from antiquity through the centuries."

"The space was brought back to life after 1,500 years."

Archaeologists also uncovered bags, cooking pots and earthenware vessels dating to the late Ottoman Empire and the early years of the Turkish Republic, suggesting the space was reused roughly 1,500 years after the mosaic was laid.

World.title: Southern university requires business suits, bans du-rags and other headwear in new dress code
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Dr. Mark Brown, president and CEO of Tuskegee University in Alabama, is bringing forward a "professional educational environment" to one of the nation's most prestigious Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCU).

Students will be required to bring a business suit and shoes to campus for business-like meetings and cannot dress unprofessionally in the classrooms or cafeterias. Head coverings will also be barred, with exceptions for those that serve religious or medical purposes.

"The university has developed a new policy for student attire on campus, classroom attendance, and cell phone use in classrooms," Brown wrote in a message to students. "Tuskegee students now have a dress code for public and professional places."

"The Student Handbook requires students to arrive on campus with a business suit and proper shoes for a business meeting," the message said. "Students are prohibited from wearing revealing clothing in class, to the cafeteria or in official settings like Convocation. They are also not able to wear bedroom shoes, bonnets, or du-rags to class or the cafeteria."

MICHELLE OBAMA ACCUSES MEDIA OF WEAPONIZING FASHION TO 'DIMINISH' HER AS A CAMPAIGN THREAT

The Alabama school is also restricting revealing and sexually explicit clothing as part of a broader push to prepare college students for the workforce.

"The goal here is not meant to restrict you from enjoying the Tuskegee Experience, but to prepare you with a solid foundation for the workforce you will enter once you leave Tuskegee," Brown, who took over as Tuskegee University president two years ago, wrote. "Employers are less forgiving and too often presentation may overrule stellar preparation.

"Tuskegee University continues to prepare the best and brightest for a lifetime of success," Brown added. "With these changes, we want to ensure every student is as prepared as they can be. I look forward to seeing you in August."

STUDENT LOAN RULE WOULD PENALIZE GRADUATES WHO ENTER MINISTRY, CHRISTIAN COLLEGE LEADERS SAY

Tuskegee’s fall orientation guidance lists business attire for career fairs, meetings, interviews and other professional occasions, but the guidance does restrict unprofessional attire in classrooms, too.

"Hats, bonnets, head scarves, caps, hoods, du-rags, bandanas, sunglasses, and other non-religious or non-medically required head coverings should be removed while in the classroom or cafeteria unless they are required for documented medical, religious, cultural, or University-approved purposes," the Dress Code Policy for Students that accompanied Brown's message read.

"Pants, skirts, dresses, and shorts should be worn in a manner that is appropriate for a professional educational environment. Clothing should fit properly and not expose undergarments or other private areas. Excessively short shorts, swimsuit bottoms, body suits, sleeveless undershirts, and similar casual garments are not appropriate for professional classroom settings," the guidance continued. "T-shirts worn as dresses and sagging pants are not permitted. Baggy or loose fitting pants must be worn with a belt that fits around the waist."

UNITED PASSENGER SAYS CREW ORDERED HIM TO CHANGE CONTROVERSIAL T-SHIRT BEFORE HE COULD TRAVEL

Faculty members will be authorized to respond when students are dressed in violation of the guidelines, though the president’s message did not specify potential penalties.

Some elements of the announcement reinforce standards that were already on the books. Tuskegee’s 2025-26 student handbook required students to dress "in good taste," prohibited sleepwear outside residence halls and barred men from wearing "do rags," stocking caps, bandanas, baseball caps and other headwear inside university buildings. It also prohibited sagging pants in academic facilities.

The revised rules have fueled a wider debate over professionalism, cultural expression and the expectations placed on students at HBCUs. Critics online have described restrictions on du-rags and bonnets as respectability politics that unfairly target clothing associated with Black culture.

Supporters argue that colleges should teach students how to present themselves during interviews, meetings and other professional situations.

Several alumni have defended the university’s approach. Tuskegee graduate Gwen McKinney told NBC4 Washington that the policy was "a breath of fresh air," saying there is "a time and place and a setting for every kind of dress."

"A critical part of being ready for and confident in business environments is being appropriately dressed," Director of the Career Education and Leadership Development Center Walter P. Cooper, Sr., said.

"We know that every workplace doesn’t require business attire – our center includes business casual and casual attire, too – but as our students prepare to enter those workplace scenarios that do, it is important that access to the right wardrobe is not a barrier."

For students that might not have the proper attire, there is The Golden Tigers Community Closet to help outfit needy students.

"One of the key pillars of Tuskegee’s Renaissance Era is our focus on career readiness for our students," Brown said. "Academically, we are equipping our students to stand shoulder to shoulder with any candidates competing for roles in the global economy.

"The Golden Tigers Community Closet is an important way to ensure that every student can also feel confidently dressed when they step into those spaces."

The dress code is part of a larger set of classroom and career-readiness rules being introduced as Tuskegee expects its highest new-student enrollment in 32 years. Cellphone use will be prohibited unless authorized by an instructor.

"Faculty will be empowered to respond to students who are inappropriately dressed based on these guidelines," Brown's message to students added.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Faculty will also be able to respond to a different classroom challenge – cell phones. Unless directed by the professor, students are no longer allowed to use their cell phones while in class. They should be turned off to eliminate any distraction from the instructor’s lesson."

Fox News Digital reached out to Brown's office and the university for further comment. VP of Stragetic Communications Thonnia Lee confirmed the details of the president's message to students and the dress code here but declined further comment.

World.title: Mackenzie Phillips says 'morals clause' led to abrupt exit from 'One Day at a Time'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Mackenzie Phillips is reflecting on the moment that ended her run on "One Day at a Time."

The sitcom star recently attended Fanboy Expo Knoxville in Tennessee, where she spoke about the "morals clause" in her contract and how it contributed to her abrupt departure from the series.

"One Day at a Time" made Phillips a household name alongside co-stars Bonnie Franklin and Valerie Bertinelli. Behind the scenes, however, the actress was battling addiction. The 66-year-old said her struggles with substance abuse led to additional provisions in her contract.

MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS SHE AND VALERIE BERTINELLI DRANK WINE, DID COCAINE DURING SITCOM BREAKS

"We all had a morals contract, but mine was a little more specific," she said at the event, People magazine reported.

According to the outlet, the actress said that if producers suspected she was "under the influence," they would "have the right to take [me] to a doctor for urinalysis."

Phillips said everything changed during a lunch break between scenes.

WATCH: MACKENZIE PHILLIPS REVEALS WILD COCAINE-FILLED BREAKS WITH VALERIE BERTINELLI

"One day, I was asleep on the couch," she recalled. "It was lunch hour. Everybody would just take a little nap. And [co-executive producer] Patricia Fass Palmer, who I hated for years, and now we're very good friends, she came up to me, and she said, 'Mac, wake up. Wake up. We're gonna take you to the doctor and have you pee in a cup.'"

Phillips told the panel her first reaction was to ask for more time, knowing that "cocaine runs through your system so quickly." Palmer, however, immediately shut down the idea.

Palmer then told her it was time to leave.

"She said, 'No, we're not waiting until tomorrow,'" Phillips said. "And I said, 'OK, well.' She said, 'All right, Mac. Grab your stuff and get it together. Get all your stuff. And leave.' So that's what I did. And that was that."

Phillips starred in "One Day at a Time" from 1975 to 1980 before her character was written off following her firing, according to People. She later returned for a guest arc before leaving the series for good in 1983, the outlet reported.

Phillips has continued to speak candidly about her struggles with addiction in recent interviews.

CLICK HERE TO 

Back in May, Phillips told Fox News Digital that one memory from her time on the show might still surprise fans today.

"Oh, I don't know. Oh, OK. So, this might surprise you — during lunch break, Valerie and I would drive to my house, get in the pool, drink wine and snort coke," Phillips said.

Phillips quickly clarified that Bertinelli has also spoken openly about that period.

"Valerie talks about it openly, so it's not like I'm pulling her covers or anything," she said. "... Valerie didn't have the kind of addiction that I had; she didn't have addiction."

The former child star said drug use was also common behind the scenes of the sitcom.

"And you know, so we would do coke together in the dressing room and stuff," Phillips said.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I just happened to be the one that got caught. And thank God I got caught, you know?"

Asked by Fox News Digital what keeps her grounded today, Phillips pointed to her faith and perspective.

"What keeps me grounded is my faith and just knowing how strong and … empowered my history has made me," Phillips said.

She said people sometimes respond to her life story with pity, but that's not how she sees it.

"Someone was just saying, 'Oh my God, I feel so sorry for everything you went through,'" Phillips recalled. "And I was like, 'Don't feel sorry for me because everything I went through, even though it was horrible and difficult, made me the woman I am today.'"

WATCH: MACKENZIE PHILLIPS SAYS FAITH AND RESILIENCE HELPED SHAPE WHO SHE IS TODAY

Phillips said she does not believe she could erase parts of her past and remain the same person.

CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

"If I could go back and just take this part out, then I might not be who I am," she said. "And I feel very blessed in my life."

The actress has been candid for years about addiction, trauma and recovery. Phillips is the daughter of John Phillips, co-founder of The Mamas & the Papas, and his first wife, Susan Adams. She chronicled her life in her memoir "High on Arrival" and later explored recovery in "Hopeful Healing."

During her conversation with Fox News Digital, Phillips said resilience has become central to how she views her life.

"I have a high, high resilience," she said. "You know, the love of my son, my family, my sisters — even though that relationship was very difficult for a long time — I just believe ... I have a strong faith, and, I mean, I had no choice. Be resilient or die."

Phillips has also used her recovery to help others. In addition to acting, she has worked in the addiction and recovery field, including as a counselor and manager at Breathe Life Healing Centers.

A Florida man is behind bars awaiting trial after allegedly killing a young woman who traveled from the United Kingdom to pay him to carry out their plan for her to be "sexually abused, tortured, and murdered," court records show.

Sonia Exelby of Portsmouth, England, was reported missing in October 2025 by her family when she failed to return home from a trip to the United States, records show.

Text communications to one of Exelby’s friends suggest she’d regretted her decision and wanted to back out of the deal she’d allegedly made with Hall to torture and kill her, records show.

FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES

But it apparently was too late.

Days later, investigators found her body in a shallow grave in a wooded area in Ocala, Florida.

Now 54-year-old Dwain Hall of Ocala, Florida, faces charges of premeditated, first-degree murder and kidnapping. His trial is scheduled for Nov. 5 in Marion County, Florida.

Hatching a deadly plan

In 2023, Hall and Exelby met on a "fetish website" where they discussed "bondage, suicide, and her desire to have someone kill her," according to court records.

Hall, a self-described sadist, allegedly started what he described as a process of "mentoring" Exelby, investigators who reviewed their messages said.

A Facebook page attributed to Hall shows a fascination with Anubis, said to be the Egyptian god of the underworld.

In the year leading up to her death, Exelby offered to "help Hall with money he owed to the IRS," their online conversation showed, according to investigators.

They allegedly agreed that Exelby would pay him $4,000 cash to pay his debt in exchange for his help achieving "what she wanted," court records show. And they allegedly came up with a "cover story," to tell their families, and potentially law enforcement, records show.

After two years of online messaging, the young woman with a love of singing booked a flight from England to a rural area of North Florida to meet Hall, investigators said.

It wasn’t the first time she’d hatched a plan for her death, reports show.

Authorities in the United Kingdom thwarted a 2024 attempt by Exelby to travel to meet "online individuals who would be willing to kill her violently," court records show. And she had "known mental health diagnoses," investigators said.

This time, court records show, Exelby left evidence on her computer indicating that she was "again suicidal and traveling to the United States to be possibly sexually abused, tortured, and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States."

Exelby flew to Gainesville Regional Airport in Gainesville, Florida, on the evening of Oct. 10, 2025. She had a return flight scheduled for Oct. 13.

Investigators said Hall picked up Exelby in a vehicle and took her to an Airbnb 40 minutes south in Reddick, Florida. She’d reserved it in her name, court records show.

Before picking her up at the airport, Hall purchased gun cleaner, 50 feet of rope, Lume spray deodorant, and sturdy, nylon, parachute cord at a Gainesville Walmart.

After paying for the items, he went back for one more thing—a shovel.

Those alleged details were gathered by investigators with the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, who reviewed Walmart receipts and surveillance video.

‘So scared’ and ‘So broken’

On Oct. 11, after spending one night with Hall, Exelby sent "long, and at times disjointed" messages to a friend through Discord, investigators said.

Exelby allegedly wrote that "last night was so bad," and Hall had her "locked in" and had taken her phone because "he doesn't trust me with it," records show. She noted there was poor cellphone signal "in the middle of nowhere."

She fretted about regret and a gruesome choice.

"I thought he'd do it quick and not give my mind time to stew," she wrote. She said she knew it would be her last communication "if I don't take his offer of shooting him," she wrote.

In the messages, she said the person she was with "made her record three disclaimer videos and write a letter to her family because he thought it was ‘funny,’" investigation notes show.

"I'm so so scared I'm so broken and in so much pain all I can do is lay here," Exelby wrote. "I'm sorry I don't even know what I'm saying and I'm trying to be quick and my time’s up."

Missing, then found

On Oct. 11, the same day Exelby messaged her friend, Hall’s bank account for his roadside assistance business charged Exelby's debit card seven times within about 10 minutes.

After Exelby didn’t show up for her Oct. 13 flight home, she was reported missing.

Shortly after, charges to Exelby’s debit card paid to Hall’s business helped lead investigators to him.

On Oct. 17, law enforcement found Exelby’s body buried in a shallow grave in a wooded area of Marion County, court records show. Four stab wounds were found on the side of her body. The label for the shovel Hall bought at Walmart was found in the top layers of dirt, investigators said.

That same day, Hall was spotted by sheriff’s deputies and was pulled over while driving his black Jeep Cherokee on Interstate 75 in the Ocala area.

DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE

Before being taken into custody, investigators said Hall allegedly messaged a friend over Facebook about a package he was sending that contained "precious and valuable personal items." "Will need this back in 6 months if this storm passes over with no lingering fallout," Hall allegedly wrote in the messages reviewed by investigators. "Please for the love of shadows don't lose this box."

Investigators later recovered the package contents from Hall’s friend. They found a bracelet and a black, seven-inch, steel knife "designed for piercing and stabbing," court records show.

The knife blade was engraved with the words: "Dorkworf pointy end goes in the other guy." The friend told investigators that "Dorkworf" was "making fun of Hall's use of the Darkwolf name while online."

DNA from blood samples recovered from the knife matched Exelby’s.

Initially, Hall denied to investigators that he knew Exelby, court records show.

But eventually, he described how he’d taken a video of her, but that she "was not behaving right so he deleted it."

Frightening video

Investigators later recovered the video that Hall recorded the same day Exelby messaged her friend. It had been deleted three seconds later, records show.

The 4-minute-and-16-second video shows a bruised, "disheveled" Exelby "sitting on a piece of furniture" in the Airbnb. World.title: America hits major marijuana milestone as daily weed use surpasses daily drinking
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Marijuana is officially leading the pack for the most-used daily drug among Americans.

New data from the 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health, from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), reveals that there are 21.4 million daily or near-daily marijuana users in the U.S.

This surpasses the 19.9 million people who smoke cigarettes and the 17.2 million who consume alcohol.

IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE

The annual federal survey of Americans age 12 and older defines daily or near-daily use as consuming marijuana on 300 or more days in the past year. Daily cigarette smokers were characterized as those who smoked on all 30 days of the past month.

The number of Americans using marijuana daily or almost daily rose about 21% between 2022 and 2025 — from 17.7 million to approximately 21.4 million. This amounts to an increase of about 3.7 million frequent users.

The biggest jump occurred between 2021 and 2022 with an increase of roughly 2.8 million users, according to SAMSHA.

This pattern in higher marijuana use is driven mostly by adults, particularly those age 26 and older, rather than teenagers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Between 2021 and 2025, the number of adults 18 and older using marijuana daily or almost daily increased about 22%, from 17.2 million to 20.9 million.

Although marijuana is now the most commonly used substance on a daily or near-daily basis, alcohol remains the most widely used substance overall. During the previous month, about 129 million people drank alcohol while 43.8 million used marijuana.

Cigarette and broader tobacco product use has been on a decline, decreasing from 20.1% of Americans in 2021 to 15.9% in 2025. Meanwhile, general marijuana use rose from 13.2% to 15.1% during that same period.

A recent report by San Francisco-based workplace mental health platform Modern Health found a concerning increase in the number of workers turning to substances to manage stress, especially THC and marijuana products.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The survey of 1,000 full-time employees in April 2026 found that 63% of the workforce engages in at least one form of self-medication after the workday, while 52% have self-medicated during the workday.

Gen Z is the only generation of workers where THC use exceeded alcohol use after work – 59% report using marijuana products compared to 50% who drink alcohol. In that group, 51% reported using THC during the workday.

Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel said the SAMHSA data reflects a "very disturbing trend."

"Too much attention has been put on the bogus or exaggerated uses of marijuana for pain, insomnia and anxiety, when in fact it increases anxiety exponentially, especially in those with underlying mental health issues," he told Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Too little attention has been paid to the growing THC content in all cannabis products, which makes it far more dangerous in terms of mental performance, judgement, memory and all forms of impairment."

THC has been associated with a growing share of fatal motor vehicle crashes, Siegel said, arguing that increased acceptance of marijuana use is "feeding a dangerous trend."

CLICK HERE TO 

"So I firmly believe that the rising use – coupled with decreasing alcohol and cigarettes – is directly due to lack of awareness of all the dangers of marijuana versus an increased awareness of all the dangers of cigarettes and alcohol," he added.

World.content:
The U.S. has agreed to pause attacks on Iran, President Donald Trump said Saturday, amid what he said were the “perimeters of a deal” being agreed upon, which would include the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump said in a post on Truth Social. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.”

The president said the U.S. was “locked and loaded and ready to go” against Iran but that he agreed to cancel attacks “subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

He added that Israel, the U.S. partner in the war with Iran, “joins me in this commitment.”

“Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE,” Trump said of a possible new agreement.

The statement came after the State Department on Saturday urged Americans across the Middle East to consider leaving the region or be prepared to depart on short notice. It also warned of flight disruptions and security risks as the conflict with Iran appeared to be escalating.

Trump earlier threatened Iran with additional attacks, saying Friday that the U.S. will be “hitting them very hard,” while Iran has vowed to “punish” the U.S. and both nations traded what some U.S. officials described as “heavy” strikes.

Responding to Trump’s announcement, Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told “Meet the Press” Sunday that the president should not trust Iran’s word.

Asked why a fresh deal would be different when the Memorandum of Understanding signed in June failed, he told moderator Kristen Welker: “Well, it may not be.”

“We only have three choices: escalate, retreat and come home, or maintain the status quo. I would maintain the status quo as long as I could,” he said.

Iran’s acting minister of defense, Iran Majid Ibn al-Reza, meanwhile said that U.S. remarks should be viewed as “psychological and cognitive warfare.”

He said on X that the threat of further strikes would be taken “as the basis for increasing readiness, strengthening deterrence, and enhancing our own power.”

Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman, a key regional player, spoke with Trump by phone Saturday. According to the Saudi state news agency, he told him that dialogue was needed to de-escalate Middle East tensions, and expressed concerns over plans for new strikes against Iran.

Residents inspect the damage caused by Israeli airstrikes last night on residential buildings in the Safatawi area of Gaza on Aug. 1. Ahmad Hasaballah / Getty Images

The State Department issued fresh security guidance Saturday for Americans in the region.

“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise caution and heightened vigilance and should be prepared for flight cancellations, periodic airspace closures, and potential travel disruptions,” the State Department said. “Some airlines in the region have postponed resumption of earlier flight schedules; others have cancelled some routes. Americans in the region should consider departing, or be prepared to depart should there be escalation.”

The State Department also urged Americans to reconsider travel bans to or through the region.

The warning was distributed through U.S. embassies in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar and Saudi Arabia.

The agency posted a nearly identical statement earlier this month, but that bulletin did not urge Americans to prepare to leave the Middle East or to reconsider upcoming trips, reflecting Washington’s growing concern that the conflict could widen.

On Saturday, the Kuwait Army said its air defense systems intercepted drone attacks from Iran.

“Kuwaiti air defenses are currently engaging hostile drone attacks following the Iranian aggression. The General Staff of the Army notes that any explosions heard are a result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks,” the army said.

Two days ago, the U.S. military confirmed it had executed a “heavy wave of strikes” on Iran, hours after Fox News reported that the president in a phone call had vowed to “beat the f-----g s--- out of” the country.

Trump has grown increasingly exasperated with the state of the war, one Trump ally told NBC News.

Displaced Palestinians inspect the destruction following an Israeli airstrike that targeted the central Gaza Strip on Aug. 1. Majdi Fathi / NurPhoto via Getty Images

“There was not a real strategy for how long or what they should do to get to the endpoint,” the ally said.

The conflict has now entered its sixth month, despite Trump’s repeated early predictions that the war would resolve itself “shortly.”

The protracted conflict has led to soaring oil prices globally and rising gas prices in the U.S.

There was a brief reprieve from fighting in June when the U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding outlining the process for talks to end the war.

But in early July, Trump declared a ceasefire to be “over” and the countries resumed striking targets in the Middle East.

World.title: At least 3 killed in Idaho In-N-Out Burger shooting; suspect dead
World.content:
Three people are dead in a shooting around an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday, authorities said.

At least five people were injured in the violence, Twin Falls Police Department said.

Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said a suspected shooter has died. It was not clear whether the shooter was being counted among the three dead.

The identity of the suspect and a possible motive were part of the investigation, Hicks said.

“We believe the threat to the community is over,” he said at a news conference. “The suspected shooter in this incident is deceased.”

Lynsi Snyder, President of In-N-Out Burger, said a worker was among those killed.

“She was taking care of our most important asset — our customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own,” Snyder said. She added: “He shot both on our property and off, and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our associate and customers, innocent people who never saw it coming.”

City, county and state authorities responded to reports of an active shooter in the area of an In-N-Out on Blue Lakes Boulevard North around 2:30 p.m., police said.

The area is also the location of multiple major retailers and a movie theater complex. Hicks said hundreds of potential witnesses were expected to be interviewed.

“Today has been a very hard day here in Twin Falls,” he said.

A shelter-in-place order for the area was later lifted and roads were being reopened as the shooting investigation continued, Palmer said.

A nearby Chick-fil-A said it was closing Saturday as a precaution.

“Out of an abundance of caution, Chick-fil-A Twin Falls will be closed for the remainder of today,” the restaurant said.

Magic Valley Mall nearby was closed and people inside were told to stay put, a public safety employee there said earlier Saturday afternoon.

The In-N-Out location, the fourth in Idaho, opened July 24, according to a news release from the California-based chain.

World.title: Truth Social launches service selling faster access to Trump posts
World.content:
Wall Street firms can now be alerted of the “most market-moving” social media posts from President Donald Trump before the general public — as long as they pay the right price.

The service went live Saturday: a subscription to his social media platform, Truth Social, that allows financial firms and other organizations to get alerts for new posts made by Trump and other top accounts before general users do.

Trump Media and Technology Group, which owns the platform, launched the new high-speed data feed called “Truth API,” describing it as giving firms “a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths.”

Trump, who has the largest following on the platform by far with 13 million followers, has used Truth Social as his go-to platform to release official statements throughout his second term, including to announce that he was imposing sweeping new tariffs or to declare major military operations.

Trump’s unprecedented use of social media to reveal updates on global affairs and economic policy has contrasted sharply with prior presidents, who generally made such announcements through more formal avenues, such as through the White House press office and the official White House website.

Many trading firms already plug into Trump’s posts through Bloomberg, Reuters or other services that scrape his posts and relay them in real time to their customers. But using this data feed on Truth Social could enable firms to access his posts seconds or even milliseconds faster than the general public.

For a high-frequency trading firm, even milliseconds could make a huge difference.

The president also stands to profit from the new service. Trump is a major stakeholder in TMTG, owning 114.75 million shares to represent 41% of the company, according to his 2025 financial disclosure.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif., have urged the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether Trump Media is violating the law by selling faster access to the president’s posts.

The senators wrote that the subscription “appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders.”

In its announcement of the new service last month, TMTG emphasized Truth Social’s impact on the market.

“Markets already move on Truth Social posts,” Kevin McGurn, interim chief executive officer of TMTG, said in a press release. “Truth API delivers a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths while advancing our strategy to monetize proprietary assets through a high-margin, recurring revenue stream.”

Trump launched Truth Social in early 2022 after he had been banned from X, formerly known as Twitter, and other social media platforms in 2021 following the attacks on the Capitol on Jan. 6.

Elon Musk reinstated Trump’s access to X in November 2022 shortly after he took over the platform as CEO. Trump also regained access to Facebook and Instagram in January 2023.

World.title: Trump rebukes Jeanine Pirro over decision to drop Reflecting Pool vandalism case
World.content:
President Donald Trump criticized longtime ally Jeanine Pirro Saturday after she agreed to drop a case against a former Olympic canoeist who was accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

“I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, on the Reflecting Pool. I don’t know what she was thinking?” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, adding “it was a pure case of VANDALISM.”

“There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS!” the president added.

Pirro’s office, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, said Friday it had obtained information that undermined “the evidentiary basis for the indictment” against David “Davey” Hearn.

Hearn was indicted on July 2 over claims that he was “forcefully and violently pulling up and removing the bottom liner” of the pool with both hands on June 19 — shortly after the pool had undergone renovations directed by the president.

Hearn pleaded not guilty and has said that “the condition of the Reflecting Pool was the same after I stepped away from the water as it was before I got there.”

Prosecutors said Friday that they received new information from the Interior Department after Hearn’s indictment that indicated that the damage to the pool “was the result of flawed installation by the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings.”

Hearn was one of several people arrested in June after the pool was seen covered in green algae and pieces of its blue sealant had peeled away in several places, resulting in chunks of the material floating on the water’s surface.

Trump, who directed a $14 million-plus renovation project that included coating the pool in “American flag blue,” has repeatedly argued that the pool’s issues were caused by vandals.

In a second post Saturday, the president argued that surveillance video clearly showed vandalism at the pool.

“Look for yourselves at the VANDALISM that took place at The Reflecting Pool. The material is being cut with a knife or a box cutter, for all to see!” Trump wrote.

On Friday, the Justice Department said it “first became aware of information showing that the damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism” after reviewing more documents.

The DOJ said that it wouldn’t have sought a grand jury indictment against Hearn had it initially received the documents that the Interior Department provided after the indictment.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum continued to stand by Trump’s claims of vandalism on Saturday, despite the findings presented by Pirro’s office.

“The evidence is clear, vandals have repeatedly caused damage to the Reflecting Pool. Some of these acts were even caught on camera,” Burgum wrote in a post on X.

Burgum wrote that his office “also provided the U.S. Attorney’s office expert and eyewitness testimony to the damage done by vandals and provided every piece of evidence they asked for in the requested time line detailing each area of damage at the pool.”

Hearn’s lawyer said in a statement Friday that the Trump administration owes Hearn an apology.

“The Government’s case against Davey Hearn should never have been brought,” Steven Levin, Hearn’s attorney, said in a statement. “Its dismissal today does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American. The government’s approach was ready, shoot, aim. The federal government owes Mr. Hearn an apology.”

Pirro’s office said Friday that it also moved to dismiss at least one of the other three misdemeanor cases against those who allegedly vandalized the pool.

World.title: Trump says he’ll revive ‘anti-weaponization’ fund if Blanche’s nomination for AG is blocked
World.content:
President Donald Trump on Saturday threatened to “push hard” to keep a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization” fund active, amid an ongoing feud between two Republican senators and the Trump administration over the president’s nomination of Todd Blanche for attorney general.

“If Senators Cornyn and Tillis, both upset because I wouldn’t Endorse them (they lost, and quit, respectively!), aren’t going to approve Todd Blanche, one of the most respected professionals, according to everybody, in the Country, to be the United States Attorney General, then I will keep Todd as Acting A.G., and push hard to get the Anti-Weaponization Bill, which takes care of those who have been so badly treated by the Crooked Joe Biden (and Obuma!) Administration (I get nothing, although I was treated horribly!), PASSED,” the president wrote in a post on Truth Social.

“Todd Blanche was a voice of reason! It will immediately be back on the table, and I will get it done. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” he added.

Sens. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Thom Tillis, R-N.C., are both departing Congress after feuding with Trump. In Texas, Cornyn ran for re-election, losing in a primary runoff to state Attorney General Ken Paxton after Trump endorsed Paxton.

Tillis, in North Carolina, opted not to run for re-election, making his plans to retire public one day after drawing Trump’s ire for opposing a GOP-backed domestic policy package.

The two senators have partially conditioned their support for Blanche’s nomination on the Trump administration rescinding its plans for the fund, which would provide compensation for Jan. 6 rioters pardoned by Trump for claims of government overreach.

In a post on X following Trump’s statement Saturday, Tillis blamed the president for Blanche’s stalled confirmation.

“Despite comments as late as yesterday that the fund is dead, President Trump clearly intends to resurrect the payout pot for punks either by inappropriately establishing another bogus fund or pushing Congress to vote for a bill that the majority of Republicans in the Senate would be against,” he wrote.

“It’s unfortunate that Todd Blanche, who I consider qualified for the job, will not be confirmed because of this reversal. Hopefully, we can resolve this by Tuesday,” Tillis added.

Blanche’s nomination has been in jeopardy for several weeks, with Cornyn and Tillis previously saying that there are other Republican senators that share their concerns but don’t sit on the Judiciary Committee and wouldn’t have the chance to vote for or against Blanche until his nomination came to the floor.

On Wednesday night, the committee postponed a vote on Blanche’s nomination because of Cornyn and Tillis’ concerns.

On Friday, at a Cabinet meeting, the president defended the fund, saying, “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t.”

“This has nothing to do with Todd,” Trump added.

The anti-weaponization fund has been blocked indefinitely by a federal judge, but the Trump administration has not pledged to stop pursuing it.

The fund was part of a settlement agreement that stemmed from a lawsuit Trump filed against the IRS. Also part of that settlement was an agreement that made the president and several family members immune from IRS audits, another provision that Cornyn and Tillis have shared concerns about.

Earlier this week, the president threatened to withdraw Blanche’s nomination and resubmit it next year, after Tillis and Cornyn have left office.

“Hey, in 158 days they can try it again, roll the dice on what the Senate confirmation process looks like next year,” Tillis told reporters at the Capitol after that threat. “It’s all on him. Certainly within his authority to do that.”

World.title: Vincent Pastore, mob enforcer on ‘The Sopranos,’ dies at 80
World.content:
Vincent Pastore, who played Tony Soprano’s best friend turned informant on HBO’s mob drama “The Sopranos,” has died, a representative confirmed Saturday.

He was 80.

Manager Robert Attermann said Pastore, a longtime resident of the Bronx borough of New York City, died at home. He confirmed that friends found his body Saturday.

A cause of death was not provided.

Vincent Pastore attends the "Stevie Van Zandt: Disciple" premiere during the 2024 Tribeca Festival in New York City. Theo Wargo / Getty Images for Tribeca Festival

“To the world, he will always be remembered as the unforgettable ‘Big Pussy,’” he said, using the nickname of Pastore’s “Sopranos” character, Salvatore Bonpensiero, “but to those of us who knew him, he was so much more.”

A longtime actor who plied his trade within the sordid and violent narratives of the Italian American mob, Pastore became a household face in 1999 when he was cast cast as Bonpensiero, mob boss Tony Soprano’s best friend, a family enforcer and ultimately an FBI informant who threatened to upend the New Jersey mob’s enterprise on the acclaimed drama.

He was born in the Bronx, grew up in New Rochelle, New York, served in the U.S. Navy, and attended Pace University, according to an IMDb biography.

Vincent Pastore, left, and Tony Sirico playing cards in a scene from "The Sopranos." Anthony Neste / Getty Images

He has said he worked in the nightclub industry. But he also tried acting, and after befriending Matt Dillon and Kevin Dillon he decided to dive in, he said during a 2015 appearance on “Good Day New York.”

According to his bio at the website for HB Studio, where he was an instructor, one of Pastore’s breakthroughs as an actor was in director Nancy Savoca’s Bronx comedy “True Love.”

He also appeared on television’s “Law & Order” and as an extra in director Martin Scorsese’s 1990 mob classic “Goodfellas.” He appeared in a string of mob narratives on New York City stages and on the big screen.

Pastore became a staple in films and television dramas about organized crime, including a role in “Once Upon a Time in Brooklyn.” But it was “The Sopranos’” six-season run that made him a true star.

“His portrayal of the complex and lovable mobster earned him widespread recognition and praise,” said the Bronx Walk of Fame, which inducted the actor in 2016. “Pastore’s ability to bring depth and authenticity to his character contributed to the show’s success and solidified his place in television history.”

The character’s nickname, Big Pussy, is rumored to have originated during his time as a cat burglar. It distinguished him from another character, Little Pussy Malanga.

From left, Tony Sirico, Steven Van Zandt, James Gandolfini, Michael Imperioli and Vincent Pastore in a publicity still for "The Sopranos." Anthony Neste / Getty Images

The actor also had a musical side and performed with bands, including fronting Gangster Squad, a band familiar to small venues in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut. The band’s Facebook group says it specialized in “a mixture of classic hits from all different music genres, Rhythm and Blues, Rock & Roll, Funk, Soul, and Reggae.”

One of his most difficult gigs in the entertainment industry was during his brief 2007 stint on television’s “Dancing With the Stars,” where he lasted one week.

He said at the time that the training was too difficult.

Pastore founded Renegade Theater NYC with fellow “Sopranos” actor Maureen Van Zandt, wife of Steven Van Zandt, according to HB Studio. His Renegade Theater bio says he wrote “Crazy Horse,” describing it as “a hit play based on the story of his life as a Rock and Roll club owner.”

Musician and “Sopranos” castmate Steven Van Zandt memorialized Pastore on social media, calling him “another irreplaceable brother” who has died.

“It never gets any easier,” he said. “Travel well Vincenzo.”

Speaking on Instagram, “Sopranos” costar Michael Imperioli​ reminisced about traveling with Pastore in the United States, Italy, and Australia.

“Lots of good times,” he said. “Lots of laughs. Vinny was a kind hearted brother who cared deeply about his family and friends. I will miss him always.”

Lorraine Bracco, who played Tony Soprano’s psychiatrist on the HBO drama, said on the same platform that Pastore was “a beautiful soul.”

“Absolutely heartbreaking,” she said.

Attermann said he represented Pastore for more than 30 years — long before his HBO fame.

“Vinny was one of the kindest, most generous people I have ever known,” he said. “He treated everyone with warmth and respect, never turning down a fan who wanted a photograph or an autograph. He genuinely appreciated the people who supported him and always made them feel valued.”

Pastore “loved being an actor” and encouraging others interested in the craft, Atterman said.

He added, “I will miss his friendship, his loyalty, his humor, and his generosity. ... May his memory be a blessing.”

World.title: This week on "Sunday Morning": The Money Issue (Aug. 2)
World.content:
The Emmy Award-winning "CBS News Sunday Morning" is broadcast on CBS Sundays beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET. "Sunday Morning" also streams on the CBS News app beginning at 11:00 a.m. ET. (Download it here.)

This week we present a rebroadcast of "The Money Issue," our annual special broadcast hosted by Jane Pauley dedicated to the many ways in which money underscores the way we live.

COVER STORY: Homebuyers chase the American Dream (Video)

A growing number of young people see themselves as "forever renters" because they can't afford to buy a home, due to short supply, higher mortgage rates, and incomes that haven't kept up with rising home prices. Correspondent Jo Ling Kent examines the difficulties of today's housing market, and checks out one Midwestern city's program aimed at attracting homebuyers from out-of-state.

For more info:

"Enameled Cents" by Stacey Lee Webber. Stacey Lee Webber

ARTS: Art made of money (Video)

Philadelphia-based artist Stacey Lee Webber has invested small coins and bills into her sculptures and jewelry – art made entirely of money. Correspondent Nancy Giles talks with the money-making artist whose creations can cost a pretty penny.

For more info:

The BYD Sealion 7 premium electric SUV. BYD

AUTOMOTIVE: Chinese EVs pull into the lead (Video)

Last year the Chinese car company BYD (which stands for Build Your Dreams) overtook Tesla as the world's top seller of fully electric vehicles, despite the U.S. market being virtually closed to them. Correspondent Seth Doane looks at how China's long-term investments in innovation are paying off in EVs – and how protective tariffs may end up hurting American automakers down the road.

For more info:

Bingo at American Legion Post 153 in Olathe, Kansas. CBS News

GAMES: Bingo! New spins on an old favorite (Video)

From American Legion halls to church basements, the simplicity of Bingo and its ability to let large groups play at once is why the game raises billions of dollars for charities and non-profits. Correspondent Luke Burbank looks at the history of this popular numbers game.

For more info:

HEALTH: Fighting health care insurers (Video)

With health insurance companies frequently denying coverage for medically-requested procedures, 73 percent of Americans surveyed say healthcare delays and denials are a major problem. Now, a company called Sheer Health says they will fight insurance battles on behalf of their clients. Correspondent Susan Spencer looks at how a form of insurance against health care denials may benefit consumers.

For more info:

AMUSEMENTS: A new high for roller coasters (Video)

Correspondent Lee Cowan reports on how the ups-and-downs of today's amusement park industry are being ridden via new technologies in roller coaster design, including the New Texas Giant (a hybrid wooden-and-steel roller coaster), and the Tormenta Rampaging Run (a "giga dive" coaster), at Six Flags Over Texas.

For more info:

TECH: Does your phone eavesdrop on you? (Video)

When ads pop up on your phone for products after you've happened to mention them, is it an indication that advertisers are eavesdropping on you? Correspondent David Pogue checks out the facts about highly-targeted advertising, and why it sometimes gets weirdly specific.

For more info:

Scarlett Johansson with correspondent Tracy Smith. CBS News

SUNDAY PROFILE: Scarlett Johansson, skin care mogul (Video)

Actress Scarlett Johansson has played many roles in her career – and now, the Tony-winner and two-time Oscar-nominee has taken on another: launching her new line of products, called The Outset, designed for people with sensitive skin (like hers). She talks with correspondent Tracy Smith about her skin struggles, and how husband Colin Jost has been a "guinea pig" for her products.

WEB EXCLUSIVE: Extended interview - Scarlett Johansson (Video)

For more info:

Correspondent Robert Costa with Kayleigh Cornell and Sarah Gabriel, of the Archbald Neighborhood Association, at the site of proposed data centers in their small Pennsylvania community. CBS News

TECH: Resistance grows nationwide against AI data center boom (Video)

To fuel their artificial intelligence initiatives, tech companies are building massive numbers of AI data centers, with more than 4,000 in operation across the country. But some communities, wary of the environmental and financial implications of such facilities in their backyards, are fighting back. "Sunday Morning" national correspondent Robert Costa examines the drive to construct AI data centers, and the debate between opponents and AI advocates.

WEB EXCLUSIVE: Extended interview - Sen. Dave McCormick on AI (Video)

In this web exclusive, Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) talks with Robert Costa about how energy and the rise in artificial intelligence go hand-in-hand; America's rivalry with China over AI; and nuclear power.

For more info:

CBS News

TOYS: American Girl: Celebrating girl power

Founded in 1986, American Girl has created dolls, books and accessories that tell the stories of young girls in every American era. On the toy's 40th anniversary, correspondent Faith Salie explores how making history come alive is also creating timeless bonds between generations that celebrate girlhood.

For more info:

NATURE: Hunting for sand dollars

In Florida, correspondent Martha Teichner goes searching for sand dollars – cousins of sea urchins and sea stars – with naturalist Kristen Williams (a.k.a. The Seashell Mermaid). She also goes to the California Academy of Sciences' Steinhart Aquarium in San Francisco to learn what makes these sea creatures so special.

For more info:

FROM THE ARCHIVES: "Once" songwriter Glen Hansard (Video)

Irish singer-songwriter Glen Hansard, an Oscar-winner for "Once" (which became a Tony Award-winning musical), died July 29, 2026 at age 56. In this March 17, 2013 "Sunday Morning" profile, Hansard talked with Anthony Mason about growing up as a street performer in Dublin, and his meteoric rise to fame as a member of the rock band The Frames and (with Markéta Irglová) half of the duo The Swell Season. Also: A web extra featuring Hansard busking on the streets of New York City.

A look back at the esteemed personalities who left us this year, who touched us with their innovation, creativity and humanity.

FROM THE ARCHIVES: Spider-Man creator Stan Lee (Video)

The creator of such superheroes as Spider-Man, Iron Man, the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, Stan Lee (1922-2018) was a comic book genius whose characters made him a superhero himself to legions of fans. In this report that originally aired Jan. 17, 2016, Lee talked with "Sunday Morning" correspondent Lee Cowan about his marvelous life story that, fittingly, was published in comic-book form.
