World.title: Indonesia: At least 5 dead in ferry fire
World.content:
Search and rescue officials report some 41 missing after a fire on a ferry near the Indonesia island of Madura. The cause of the blaze remains unclear.

At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed.

The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi.

Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing.

Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said.

What have Indonesian authorities said?

"Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation.

"The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added.

The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since.

Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia?

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards.

Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi.

At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation.

World.title: Poland: Prime Minister Tusk defies anti-Ukrainian violence
World.content:
Anti-Ukrainian sentiment in Poland is on the rise, with numerous attacks against refugees from the war in Ukraine. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has spoken out against the violence and warned of the danger from Russia.

The Polish leader didn't mince his words. "We must wage a resolute fight against this violence, because thugs, hooligans, and this culture of violence are becoming increasingly brazen and insolent — and also because they have received political support," Donald Tusk said on Tuesday, before a Polish cabinet meeting in Warsaw. The liberal-conservative prime minister said he deplored the fact that "more and more such incidents" are taking place all over Poland.

Tusk's comments came in response to an incident in Wroclaw two days earlier, in which three Polish men brutally beat up a young Ukrainian man and his girlfriend on the street. Cellphone videos show the attackers kicking the Ukrainian man as he lies on the ground. The woman was also hit, sustaining injuries to her neck and ear.

The attack came after an argument in a shop; the attackers took exception to the couple's Ukrainian accents. Polish police acted swiftly: Two of the attackers, both of whom have previous convictions, are already in custody, and a third is being sought.

Tusk warned that such incidents negatively impact Poland's image abroad. The country's reputation was greatly enhanced by its willingness to provide assistanceafter the start of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. This could be destroyed, said Tusk, "if we allow thugs, hooligans and common criminals to beat and humiliate people just because they have a slightly different accent."

Mood is turning against Ukrainians

Poland provided military and humanitarian assistance to its neighbor from the very beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. It took in more than one million refugees from the war, and around 1.5 million Ukrainians are currently living in Poland. The majority of them work, pay taxes, and contribute to the Polish economy.

Ukrainian refugees in a reception center in the Polish capital, Warsaw in April 2022, two months after the start of the war Image: Attila Husejnow/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO

But four and a half years after the start of the war, the mood in Poland has changed. More and more often, Ukrainians are being verbally and physically attacked in public. Last Wednesday a Polish manager on a construction site in Skawina, near Krakow, was filmed aggressively insulting Ukrainian workers. In another incident on a local train near Warsaw, two drunken men shouted verbal abuse at a Ukrainian passenger. On July 11, a man on a bus in Bielsko-Biala insulted and threatened two Ukrainian girls who were trying to take a selfie. Even schoolchildren, including teenagers at a playground, have fallen victim to the new climate of hate.

According to the police, 180 hate crimes against Ukrainians were recorded in the first six months of this year — a third more than in 2025. And on Friday (31.07.2026) the newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza warned that the internet is full of fake news about crimes Ukrainians are supposed to have committed against Poles.

Award of honorary title considered a provocation

Anti-Ukrainian slogans were already apparent during the presidential election campaign last year. But this May was a big turning point. The Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy prompted outrage in Poland with his decision to award a special unit of the Ukrainian army the honorary title of "Heroes of the UPA."

Poland holds the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) responsible for the mass murder of tens of thousands of Polish civilians in Volhynia between 1943 and 1945. Ukrainians, on the other hand, revere the soldiers of the UPA as heroes in the fight against the Sovietization of their country. Individual UPA units continued to fight against Soviet rule well into the 1950s.

Memorial march in Krakow in July 2026 for victims of the Volhynia massacre committed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army during WW2 Image: Beata Zawrzel/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Along with Polish opposition politicians, Tusk is also critical of Zelenskyy in the row about the UPA. However, he believes that the reactions on both sides are exaggerated and counterproductive. Poland's president Karol Nawrocki revoked the award of Poland's highest order to his Ukrainian counterpart, which had been made in 2023. Zelenskyy returned the award by courier to Warsaw.

Avalanche of hate

These demonstrative gestures by both leaders have set off an avalanche. The Polish internet is flooded with hatred for Ukraine. Przemyslaw Czarnek, the prime ministerial candidate of the leading opposition Law and Justice party (PiS), demanded that all military aid for Ukraine be stopped until Kyiv backs down in the row over the interpretation of history.

Current opinion polls speak for themselves. According to a survey by the CBOS institute, for the first time since the start of the war a majority of respondents (54%) were opposed to taking in more Ukrainian refugees. Only 42% supported maintaining the policy to date. In 2022, at the start of the war, 94% of Poles wanted to offer sanctuary to refugees.

Another poll, by the Opinia24 institute for the weekly newspaper Polityka, found that 44% were against providing further aid to Ukraine, and 41% in favor. 54% of respondents opposed Ukraine joining the EU. Only 33% supported Kyiv's desire to become part of the European Union.

The Ukrainians who were attacked in Wroclaw spoke to the NEXTA Polska news service and urged their fellow countrymen to be careful while in Poland. They advised them to avoid any kind of conflict and to "speak less Ukrainian" in public, as a precaution.

Tusk wants to de-escalate the row with Ukraine

Poland's center-left government under prime minister Donald Tusk has emphatically condemned the anti-Ukrainian attacks. The Polish police and judiciary have also acted swiftly and decisively. After the incident in Wroclaw, Tusk urged President Nawrocki to "break his silence" and condemn the violence. So far, Poland's head of state still has not commented. During the presidential election campaign, Nawrocki, a former boxer, admitted that in his youth he took part in an organized brawl between fans of rival football clubs, violence he described as a form of "noble, masculine combat."

Tusk agrees with the opposition's criticism in the row about the UPA. All the same, he is trying to pour oil on troubled waters. On Wednesday, he met with the Ukrainian president Zelenskyy in private for the first time since the UPA crisis. "We also talked about the security challenges that, unfortunately, affect our people as well: it is important that Ukrainians who have left their homes because of the war and found refuge in Poland feel safe," Zelenskyy wrote afterwards on social media, and thanked Tusk.

Continued support for Ukraine

Polish-Ukrainian cooperation is vital for both countries, as demonstrated by an incident in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday (30.07.2026). During a massive Russian attack on Ukraine, a Russian rocket crossed into Polish airspace, landing in a field near a village around 90 kilometers inside the Polish border. The explosion left a crater ten meters wide.

"I know it's not very popular these days to speak well of Ukraine," Tusk said after visiting the scene. Nonetheless, the Polish leader continued: "Poland's security directly depends on the effective actions of Ukrainian forces, including in the air." Tusk stated: "I know where the enemy stands," and added that, despite protests by the Polish opposition, he remains committed to supplying weapons to Ukraine.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany: Islamism and right-wing extremism — a story of mutual radicalization
World.content:
Following the attack on a Berlin Pride festival, the focus in Germany is turning to Islamist terrorism. An expert warns: Looking only at Islamists overlooks the parallels with right-wing extremism.

The terror attack on Berlin's Pride parade has shocked Germany. The perpetrator, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, was a German national and known to German security forces as an Islamist who had tried to join the "Islamic State" group. He had already been convicted of criminal offences twice, and was awaiting a decision about a possible prison sentence at the time of the attack.

The LGBTQ+ community is not a surprising target, according to Jakob Guhl, a director of policy and research at the London-basedInstitute for Strategic Dialogue who has studied Islamist extremism for many years. "The ideology is deeply homophobic and hostile to the queer community. The 'Islamic State' terror group, when it held territory in its so-called caliphate, executed people it accused of homosexuality," Guhl told DW.

In recent years, there have been several attacks on Pride events, Guhl said: In London, Oslo, Zurich and Vienna.

Was the Berlin Pride attack inevitable? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Parallels between different extremist movements

Guhl has also noticed that Islamist extremism has a close relationship with far-right extremist movements. Both ideologies strengthen each other and profit from one another, he argues: "Both are of the view that peaceful coexistence between Muslims and non-Muslims is impossible."

Young Muslims' experiences of discrimination in Germany, being marginalized, and negative reporting about Islam are cited as proof of the German state's hostility towards Islam, according to Guhl.

"In the view of the Islamist extremists, right-wing extremists are representative of Germans as a whole, and on the other hand the right-wing extremists say that Islamist extremists essentially represent Muslims," Guhl says. "There is an attempt to split society into two camps."

Both ideologies overlap in numerous attitudes: contempt for Western liberal society, the propensity toward conspiracy ideas, mistrust of government institutions, anti-feminist attitudes, and hate of the LGBTQ+ community.

"Their reasons for disliking the LGBTQ+ community do vary. On the one hand, from the religious ideological perspective, they believe it goes against the instructions of God," Guhl explained. "On the far-right extremist side, it mostly stems from a biological-racist perspective that it lowers the birthrate and weakens the health of the nation."

Berlin attack: When deradicalization programs don't work To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Germany, security authorities have for years observed the formation of a new generation of young, violence-prone, far-right extremists who are mobilizing against Pride parades.

In a 2018 study entitled, "Loving hate. Anti-Muslim extremism, radical Islam and the spiral of polarization," Guhl and other authors described the common interest of both ideologies: Social division, itself a breeding ground for extremism.

Fuel for extremism: Hate speech on social media

To combat the proliferation of such ideologies, the authors recommended a tougher approach toward hate speech on social media. They also call upon traditional media to avoid one-sided reporting and finger-pointing, which only fuels the polarization spiral.

According to Guhl, one example of this is the current discussion about the background of the attacker of the Berlin Pride event. "I find the question of the nationality of the perpetrator problematic: You quickly run into the danger of creating a two-tier society between different affiliations. That is counterproductive when it comes to the dynamics of radicalization."

For Guhl, it is also important to keep pointing to what Muslim and non-Muslim communities have in common: "We share many more things than those which divide us."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany: As temperatures rise, so does climate skepticism
World.content:
Some 98% of active climate scientists say climate change is happening, and is man-made. Nonetheless, a new study shows the number of climate-change skeptics in Germany has increased. Why is that?

Climate skeptics are no longer a small but noisy minority. They are now "a mass phenomenon," according to researchers at Flensburg University.

In a study published in the scientific journal Global Environmental Change , authors Katharina Gies and Emanuel Deutschmann reported that between 2022 and 2023 there was a big jump in skeptical attitudes to climate change among the majority of the 3,074 people surveyed. Some 59% said they had more doubts about climate change in 2023 than they had had in the previous year.

The researchers wrote that the respondents' individual economic situations could not be considered the primary explanation for the increase in skepticism. Other factors, they said, were much more decisive: A right-leaning political orientation, distrust of state institutions, and dissatisfaction with democracy.

Social psychologist Marlene Altenmüller said the Flensburg publication is important and fascinating, though she has doubts about its alarming tone. Other studies show that "the number of people who have doubts is still very small," she says. Altenmüller, a junior professor at the Leibniz Institute for Psychology in Trier, conducts research into science reception: How people perceive scientific evidence, and what they think about the scientific system and its researchers.

Altenmüller's research indicates that people in Germany do not have fundamental doubts about scientific evidence. Rather, it varies depending on the topic, and the view the group to which people feel they belong has of the topic.

Extreme heat: Can Europe adapt to climate change? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If a group has doubts about climate change, so do its members

Her work, and that of many other researchers, also shows that politically right-leaning people express more skepticism about climate change.

"If right-wing parties were suddenly to discover that we should in fact take action against climate change, my assumption is that the followers of these parties would also believe in climate change and would support political measures," Altenmüller said.

Nor does she believe that climate skeptics have a different personality structure. Instead, climate skepticism is more likely to be down to the fact that "people orientate themselves according to their group and its identity." The credo for most people is that content is secondary, or, as Altenmüller calls it, "Party over policy."

Underlying this is something psychologists call motivated reception. People always see the world through the lens of their own desires, ideas, values, and political ideologies, and anything that cannot be squared with their own ideas and values tends to be disparaged. Altenmüller's research demonstrates that all of us are predisposed to seeing the world through our own filters.

From climate skepticism to conspiracy theories

Both Altenmüller and the Flensburg researchers emphasize that climate change skepticism comes in different guises. One form is the rejection of climate policy measures. The basis for this may be the assumption that it won't be all that bad, or doubt that human activity is the cause. Another is the belief that all the talk about climate change is simply a con, a conspiracy.

This is the focus of research of Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive science at the universities of Bristol and Potsdam. Among other things, he examines the persistence of misinformation and conspiracy theories, and is interested in the parameters that determine whether people reject or accept scientific proofs, especially in connection with vaccines and climate change. "Certain people are more susceptible to conspiracy theories than others," he said.

The COVID-19 pandemic made this very apparent. Lewandowsky argues that for some people, conspiracy theories that apportion blame for a particular situation provide a welcome opportunity to escape from feelings like fear and loss of control. "That offers some brief psychological comfort to people," Lewandowsky says.

However, he goes on to explain that the comfort they derive from assigning blame does not last long. "There's good evidence to suggest that people who do fall into that rabbit hole over time are suffering," he said. "They're less likely to hold their jobs. They lose social contacts. They become mentally challenged."

How climate change forces Indian farmers to stay single To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why climate skepticism is hardly an issue in India

Climate skepticism and conspiracy theories are mostly a Western phenomenon. Researchers observe them the most in the US, Europe, and Australia. In India and other countries of the global south, climate change is already a question of daily survival, and has been for some time. "In India, a lot of people still suffer from [not] getting access to clean drinking water," says Jagadish Thaker, senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, Australia, and an expert in climate change communication.

For years now, he says, people in the global south have been experiencing first-hand the ways that climate change is exacerbating problems through rising temperatures and extreme weather events.

Consequently, measures to reduce emissions and adapt to changing living conditions are not seen as a matter of political ideology. According to Thaker, people in India are trying to counteract their own vulnerability to climate change while still trying to develop economically.

Countering climate skepticism with respect

Heatwaves and other extreme weather events are a direct threat to human life in Germany, as has become apparent during this summer's heatwaves, which are reported to have killed as many as 10,000 people already.

This is why the authors of the Flensburg study are urging people to take climate change skepticism seriously if they are to successfully anchor climate protection measures in society.

Thaker believes the media plays a decisive role. He believes there is still a general lack of information and understanding of the effects of climate change. "The media coverage of extreme weather events, while it's a lot, it is dramatic, and unfortunately doesn't mention climate change."

Altenmüller says it's important to keep emphasizing that there is a scientific consensus that climate change is anthropogenic, or, caused by human activity. Sometimes, she says, it does matter who says it. Research shows that some scientific disciplines are perceived as more biased than others. Consequently, economists have a better chance of their message reaching a wide audience than sociologists.

Taking the values of people who express skepticism into account could also help to communicate a different point of view to them, says Altenmüller. Communication must emphasize not only the restrictions that need to be imposed through political measures, but also the opportunities arising from this.

People who have themselves experienced extreme weather events probably find it easier to shift their perspective. This is why Lewandowsky is hopeful that the this year's heatwaves and wildfires will make a difference. "At some point, people's personal experiences matter," he says.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: China: Dozens dead in Gansu flash floods
World.content:
Chinese authorities will launch an investigation into the floods, amid warnings of further landslides as the rainy weather continues.

The death toll after a flash flood in the northern Gansu province of China has climbed to 25, according to state media reports.

The flood has left 23 others injured, the ⁠official Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday.

What do we know about the Gansu flash floods?

The Shuangshimen Scenic Area, a popular tourist spot for camping, was hit by a flash flood on July 26, with state media initially reporting 10 deaths and 23 injuries.

The country's national commission for disaster prevention said it would oversee an investigation into the event.

Videos of the flood show a deluge ripping through a valley where several tents and cars were parked.

China has been hit by extreme weather this summer, with flooding affecting various areas in the country Image: Lang Bingbing/Xinhua/IMAGO

Authorities have warned of further landslides, including in ‌Dingxi, ​as heavy downpour continues in the annual flood season.

Beijing and Inner Mongolia also issued weather warnings on Sunday as China's ​weather observatory warned of heavy rain, high winds and thunderstorms across a large stretch of the country from ⁠the southwest ​to the northeast.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: On the front line of Europe's battle against wildfires
World.content:
French firefighters have won out over a massive blaze, with almost 200,000 evacuees returning home. But Europe's climate-fueled wildfire season is far from over.

The signal to move comes suddenly — and within a minute or so the fire truck is full and speeding off into the distance, a cloud of orange dust swirling in its wake. "There's always a bit of adrenaline when you get the call," marine firefighter Julien says. "But we're trained; we're prepared."

Maitre Julien — whom DW can only identity by rank and first name — is part of Marseille-based battalion deployed to France's Gironde region to tackle a wildfire which prompted the largest evacuations in the country since World War II.

Some 264 firefighters were injured in the fight against the Gironde fire, four of whom lost their lives. In nearby towns, French flags still fly at half mast to mark the loss. "It's always on our mind," Lieutenant Damien, another marine firefighter, explains as his team members haul the firehose out behind him.

Firefighters are still tackling a wildfire near Bordeaux Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance

Big battles on little sleep

Letitia, a firefighter and medic, said she tries to ask how colleagues are feeling "without being too intrusive."

"It's the fatigue above all," she says when asked about the most common problem affecting her colleagues. "They're sleeping very little."

"Do you see all all of that?" Maitre Julien asks, gesturing out the car window as he drives past rows of blackened trees and swathes of scorched earth at the roadside. "All of that's already burned. But you can see small peels of smoke here and there. We absolutely have to extinguish those so fires don't restart."

When Julien pulls up at another hotspot, the risk of flare-ups comes sharply into focus: The air smells burned and a cloud of white smoke fills the sky. Within about 20 minutes, the smoke turns thick and black, and the fire — previously under control — was visible burning bright again through the trees.

No respite for France's firefighters battling wildfires To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Here by the firefighters' side are improvised teams of local volunteers — farmers and tradesmen and women who took it upon themselves to use their tractors or vans or four-by-fours to transport water to firefighters on the front line, and often head into the blazes themselves without proper protective gear or training.

"We're here because we're needed. And because we want to help," Steven Page, one volunteer, told DW. Maitre Julien said they played a "primordial" role, saving firefighters "precious time" in the fight.

Winning a 'David and Goliath' fight, together

At times, firefighters said, this felt like a "David and Goliath" battle. But they came out on top. By Saturday, France's Interior Ministry declared the fire was no longer progressing. Most of the 220,000 evacuees were allowed to return home.

Elsewhere in Europe, the heat of battle is far from over: Wildfires have also been raging in Greece and Spain — other countries are likely to face fires in the coming months too.

That's keeping EU crisis management chief Hadja Lahbib busy. She visited Bordeaux on Thursday, meeting local officials in Ornano fire station's crisis room and learning how they felled trees and vegetation across 150 kilometers (93 miles) of land to create tactical firebreaks and prevent the flames from reaching the city.

Dotted around the green lines on the map representing firebreaks are different European flags: Germany, Slovakia, Portugal, Spain, Belgium, Sweden, Czechia, Switzerland, Turkey — some of the countries that sent firefighting aircraft, firefighting crews, and technical teams through the EU's crisis management mechanism.

Maitre Julien is expecting more fires to flare up in August and September Image: Rosie Birchard/DW

More EU funds to fight climate-fueled fires?

"Climate change isn't knocking at our door. It's here," Lahbib told DW on Thursday. Last year, her team laid out an EU crisis preparedness plan designed to better anticipate and prevent wildfires and other disasters through EU cooperation. "For that we need the means," she said.

"We proposed a budget of €10.7 billion ($12.3 billion), which is an important amount of money, but at the same time, it pays back," she said. "It's better to prevent — to anticipate — then to recover. So I hope that member states will follow our proposal."

EU states pay into a communal seven-year budget for the bloc. Some national governments facing their own financial woes — including Germany — are skeptical about the EU Commission's bid to lock in its biggest-ever global budget.

Lessons for the future

Climate campaigners also accuse the EU of walking back on big green promises as the bloc pursues a red-tape-cutting agenda to better compete with the likes of China and the US.

"This isn't 'just nature.'⁣ Decades of burning coal, oil and gas are making wildfires more frequent and more destructive," Greenpeace wrote in a statement last week.

But ⁣Lahbib gave a cautious response when asked about allegations that EU states were dragging their feet on climate action. "This is not the moment for controversy and so on. This is a moment of solidarity," she said. "We will have the time to draw on the lessons learned."

EU crisis commissioner Hadja Lahbib says the EU needs to put more resources into crisis prevention Image: Rosie Birchard/DW

In Brussels, where a small monitoring and decision team runs a bloc-wide crisis response center, unit chief Maria Zuber is already busy planning.

"We need to think of informing the population," she said. "We need to think of evacuation plans. We need to invest in early warning tools. So all this is something that we we are mapping. I think that is the main challenge — that we need to change our mindset."

Wildfire season far from over

Back in Gironde, Maitre Julien is all too aware of what's ahead. "We know we'll have more intense fires like this one more frequently," he said. Even this year's wildfire season isn't over yet — Julien and his team still have all of August and September to get through.

But for now, there's a moment of reprieve. At a hastily setup command center in Lège-Cap-Ferret, firefighters can get a meal and some rest before heading back home, or out on their next shift. There's little privacy — just rows of camp beds in a sports hall full of people. Outside, some firefighters prefer to lie on the ground in the shade of empty firetrucks.

"It's a little moment of cohesion," Maitre Julien explains as he sips coffee and jokes with volunteers. "We're not with our family, so we make this sort of temporary bubble to stay well. So that it's more like home."

Tessa Walther contributed to this article.

Edited by Ben Knight

World.title: El agua que hace crecer la población de toda una comarca
World.content:
Las plantas de Bezoya en Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) son un ejemplo de cómo innovación, adaptación, sostenibilidad y responsabilidad empresarial consiguen retener a vecinos de toda la zona que quieren trabajar y vivir en el mismo lugar

Carla Pardo era una niña la primera vez que pisó la embotelladora en la que hoy trabaja; fue en una excusión escolar. Desde su pueblo, San Cristóbal de Segovia, se tardan apenas cinco minutos en coche hasta la fábrica, situada en Trescasas, y esa proximidad marca la diferencia en su día a día: “Es calidad de vida, un lujo que no se compensa con otras cosas”, confiesa esta joven de 32 años, responsable de Calidad de las dos plantas de Bezoya en la provincia de Segovia. La segunda también está cerca, a unos 25 kilómetros de distancia, en Ortigosa del Monte. La combinación ha supuesto que Pardo haya podido quedarse donde se ha criado; de hecho, acaba de comprarse una casa.

Pardo no es una excepción. La mayor parte de la plantilla de estas dos embotelladoras está formada por vecinos de la zona. Su compañero Sergio Moreno (Otero de Herreros, 41 años) entró en la de Ortigosa del Monte hace 10 años por una baja, pasó a tener un contrato indefinido y escaló: “Empecé aprendiendo a manejar distintas máquinas y carretillas”, recuerda. Actualmente es jefe del equipo de Producción. “Si respondes bien, puedes ir creciendo”, explica. “Fue la mejor decisión de mi vida a nivel profesional”. Él también es de los alrededores, vive tan solo a cuatro kilómetros de su puesto de trabajo. “He nacido aquí y no me iría ni a Segovia capital. La tranquilidad, la naturaleza y la cercanía con los vecinos son fundamentales para mí”.

Sergio Moreno, jefe del equipo de Producción, sujeta la botella de agua PI (de 3,14 litros), uno de los nuevos formatos de la marca. Santi Bur

Para Carla Pardo, “cada vez más personas pueden desarrollar una carrera profesional en un entorno rural gracias a la existencia de empresas con empleo sólido”. Su testimonio refleja una de las principales apuestas de Bebidas Bezoya, como subraya su director general, Sergio Bravo (Santander, 48 años): “Tenemos en las plantas 170 empleados y en la compañía somos 230 en total; es una plantilla muy estable a la que iremos incorporando más personas”. Los tres, Pardo, Moreno y Bravo, son el ejemplo de cómo el viaje del agua del manantial a los negocios o casas retiene el talento de los pueblos.

Diseños innovadores y más sostenibles

En embotelladoras como estas se necesitan, además, personas de muy distinta cualificación. Como afirman desde Bezoya, la empresa tiene dos objetivos: la sostenibilidad y la adaptación a las demandas de sus clientes. Como explica Bravo: “La sostenibilidad es un eje clave en Bezoya, y no solo la económica y social, también la medioambiental”. Esa gestión responsable está vinculada a la innovación y a crear nuevos productos, dos pilares que se refuerzan mutuamente. Por ejemplo, han renovado los formatos pequeños y medianos para que sean más ligeros, ergonómicos y sostenibles. Su opción de bag in box (una caja de cartón con dispensador) utiliza un 70% menos de plástico que una botella convencional de capacidad similar. Además, han lanzado la botella PI de 3,14 litros, diseñada con menos material que otras alternativas equivalentes. “Permite la comodidad de una garrafa, pero es fácil de almacenar, de servir y cabe en la nevera”, describe Bravo.

Pero el objetivo de ser más responsables medioambientalmente es transversal, y empieza por el origen. “Cuidamos la diversidad del entorno del manantial”, asegura su director general. Lo hacen de la mano la Red Natura 2000, fundamental para la conservación de la naturaleza en la Unión Europea, cuyo propósito es asegurar la supervivencia a largo plazo de las especies y los tipos de hábitat. Esta red asegura la compatibilidad entre las actividades humanas y el uso adecuado del territorio.

Las fábricas de Bezoya emplean energía 100% renovable. Además, valorizan más del 90% de residuos y compensan la diferencia con reforestación, según Bravo. Toda la flota comercial es híbrida o eléctrica y las botellas están hechas en su totalidad de otras botellas recicladas.

Para trabajar en estos propósitos de forma más eficiente, en febrero la empresa matriz, Pascual, lanzó el Proyecto Aura, una reorganización que ha convertido sus distintas áreas de negocio en cinco compañías especializadas (Lácteos, Café, Distribución e Internacional, además de Hidratación). Todas mantienen un gobierno común, pero cada una cuenta ahora con un equipo propio y una hoja de ruta para adaptarse mejor a su mercado. En el caso de Bezoya, “el objetivo es trascender el agua mineral sin gas y consolidarse como una compañía centrada en la hidratación saludable”, describe Bravo, al frente de esa unidad.

Sergio Bravo, director general de Bebidas Bezoya, posa desde la embotelladora de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia) con la Sierra de Guadarrama de fondo. Santi Burgos

Un agua de calidad

El consumidor es cada vez más exigente. “Su preocupación van más allá del precio, pide productos que no solo le ayuden a cuidar su salud, también quiere impactar lo mínimo en el medioambiente”, afirma Bravo. Por eso, responden con “máxima coherencia” y con mineralización muy débil (’Para vivir muy fuerte’, dice su lema). Como apunta Pardo, esta tipología “puede generar en el organismo una especie de limpieza. Las células del torrente sanguíneo están cargadas con distintos minerales y, al tener el agua una mineralización muy baja, si esa concentración es alta, la arrastra”. En cambio, si el agua tiene una mineralización media, el equilibrio se mantiene y, si es alta, aporta más electrolitos y minerales, “lo que ayuda a recuperar las sales”.

Pardo, como responsable de Calidad, se asegura de que el producto llegue al consumidor con las mismas propiedades con las que emerge del manantial. “El agua viene así de la montaña: es buena y pura, con una composición estable químicamente”, explica. La travesía hasta que llega al envase da comienzo en la sierra de Guadarrama, en un perímetro de protección al que llaman la zona de captación. Allí, la pluviometría (la lluvia o la precipitación que cae) se filtra por un terreno granítico, un tipo de suelo que deja esa mineralización tan baja.

Carla Pardo, la responsable de Calidad de las plantas de Bezoya, en el laboratorio de Ortigosa del Monte (Segovia). SANTI BURGOS

El alumbramiento, la primera vez que se ve el agua, es ya dentro de la botella. Después pasa por el etiquetado, el loteado y el empaquetado, y ya queda lista para que el consumidor la beba. En todo momento, su temperatura se mantiene fría. “En invierno es aproximadamente de 9 grados y en verano puede llegar hasta los 13″, indica la experta.

En la zona de captación “no hay absolutamente nada; ni pozos ni ninguna extracción externa, porque el agua nos llega por gravedad”, describe la segoviana. Tampoco realizan intervenciones en el entorno más allá de la construcción necesaria para la planta que, en los últimos años, se ha ampliado. Sergio Moreno ha sido testigo de esta evolución: “Me motiva haber llegado desde abajo y ser parte de estos cambios; la fábrica, la línea, la formatos... Todo se ha modernizado”. Una evolución que, más allá de la adaptación a las demandas de los clientes y a la sostenibilidad, permite que el trabajo perdure, los puestos se mantengan y la comarca logre una población estable.

A Moreno el trabajo en cadena le gusta; le permite ayudar al compañero que va antes y al que va después. “He podido coordinar equipos y conocerles de primera mano. Algunas veces ayudo a personas que ya estaban cuando entré, y noto cómo he crecido. Es muy bonito”, confiesa. También se enorgullece del resultado, del producto final: “Vas de vacaciones y ves botellas de Bezoya. Además, a la gente le encanta. Es muy gratificante”, resume.

World.title: Rosa Vañó (Castillo de Canena): “Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego con las que he trabajado”
World.content:
Economista de formación, dejó su exitosa carrera de directiva en Coca-Cola para desarrollar, junto a su hermano Francisco, la explotación olivarera que había creado su padre en Jaén. Además, conoce muy bien el mundo de las discográficas ya que trabajó para Warner Music y Universal

Es la gran dama del aceite español. Rosa Vañó (Madrid, 63 años), economista de formación, abandonó una exitosa carrera como directiva de Coca-Cola, donde se dedicaba al desarrollo de nuevas líneas de negocio, lanzamientos y reposicionamiento de productos, para dedicarse, junto a su hermano Francisco, al sueño que inició su padre, Luis Vañó: impulsar Castillo de Canena, una explotación olivarera con almazara situada en Canena (Jaén), propiedad de su familia y reconocida con numerosos premios nacionales e internacionales. Anteriormente trabajó en las discográficas Warner Music y Universal, “donde aprendí a gestionar egos y a entender que hay que contar con los medios de comunicación como embajadores y transmisores de la creatividad y el valor añadido de los músicos”. Ejerce también como tesorera de la Real Academia de Gastronomía.

Pregunta. Con este bagaje, decide desarrollar su propio negocio.

Respuesta. Sí, porque teníamos la enorme suerte de tener campo, almazara y también el castillo. Se puede empezar de cero, pero de distintas formas. Es un recorrido profesional que te va formando y quitando miedos. La ignorancia es muy valiente y te hace creer que puedes hacer las cosas mejor, de forma diferente y de manera especial. Todo esto cuesta mucho trabajo. Primero, porque no es fácil hacerlo y porque hay mucha gente que lo hace igual o mejor que tú. Al final, la fórmula no es otra que trabajo, pero bien entendido.

P. ¿Qué significa esto?

R. El trabajo no son horas, es calidad y flexibilidad. Los peores resultados los he tenido cuando he trabajado 14 horas al día. He sido menos resolutiva y creativa. Me parece importante la conectividad para mi conciliación como madre, como hija y como profesional. Son las tres prioridades de mi vida. El teléfono me permite tener mi sitio de trabajo en cualquier lugar.

P. Comentaba que sabe manejar los egos. ¿Se ha encontrado con muchos?

R. Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego que he conocido y con la que he trabajado en mi vida. Me tocó trabajar con ella en promoción y en gira. Por el contrario, con Phil Collins o los hermanos Young [Malcolm y Angus], de AC/DC, me he divertido mucho. Son personas que han dejado el ego a un lado. Y no tiene nada que ver con que sean hombres o mujeres. Por ejemplo, Prince era un hombre que tenía inseguridades, pero con una gestión muy peculiar de su ego. Porque el ego no es solo el de tipo Madonna, en el que tienes que interpretar su gestión, sino también cómo se siente, cómo es su timidez y cómo tienes que relacionarte con él. Seal tampoco era una persona fácil. Fue mi primer artista y era complicado de manejar.

P. ¿Qué se hace en esos casos?

R. Callar, entender y destensar la situación, aunque no tengas la culpa. Hay que intentar destensar y tratar de ser empático y resolutivo. El ego es más complejo que creerse superior, por eso hay que entender cómo es la personalidad de cada uno. Ha sido una gran escuela de vida.

P. Salir a vender aceite por el mundo habrá sido mucho más fácil, ¿no?

R. La primera vez que salí a vender aceite fue en España. Entré en un restaurante, que no voy a decir cuál, por la puerta principal. Me preguntaron a qué iba y les dije que a vender aceite. Me dijeron que eso era por la puerta de proveedores, que estaba por detrás, donde estaban los cubos de basura y los cascos de botellas. Entré por ahí. Hoy, si no me dicen lo contrario, siempre entro por la puerta de proveedores. Entiendo que, si el cocinero me tiene que recibir en su cocina para probar el aceite, esa es la puerta. Hay que entender cada situación.

P. ¿Ha hecho mucha calle?

R. Al principio hay que hacer mucha calle. Ahora también, pero tenemos más gente que te ayuda. Estoy en un momento de mi vida en el que tengo que mirarlo todo con mucha positividad. Lo mejor es hoy y tengo que estar preparada para el día de mañana. Debe haber un relevo. Hay decisiones que ya no me toca tomar a mí, sino al equipo, a mi sobrino y a mi hijo [ambos se llaman Luis y llevan el apellido Vañó]. Me pueden pedir opinión, pero no puedo empecinarme en que la decisión es mía porque hay gente alrededor que tiene que liderar. Odiaría ser la típica persona que es la primera que llega a la oficina y la última que se va. O la que va todos los días, con 80 años, a ver qué pasa.

P. ¿A qué dedica el resto del tiempo cuando no trabaja?

R. Voy a ir por orden de frivolidad. Me gusta jugar al golf; hago pilates tres días a la semana, que me divierte mucho, y camino. Soy una gran aficionada a viajar, pero con causa. Mi afición siempre ha sido la antropología, la arqueología y el arte antiguo. Me ha interesado saber cuándo el hombre deja de ser animal y adquiere un toque divino o humano. Me gusta viajar con contenido, por ejemplo, para ver el románico del norte de España, el misterio de las catedrales, conocer culturas antiguas... Es algo que no he hecho en los últimos años todo lo que me habría gustado y me gustaría retomarlo. Coger un barco y recorrer las esclusas francesas, pararte en los vignerons y vas viendo el paisaje, me gusta. Me voy a dedicar a viajar más. También he descuidado mucho mi afición a las exposiciones. Antes iba prácticamente todos los meses a ver dos exposiciones en Madrid y, si tenía que irme fuera, también lo hacía. Pero ahora, por mi situación personal, he descuidado un poco esa faceta. Me encantaba ir con toda la familia a ver una exposición y luego irnos a comer. Me parece gratificante. Adoro leer.

P. ¿Cuál es su género preferido?

R. Leo mucha historia, pero como formo parte de varias tertulias literarias me hacen leer todo tipo de libros. Uno de los más recientes ha sido Historia de una escalera. También acabo de leer varias obras de Hermann Hesse para una tertulia. Me esfuerzo por leer cosas diferentes de las que suelo leer durante el insomnio.

P. ¿Qué lee en esas noches en vela?

R. Leo a Agatha Christie y a sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Quiero lecturas ligeras para quedarme dormida. La ópera me ha encantado toda la vida. He estado en distintos teatros, como el Bolshói o La Scala de Milán. Verdi y Puccini me encantan porque mi madre me los ponía de pequeña. Voy a cuatro o cinco óperas al año. También me encanta la música barroca. No me pierdo los ciclos de Händel en el Auditorio Nacional de Música de Madrid.

P. ¿Qué restaurantes frecuenta?

R. Tanto de producto y muy clásicos como sorprendentes y de vanguardia. Me gustan los dos extremos. Estuve hace poco en Desde 1911 y trabaja con un gran producto. También me gustan las verduras de Saddle o el ganso de Navidad, que tomo con mis hijos. Los atunes guisados de El Campero me encantan. No me gustan los crudos. Estuve hace poco en Tetsu y me pareció espectacular y divertido. De Jaén me gustan Juan Carlos García, de Vandelvira, y Pedro Sánchez, de Bagá; también Dani Carnero, del restaurante Kaleja en Málaga. Son maravillosos. Y José Álvarez, en la costa de Almería, con su proyecto de tomates.

P. ¿Su desayuno preferido?

R. Una tostada de pan bien caliente, restregada con ajo, aceite de oliva virgen extra y sal. El ajo es maravilloso de todas las maneras. No soy muy cafetera, tomo uno al día. Me gusta su olor, pero no tanto el sabor.

P. ¿Le gusta darse caprichos?

R. No, salvo gastronómicos. Comprarme ropa siempre tiene que ser algo organizado. Hace años, una compañera de trabajo me dijo que salía con la misma ropa en todas las fotografías. Nunca se lo agradeceré lo suficiente porque no había caído en ello. Soy muy estructurada con lo que me pongo, pero ir de compras me aburre. También me aburren las obras en casa y comprar cosas para decorarla.

P. ¿Tiene algún viaje pendiente?

R. Cuando era pequeña leí los libros de Jack London y sus viajes a los mares del Sur. Por eso me atrae la Polinesia, aunque luego quizá sea un coñazo y tenga que llevarme 200 libros, preguntándome qué hago yo en un palafito. Me gustaría conocerla. También me gustaría ver una aurora boreal. La Antártida me resulta muy atractiva. Y me apetecería hacer un viaje en barco entre Moscú y San Petersburgo.

P. ¿Algún remedio para el insomnio?

R. La edad no perdona. He probado todo lo que no es químico y, a veces, funciona y otras no. Ya convivo con él, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones en Granada, frente al mar Mediterráneo, al que tanto quiero. Lo que no me gusta es pensar por la noche porque es muy mala compañera. También escucho pódcasts ligeros y de true crime; eso me evade y evita que me invadan los malos pensamientos, porque soy una persona muy positiva y estable.

World.title: “Amsterdam’s gay tourism scene doesn’t stretch beyond the city”
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

For over two decades, Michiel Hoogkamer has single-handedly managed Leiden’s sole gay bar. As it approaches its final weeks in business, he and others speak to Brandon Hartley about the challenges facing the country’s ‘homohoreca’ [gay nightlife scene].

Michiel Hoogkamer, the owner of De Roze Beurs, Leiden’s only gay bar, is ready

to call it quits.

After 24 years of catering for everyone from introverted university students to boisterous drag queens, the final night has been set for 15 August.

There’s no single reason why Hoogkamer decided to close down the bar he lovingly described as his child during an interview with Dutch News, but it comes at a difficult time for LGBTI+ oriented businesses all across the Netherlands.

While De Roze Beurs continues to host a stream of regulars, similar businesses across the country have struggled over the past decade.

“Here in the Netherlands, little bars like this one aren’t doing well,” Hoogkamer said. “Young people aren’t loyal to one place anymore. They go to monthly or quarterly parties at nightclubs instead or go to restaurants in the middle of the day.”

Hoogkamer and others say the country’s homohoreca is facing an increasing number of challenges.

Homohoreca is a Dutch term for hospitality businesses that cater for a gay, lesbian, transgender, and bisexual clientele, such as bars, saunas, nightclubs, and restaurants.

Saunas disappearing

Even Amsterdam is not immune. Cafe Getto, a popular gay-oriented restaurant that became famous for its ‘Diva Burgers,’ closed down a few years ago.

Lola the Green Aardvark, a queer food bar, and the lesbian/bisexual/queer café B’Femme both shuttered in 2025.

“The decline is drastic among gay saunas,” Peter Koop told Dutch News. “In 2020, there were still 12 gay saunas, but only eight remain.

“The closed saunas have not found successors. This is likely because there is hardly any interest in such establishments among young people anymore.”

Koop is the current writer and editor of homohoreca.nl, a website that has been tracking the industry since 2001.

However, a precise forecast of what’s to come could prove more difficult than predicting the weather in April.

“Although we do not have hard figures, we also have the impression that there are fewer bars and clubs aimed at the LGBTI+ community,” Philip Tijsma, spokesperson for the national LGBTQ+ rights group COC Nederland, said.

Changing habits

Many clientele are less reliant on these businesses to serve as safe spaces or

dating venues.

“We also have the impression that people’s nightlife behaviour has changed,’ Tijsma said.

“People go to a bar or club less often, and are more likely to attend a large LGBTI+ party or festival a few times a year. General nightlife venues have also sometimes become more inclusive and LGBTI+ people feel at home there more often.”

“In the Netherlands, there is indeed a decline in the number of gay bars, but that decline is very slow,” Koop said.

He said an average of two close in the Netherlands every year, but at least one new one usually appears.

Gay tourism

Koop also noted that, despite a downturn between 2010 and 2015, the number in Amsterdam has been holding steady.

“Amsterdam’s gay establishments benefit from gay tourism, which is not the case in the rest of the Netherlands,” he said.

The decrease is less severe than many people think, but the blow can be hard locally, as is the case with Leiden.”

The city still has a local chapter of COC Nederland but, aside from periodic club nights, it’s more of an advocacy centre than a social organisation.

Potential buyers

The building that houses De Roze Beurs has primarily served as a bar since it was built in 1636.

The name is somewhat difficult to translate into English, as beurs can mean various things such as stock exchange, marketplace and coin purse.

Hoogkamer said the name is partially a tribute to the years it was used as a meeting hall for officials and accountants from the Beestenmarkt, a nearby square where livestock was once sold.

He doesn’t know what the future holds for the building, but he doubts it will remain a gay bar.

A few interested parties have approached him about taking over De Roze Beurs, but the discussions didn’t go far. His landlord will make the ultimate decision about what happens next.

Homophobia increasing

Additional challenges new owners might face include what Hoogkamer says has been a rise in anti-gay hostility.

He said his first few years behind the bar could be rough at times. At one point in the early 2000s, the building was attacked by someone who threw paint bombs at the windows.

Things were largely quiet throughout the 2010s, but there’s been an uptick in aggression after De Roze Beurs reopened following the pandemic.

The rainbow flags out front have been stolen several times. On a busy Saturday night, a vandal smashed one of the windows and shouted anti-gay slurs at his customers.

Berlin attack

Hoogkamer also says there’s been an increase in passers-by heckling patrons seated outside on the terrace.

Recent studies suggest gay tolerance has declined in the Netherlands, especially among youths.

The Berlin Pride attack paints an even darker picture of the situation elsewhere

around the world.

“With the extreme right coming up, like Wilders and the FvD, it’s getting worse,” Hoogkamer said.

“They all say they’re woke and they’re attracting a lot of young people, but it simply isn’t true.”

Late nights

There’s also no denying that running any sort of bar can be incredibly difficult, especially once you enter middle age.

De Roze Beurs is essentially a one-man operation. “It’s hard work and I sometimes have 80-hour working weeks,” Hoogkamer said. “As you get older, you start to feel it, and there’s the long nights.

“I don’t get to bed until four or five in the morning. Everybody else gets to go home and I have to stay here and clean the toilets.”

When Dutch News recently visited De Roze Beurs, many of the rubber ducks that once stood watch over the bar itself had been packed up and placed into bags with other memorabilia.

Stripper pole

Along with an iconic stripper pole and pretty much everything else, the ducks will be sold at an auction scheduled for 20 August hosted by local drag queen Christine Carrington.

Hoogkamer will be sad to see it all go, but he said he was ready to move on.

“I’m going on sabbatical for a year,” he said. “I’m 46, I have good legs, and I want to see something of the world after managing a bar for so many years.”

While he himself wouldn’t take over a gay bar nowadays, he said Leiden could still use one, especially if there’s a person out there who knows what they’re getting themselves into.

“There’s plenty of potential in this city for a gay or queer bar, but you have to work hard,” he advised. “You’re not going to get rich and your social life is forever on hold.

“You can’t go to parties and you can’t go to birthdays because they’re all on Fridays and Saturdays. When do you make your money? On Fridays and Saturdays.”

World.title: Dutch unions call 24-hour public transport strike on September 9
World.content:
Public transport workers across the Netherlands are to stage a one-day strike on Wednesday, September 9, bringing buses, trains, trams and metro services almost to a standstill.

The FNV union has called the strike in the latest escalation of its campaign against the government’s social welfare reforms, which it says will lead to lower living standards for millions of working people.

The three major unions FNV, CNV and VCP have vowed to fight the cabinet’s social welfare reforms, which are designed to secure €6.5 billion in cost savings during the goverment’s four-year term.

Social affairs minister Hans Vijlbrief scrapped a plan to increase the statutory retirement age faster by raising it in step with life expectancy, but the unions want the cabinet to go further by abandoning cuts to unemployment pay and long-term disability benefits.

Staff working for NS, ProRail, urban and regional transport sevices and DB cargo will down tools for 24 hours on September 9, making it impossible to run timetables.

Delays inevitable

“We are aware that a 24-hour strike will cause disruption,” said FNV official Edwim Kuiper. “We regret that deeply. But the consequences of the dismantling of our social security are much greater for everyone and will last much longer.”

National train operator NS said it could not say exactly what the impact of the stoppage would be because it had not been officially notified by the union.

Lobby organisation OV-NL, which represents nine smaller public transport companies such as Arriva, QBuzz and the major city network operators GVB, RET and HTM, said it “understood up to a point” the reason to call a strike.

But it said it was “very unfortunate that passengers are being disadvantaged by a social and political debate”.

Union leader Henri Janssen said that the strike was being called on behalf of commuters. “Every working person has to deal with sickness, work incapacity or involuntary unemployment. They should be able to count on a decent social safety net,“ he said.

World.title: Amsterdam steps up Pride security in wake of attack in Berlin
World.content:
Amsterdam has stepped up security around this weekend’s WorldPride street parties and the annual canal parade in the wake of last week’s attack in Berlin.

A total of 250 concrete blocks have been placed along the canals and nightclubs are carrying out extra bag searches during the two-week event, which runs until August 8.

Richard Keldoulis of Club Church, one of Amsterdam’s best known gay clubs, told NOS: “I’ve never known anything like this.”

Venue owners are in constant contact with the police and intelligence services about appropriate security measures, although they conceded that it is almost impossible to prevent a so-called “lone wolf” attack by one person using a knife or a vehicle.

Last Sunday a woman was killed and 29 people were injured when a man drove a car into a crowd near the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, where the annual Christopher Street Day parade, Germany’s main Pride event, was taking place.

The suspect, Abdul B., was later shot dead by police, who have said they are treating the incident as an Islamist terrorist attack.

Lone wolf attacks

“I come from Berlin and I was at the scene of the attack last week. I left the party few minutes before it all went wrong, but my friends were still there,” Keldoulis said.

“It’s always nice to feel safe, but ultimately you can never rule it out altogether. There were barriers and security measures in Berlin as well, but it still went wrong.”

Michel Peters, chair of the gay police association Roze in Blauw (“pink in blue”), said police would maintain a high-visibility presence during the weekend.

“We are there mainly to maintain contact with the [LGBTQI+] community,” he said. “We want to do more to show that we are there in the coming dys, so that people know they can approach us when something is going on.”

On Tuesday evening thousands of people in Amsterdam gathered at the Homomonument, the national memorial to victims of homophobic persecution, to commemorate the victims of Berlin.

City mayor Femke Halsema addressed the crowd, calling for courage and resilience. “We will win if we keep spreading hope loud and clear,” she said.

World.title: Dutch inflation rises to 3.1% in July as fuel costs soar
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Inflation rose slightly to 3.1% in July, sustaining the above-target trend of the last two and a half years, according to statistics agency CBS’s latest flash forecast.

A 9.7% spike in energy prices, including motor fuels, was the main driver of the increase as overall inflation ticked up from 2.9% in June.

Services inflation was measured at 4.1%, the same level as in June, while purchases abroad were 4.8% more expensive, down from 5.7% a month ago.

The harmonised European rate, which does not include the costs associated with owning or renting a home, was measured at 2.9%, up from 2.5% in June.

Since January 2024 inflation in the Netherlands has been persistently above the European Central Bank’s target level of 2%, peaking at 4.1% in December 2024 and April 2025. Its highest level so far this year was 3.5% in May.

The Dutch government has so far resisted calls to cut prices at the pumps, even though the Netherlands has the most expensive fuel in Europe, at €2.35 for a litre of petrol and €2.39 for diesel.

The CBS will publish the confirmed results with a more detailed breakdown on August 11.

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A woman in Twente was enjoying the sunshine in her garden on Wednesday when she came face to face with a tarantula the size of a dinner plate.

Dierenambulance Enschede posted photos of the poisonous spider on social media after they were called to the town of Oldenzaal to retrieve the arachnid.

The woman spotted the creature in her yard and informed the regional animal ambulance, who were able to capture it by placing a container over the creature and slowly sliding the lid underneath.

Tarantulas do not live in the wild in the Netherlands and it is suspected the spider escaped from a neighbour’s house.

According to the Dierenambulance Enschede, tarantulas are largely harmless. Their bites are akin to a wasp sting.

A number of people admitted they would not have had the woman’s composure. “If I had found the spider, this spider would now be the new owner of my former house,” one commenter wrote on the animal organisation Facebook post.

World.title: Arne Slot rules himself out as next Netherlands head coach
World.content:
Former Liverpool and Feyenoord coach Arne Slot has ruled himself out as the next manager of the Dutch men’s national team, saying he wants to keep working in club football.

The 47-year-old was one of the names put forward to succeed Ronald Koeman, who resigned after the Netherlands were knocked out of the World Cup by Morocco in the round of 32.

Slot has also been courted by AC Milan and English Premier League side Fulham since he was sacked by Liverpool at the end of May after two seasons in charge.

The Dutchman, who arrived after steering Feyenoord to only their second Eredivisie title since the turn of the century, won the Premier League in his first season but could only manage fifth place last term.

The Dutch football association KNVB wants to appoint a manager well ahead of the next UEFA Nations League match against Germany on September 24.

Two other potential successors have also dropped out of the running. PSV manager Peter Bosz has extended his contract at the Eindhoven club, while former Ajax head coach Erik ten Hag recently joined his home town club Twente Enschede as director of football and has said he wants to continue in that role.

World.title: “I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam”
World.content:
Originally from the Philippines, Deepa Paul moved to Amsterdam nearly 15 years ago after her husband took a job in the capital. Her book about opening up her marriage, Ask Me How It Works, was longlisted for the Women’s Prize for Non-Fiction. She loves how the Dutch do kids birthday parties, strongly advises tourists not to cycle and wishes she could have met Mata Hari.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?

I was born in the Philippines to a Bengali father and Filipina mother. I met my husband at university in Manila. I was studying communication but also had a crazy pipe dream of going to Europe to train as a classical singer. His first job ended up being in Singapore, so we had a long-distance relationship for four years while I lived in Manila. After we were married, I moved to Singapore to be with him and found work as a writer and producer in TV. But Singapore wasn’t really my bag.

I pitched my husband the idea of one last adventure before having a baby: a round-the-world trip, him on unpaid sabbatical, me writing freelance. He thought I was crazy and suggested finding a job abroad instead.

A friend working at a Dutch multinational offered to put him in touch with a VP at their Amsterdam HQ. I remember thinking that the cold email my husband wrote sounded way too direct and maybe a bit too much. Turns out the Dutch are a direct culture: it worked! One job offer and six months later, we were on a one-way flight to Amsterdam.

How do you describe yourself – an expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?

I am an immigrant.

How long do you plan to stay?

I don’t see an end date. I will always want to have a home in Amsterdam, although I often fantasise about living a parallel existence somewhere warm in the winter.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?

There’s nothing glamorous about how I accumulated the Dutch I speak now, which I’d describe as pretty passable for daily social life. It was one awkward conversation with one school parent at a time, lots of listening to how people actually talk, and relying on context clues to fill in the 20-30% I might not be grasping accurately when people talk fast.

My husband had negotiated 30 hours of Dutch lessons for both of us, through his employer, when he started his job. I paused for a year or two after I gave birth to my daughter, then went back and took classes at the Volksuniversiteit.

I find that when Dutch people switch to English with me, I can push back. My go-to phrase is ‘ik ben grappiger in het Engels’ [I’m funnier in English]. Humour is disarming, it smooths over the switch in social situations..

My greatest achievement was being interviewed live on NPO Radio 1 about my book in Dutch. The segment was only supposed to last 8 minutes, but it was the longest 11 minutes of my life! Turns out talking about love, commitment, sex and open marriage is far more complicated than chatting about the weather.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?

You’re asking a polyamorist to choose just one?! I love the mobility and freedom of cycling. Gezelligheid. The simplicity of young children’s birthday parties. The straightforward ease of voting — if you don’t come from a culture of systemically corrupt and murderous elections, as I do, you might not appreciate what a privilege and relief that is. The progression of flowers in the spring, from tulips to hyacinths to cherry blossoms to peonies to roses to dahlias: what a gift it is to have a reliable abundance of beauty.

How Dutch have you become?

Not much — I’m still too short (1.56m). I would argue that living in the Netherlands has given me the space and independence to become more myself, rather than more Dutch.

Having said that, I am a lot more direct now, and I not only can handle direct communication, I prefer it. It’s quite a relief actually, coming from a conflict-avoidant, high-context culture. I’ve been nearly cured of my lifelong affliction of Filipino time, which means I’m only mildly late most of the time, and actually punctual the rest of the time.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?

Anne Frank, who inspired me to start keeping a journal at the age of nine. She was the first person to show me that writing about my inner world and observing my own life, no matter how small and ordinary, is a worthy endeavour.

Rachel Ruysch, the most prolific and commercially successful female artist of the Dutch Golden Age, whose floral still life paintings sold for more than Rembrandt’s paintings in that time.

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in Friesland, a bold free spirit who harnessed her eroticism, feminine power and artistic expression to live a courageous life and extraordinary life for a woman of her time. Later biographies exonerated her of espionage in World War I, but her image as a powerful and mysterious femme fatale endures to this day.

What’s your top tourist tip?

Please don’t cycle in Amsterdam, especially not with your selfie stick out. It’s not Disneyland with tulips and windmills along every cycle path. Some of us have things to do and places to get to.

On a less grumpy note, try to book a visit to the Six Collection in advance. It’s a private art collection that spans over three centuries and 10 generations of the wealthy and influential Six family, who have one of the most celebrated Rembrandt paintings you’ve never seen hanging right in their living room.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.

When I gave birth in 2013, I was taken aback that official paternity leave was two days — one day for the actual birth and a second day for the father to register it. It ran completely counter to the image of the Netherlands in my mind as egalitarian, progressive and liberal. It turns out that it’s still deeply patriarchal in small, hidden and entrenched ways.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?

If I’m not panicking about making sure everything is packed and ready to go, cycle around my neighbourhood and have a coffee at my favourite spots. If the weather allows, go for a walk and read in the sunshine at Westerpark, then go for a dip in the IJ.

Throw a big party at home for all the friends I’ve made over the last 15 years, all the people who have become part of my story (except those I’ve revoked access to). My husband will cook enough Filipino food to feed everyone one last time. Eat, drink, laugh, cry, hug and dance, maybe stay up talking until the sun comes up.

If we make it out early enough, go dancing until my legs give out or the club kicks us out. Cycle home as the sun rises and enjoy one last sleep in my own bed—or not.

Deepa was speaking to Molly Quell.

Ask Me How It Works is available for sale at the American Book Center. You can follow Deepa on Substack and Instagram.

World.title: Drugs baron Bolle Jos convicted in absentia in Belgium
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch drug criminal Jos Leijdekkers, known as Bolle Jos, has been convicted by a Belgian judge and sentenced to 14 years in prison.

The 35-year old was not present at the court in Antwerp when the verdict was announced on Thursday, having been on the run since 2024.

Leijdekkers was sentenced for his part in the Costa drugs case, in which a total of 56 people were accused of smuggling 25 tonnes of cocaine through Antwerp and money laundering. The drugs had a street value of €3.5 billion.

An investigation by Follow The Money revealed that the Brabant drugs baron has been living in Sierre Leone and is in a relationship with the president’s daughter.

Two years ago, a Dutch judge sentenced him to 24 years in 2024 for cocaine trafficking through the ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam.

In total, he has been sentenced to 103 years in prison across 10 trials.

The Dutch have requested his extradition from Sierre Leone, but the government denies any knowledge of his presence in the country.

According to drugs experts, the West African country has become a major logistical hub for the smuggling of drugs from South America to Europe.

Earlier this year, Spanish authorities intercepted a ship that had departed from the country and discovered 30,215 kilograms of cocaine, the largest intercepted cocaine shipment ever.

A Canadian multinational operator of convenience stores, Alimentation Couche-Tard, has announced plans to acquire Poland’s Żabka Group, which runs Europe’s largest chain of convenience stores. The company has offered 32 zloty per share, valuing Żabka at 32.6 billion zloty (€7.56 billion). Żabka’s main shareholders have agreed to sell their stakes, with final approval still required from stock market investors. If the transaction is completed, Żabka is likely to be delisted from the Warsaw Stock Exchange just two years after its market debut. Właściciel Circle K chce przejąć 100% Żabki. A group of major individual shareholders, together controlling 9.6% of Żabka’s shares, has also agreed to sell its holdings to the Canadian buyer. The investors include members of the company’s management and former executives. They have also agreed to reinvest part of the proceeds from the sale into Alimentation Couche-Tard shares. The tender offer for the remaining shares was announced on Friday by Ipopema Securities, which is acting as the intermediary in the transaction. Alimentation Couche-Tard and Żabka expect subscriptions for the offer to open around 26 August, following a review of the tender document by the Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF). The companies foresee the transaction closing by the end of the year. The Canadian company expects Żabka to continue operating independently, under the leadership of its current management team, and to retain its brand. Żabka shares jumped after the announcement, rising from 29.26 zloty to around 31.60 zloty on Friday afternoon, an increase of about 8%.
