World.title: Croatia’s War Crimes Prosecutions are Stagnating, Watchdog Warns
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Bozica Ciboci, Vesna Terselic and Veselinka Kastratovic. Photo: Documenta

Since Croatia joined the European Union, the effectiveness of its war-crimes prosecutions has stagnated while crimes committed against Serbian civilians and prisoners-of-war are almost never investigated, a report presented on Friday by Documenta – the Centre for Dealing with the Past, says.

“The number of proceedings is declining. We have recorded 33 criminal proceedings in the trial phase before county courts, involving a total of 91 defendants,” Documenta head Vesna Terselic said, presenting the 2025 Report on Monitoring Criminal Proceedings for War Crimes.

By comparison, there were 54 criminal proceedings in 2024, 64 the year before, and 61 in 2022.

Of the 91 defendants in war-crimes proceedings in 2025, 87 were members of Serbian paramilitary and police forces. The remaining defendants included three former members of the Croatian Army and one member of the Croatian Defence Council, HVO.

Terselic said many dedicated professionals work in the State Attorney’s Office, the police, the courts and the Ministry of Croatian Veterans, but that county state attorneys’ offices lack the capacity to investigate unresolved war-crimes cases.

“Recently, a final verdict brought to an end one of the longest war crimes trials, in which Branimir Glavas was convicted. That trial would not have happened if witness Krunoslav Fehir had not spoken out. It would not have happened if Vladimir Faber had not investigated the case while serving in the police. It was an extremely difficult crime to investigate, and many institutions failed to support the investigation,” Terselic recalled.

She said recent legislative amendments had improved the position of civilian victims of the 1990s Homeland War, but that changes to the law on the rights of victims of sexual violence during the armed aggression against Croatia were still needed.

“Unfortunately, today, there is not a single active trial for crimes committed during Operations Storm and Operation Flash. No one disputes the right of the Croatian Army and police to liberate occupied parts of Croatia and re-establish state authority there, but no one gave them the right to follow that with criminal acts,” said Veselinka Kastratovic, legal adviser at the Centre for Peace, Nonviolence and Human Rights Osijek.

“We cannot say it did not happen. We all know in Croatia that it happened; some people simply choose to look away,” she added.

Documenta’s report also criticises public statements by some high state officials, saying they reflect “one-sided and simplified interpretations of recent history”.

More positively, the report highlighted the commemoration of the killings in Varivode, where then-President Ivo Josipovic and Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic delivered messages of remembrance.

In Varivode, Croatian soldiers killed nine elderly Serb civilians after Operation Storm, a key Croatian Army operation in 1995, which overwhelmed a self-proclaimed Serbian statelet on Croatian territory.

Bozica Ciboci of Documenta called on countries across the region to “sign agreements aimed at improving the prosecution of war-crimes perpetrators and preventing the politicisation of war crimes trials.”

World.title: Week in Review: Cocaine Busts, Changing Goals, Tourism Woes
World.content:
Democracy promotion is out and energy and commercial interest are in. That, in a nutshell, sums up the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans.

In her latest ‘Letter from Washington’ column, Jovana Djurovic takes a look at what the recently initiated “strategic dialogue” between Belgrade and Washington is all about. The latest twists and turns in Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik’s efforts to ingratiate himself with the MAGA world also receive scrutiny.

World.title: Albanian Graduates Hit Hardest by ‘Outdated’ North Macedonia Ranking System
World.content:
In early 2025, when Emine Haxhiu Memishi applied for the post of Junior Associate at North Macedonia’s Ministry of Economy and Labour, she did so armed with a degree in economics from Istanbul Commerce University, an average grade of 9.88, a year of professional training behind her, and a readiness to return to her homeland when so many like her do not.

There was another grade, however, that Haxhiu Memishi hadn’t factored in, one that did not feature on her diploma, in her grade average, or the recommendation letters written by her professors – 0.5, the coefficient assigned by North Macedonia to any foreign university that does not feature on the three big international rankings lists.

Haxhiu Memishi fell at the very first stage of the recruitment process.

“I felt disappointed and treated unfairly,” the 31-year-old told BIRN.

World.title: Money the Greatest Challenge Facing Serbia’s Small, Independent Media
World.content:
For Serbia’s small independent newsrooms, pressure comes not only in the form of intimidation, spurious lawsuits, or physical assault. Increasingly, it is financial.

The Serbian media landscape is sharply divided between outlets close to the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and independent newsrooms.

Research has found that media loyal to the ruling party are the primary beneficiaries of co-financing and advertising from public bodies. Independent media are starved of such funds.

This helps explain why pro-government outlets can operate without the same financial pressures, while independent newsrooms struggle to cover basic overheads and remain vulnerable to political and economic pressure.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Danube Falls to Lowest Levels in 30 Years
World.content:
Suspected Russian missile lands in Poland; extradition of former justice minister sought

A cruise missile crossed into eastern Poland early on Thursday, striking a field and apparently exploding on impact, during another large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine. Poland’s Operational Command said radar detected an unidentified object moving west at 03:40 and dispatched an F-16 to identify and intercept it. Six minutes later, the object disappeared from radar. A Mi-24 helicopter traced its probable impact point to an uninhabited area near Tarnawa-Kolonia in Lublin province. Police arriving at the site found fragments spread around a crater approximately 10 metres across, some 2 kilometres from the nearest homes. No one was injured and no buildings were damaged. The area was checked for explosive and radiological hazards before investigators began examining it. Speaking to reporters, PM Donald Tusk said the preliminary evidence pointed to a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile, but stressed that this still had to be confirmed. He said there was no reason to believe Poland had been the intended target, and that Polish forces were prepared to shoot the missile down had it continued flying. “This war is full of surprises, and we must learn very quickly from new situations and possible new threats,” Tusk said. “For now, the reports – particularly the military ones – indicate that everything worked as it should.” Maksymilian Dura, a retired naval commander and Defence24 expert, said it was possible that the Russians had deliberately directed the missile over Poland. “Given Russia’s desperation and the difficult situation it is now in, they may simply be probing us. Such incidents will happen again,” he told PAP. The episode adds to a growing record of the war crossing Poland’s border. In September 2025, 19 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in a single night, prompting allied NATO aircraft to intervene.

Poland this week formally requested the US detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted over alleged abuses of the Justice Fund under the previous Law and Justice government. Spokeswoman for the National Prosecutor’s Office Anna Adamiak said the request, submitted through diplomatic channels on Monday, covers 19 of the 26 offences prosecutors have attributed to Ziobro. Prosecutors accuse him of directing a criminal group, exceeding his powers and steering grants towards selected organisations. Ziobro, in the US since May, has not been questioned in the investigation and denies fleeing Poland. He had previously received protection in Hungary, but the new government there later withdrew his refugee status and invalidated his travel documents. The US Justice Department will first assess whether Poland’s request meets the treaty’s formal requirements. A federal judge would then rule on whether extradition is legally permissible, before the final decision passes to the US secretary of state. Polish prosecutors say the process could take anywhere from several months to several years. Responding on X, the former justice minister said he trusted the independence of American institutions and expected them to examine what he called the case’s political context. “Donald Tusk, Adam Bodnar and Waldemar Zurek repeatedly publicly prejudged my guilt before any independent court had examined the case,” he claimed.

World.title: Bosnia’s Mainly Serb Entity Ramps Up Lobbying Outlay under Trump
World.content:
In 2021, under the Democrat administration of President Joe Biden, lobbyists hired by the Republika Srpska authorities were focussed mainly on forwarding messages from Banja Luka to US senators, including Marco Rubio, now US Secretary of State.

In early 2022, however, the focus shifted to direct conversations with, for example, Robin Brooks, the then director of the Department of Human Rights and Humanitarian Affairs at the US State Department and Republican congressman Robert Aderholt.

“Our goal is a network of relevant interlocutors who share key principles: respect for Dayton, appreciation of reality, and readiness for rational cooperation,” said Ana Trisic Babic, director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republika Srpska.

Trump’s return to office in January 2025 brought a significant hike in spending by the Republika Srpska in the US. Since then, the entity has hired four new lobbying firms: Zell & Associates International Advocates, Stokes Strategies, GS2Law and Continental Strategy.

Zell & Associates International Advocates was paid around a million euros, though almost half of that went to an Israeli subcontractor called Gilad Government Relations and Lobbying.

One of the most influential lobbying firms in Israel, Gilad is co-owned by Ariel Sender, who headed Trump’s campaign among US citizens in Israel during the 2016 and 2020 elections; in 2012, the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, temporarily revoked the entry passes for Gilad staff amid an ethics scandal.

Zell & Associates did not respond to a request for comment.

Republika Srpska also paid around half a million euros to Stokes Strategies, whose submissions to FARA show it focussed on building relations with conservative organisations and meetings in Congress.

Stokes paid Christine Czerjenewski of Firefly Communications some 50,000 euros for research work. Czerjenewski has connections in US conservative circles and the Republican Party and is a former fellow of the conservative public policy group The Heritage Foundation, described by The New York Times this week as a “bastion of American conservatism”.

Neither Stokes Strategies nor Firefly Communications responded to requests for comment.

A month before the US lifted sanctions on Dodik & Co, Republika Srpska authorities hired GS2Law to the tune of 130,000 euros.

According to their FARA report, GS2Law was tasked with legal research and preparation of a lawsuit “in connection with the previous listing of certain citizens and entities of Republika Srpska on the OFAC [sanctions] list”.

GS2Law did not respond to a request for comment.

Continental Strategy was hired earlier this year, on a contract worth around 660,000 euros. The firm is led by former Trump adviser Carlos Trujillo.

World.title: Serbian Feminists Expect Boost From Montenegro’s Menstrual Leave Law
World.content:
Serbian women’s rights organisations say they feel encouraged by developments in neighbouring Montenegro, which has adopted law changes introducing two paid days of “menstrual leave” per month for women diagnosed with secondary dysmenorrhea, or severe menstrual cramp.

“It has generated considerable enthusiasm among women. It feels like a very progressive idea and a major step forward, especially if we take into account that no country in the wider region has a law introducing such measures,” said Ljiljana Todorovic Jovanovic, founder of the FemIn Collective, a women’s rights NGO from Pozarevac.

The news from Montenegro has been hailed by Serbian women’s rights groups but criticised by some of the general public, activists said.

“Part of the general public welcomed the move and expressed hope that something similar would be introduced in Serbia. However, another part interpreted the news as meaning that women had been granted some kind of privilege,” Ana Mirkailo, an activist from Befem, a Belgrade-based feminist cultural centre and NGO founded in 2009, told BIRN.

She added that this divided reaction didn’t surprise her but “served as a reminder of how much work still needs to be done in this area”.

Spain was the first country in Europe to introduce paid “menstrual leave” in 2023, followed by Portugal, which has allowed up to three consecutive paid days off per month since 2025 for people experiencing disabling pain caused by diagnosed endometriosis or adenomyosis.

The Montenegrin measure applies to women suffering from serious conditions such as endometriosis, uterine fibroids, endometrial polyps, ovarian inflammation and polycystic ovary syndrome.

According to the explanatory note accompanying the legislation, the amendments are intended to properly regulate diagnosed pathological conditions, eliminate prejudice against women in the workplace, and help balance their health needs with professional obligations.

Todorovic Jovanovic said women in Serbia with menstrual health problems can already take ordinary sick leave, during which they receive 65 per cent of their salary. The problem, however, is that employers do not always respond well when employees request sick leave.

“On paper, the law allows workers to take sick leave simply by visiting a doctor, but there are employers and workplaces where taking leave is effectively impossible – whether to care for a child, because of illness, or due to menstrual health problems,” Todorovic Jovanovic said, adding that even if a similar law as Montenegro’s were adopted, the question of implementation in practice would remain.

For years there have been attempts in Serbia to address menstrual health issues as part of women’s general health, and put them up for discussion.

Last year, a Menstrual Justice Initiative was established in Serbia, bringing together researchers and several women’s organisations from across the country. The initiative was created to advocate for greater recognition of menstrual health and related rights.

The latest law changes in Montenegro have given Menstrual Justice Initiative fresh momentum.

“Women’s organisations actively monitor and listen to the communities they work with, and it is important to respond to that momentum. Legislative initiatives of this kind should originate from women’s organisations and be developed in cooperation with political actors who demonstrate a genuine willingness to support them,” Mirkailo said.

Both Todorovic Jovanovic and Mirkailo agreed that menstrual leave is not a “privilege” and that the question of menstrual leave is not only a question of health but of obtaining work-based rights for those who need them.

Todorovic Jovanovic, from Femin Collective, which is a member of the Menstrual Justice Initiative, explains that two main advocacy models are being pursued in the region. The first focuses on reducing VAT on menstrual products, while the second concerns the introduction of “menstrual leave”, as in Montenegro.

North Macedonia currently has the lowest VAT rate on menstrual products in the region, at 5 per cent, compared with 20 per cent in Serbia and 21 per cent in Montenegro.

“What we have been considering is initially directing our advocacy efforts towards reducing VAT, based on research conducted by the Gender Knowledge Hub, which reported in 2023 that women needed about 8,300 dinars (70 euros) a year to cover the cost of menstrual products,” Todorovic Jovanovic said.

She explained that this becomes particularly significant when it is considered how many women come from socially disadvantaged groups and cannot afford these essential products.

World.title: Live From Manhattan: Bosnia’s Republika Srpska and a Selective View of the Past
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

In late July, Denis Bojic, the director of the Republika Srpska Memorial Centre, told the Serbian daily newspaper Politika: “The politics of memory is a means of survival.”

Bojic was commenting on the Centre’s recent campaign in New York, in which billboards bearing photographs and accounts testifying to the ‘suffering’ of the Serb people travelled through Manhattan.

Bojic’s words offered perhaps the clearest explanation of the campaign’s political significance. If Republika Srpska, the predominantly Serb-populated entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were denied the right to tell the world about Serb suffering, he said, it would mean “the end of the existence of Republika Srpska”.

‘Learn About Serbian Suffering’ was presented in New York on July 10 and 11 by the Memorial Centre, a public institution established by the Republika Srpska government in 2024.

According to the organisers, the exhibition appeared at a number of prominent locations in the city, including near the headquarters of the United Nations. A QR code was displayed, directing interested passers-by to a digital collection of testimonies and archival material.

Even the timing of the exhibition was political.

World.title: The 3,500-Year-Old Sunken Settlement Near Zadar You Can Swim to
World.content:
August the 2nd, 2026 – There’s an absolutely fascinating 3,500-year-old sunken settlement not far from Zadar that you can swim to and explore yourself.

Hidden beneath the waters near Zadar lies an incredible archaeological discovery, an interesting prehistoric settlement dating back around 3,500 years that can be reached by swimming from the coast. Putni kofer writes that this ancient submerged site is located near the small island of Ričul, close to Turanj and near Galešnjak, the famous heart-shaped “Island of Love.” The remains lie in the Pašman Channel, only around 50 metres from the shore, at a depth of just two to three metres.

Although it is often described as a “sunken city”, archaeologists explain that it is actually a prehistoric settlement and harbour from way back during the Middle Bronze Age, a period about which relatively little was previously known in northern Dalmatia. The discovery revealed the remains of a large prehistoric harbour structure, including a stone embankment around 300 metres long that once connected the mainland area, known as Tukljača, with the island of Ričul.

Archaeologists also discovered thousands of artefacts, including fragments of pottery, tools, animal bones, wooden objects, and fishing equipment. One of the most remarkable finds was an olive stone believed to be the oldest discovered on the eastern Adriatic coast.

Researchers believe this settlement played an important role in protecting and controlling maritime routes along the eastern Adriatic coast. Its location made it strategically valuable for people who lived and travelled by sea thousands of years ago. The settlement belonged to a population that lived in the area before the emergence of the Liburnians, the ancient people who later became known as skilled sailors and traders of the Adriatic.

Today, the underwater archaeological site near Ričul offers a rare glimpse into prehistoric life on the Croatian coast. With the remains lying so close to shore and in shallow water, it is one of the most fascinating examples of Croatia’s very rich, hidden underwater heritage.

World.title: The Slavonian Banovac: The Croatian Town That Had Its Own Money
World.content:
August the 2nd, 2026 – Few have heard of the Slavonian banovac, but there’s a small, totally overlooked Croatian town that had its very own money over 770 years ago.

Long before Croatia existed as we know it today, and long before it had the kuna or the adopted the euro, a small town in Slavonia was already making history with its own currency. Turning the clock all the way back to the 13th century, the town of Pakrac was home to one of the first Croatian mints, where the famous Slavonian banovac was produced. Putni kofer writes that over 770 years later, this special medieval silver coin remains one of the most fascinating reminders of the town’s importance in Croatian history.

The first reliable written mention of Pakrac dates back to 1256, in a charter issued by King Béla IV. The same document mentions a mint located in the town, one of the earliest known mints in Croatia. Between 1256 and 1260, silver Slavonian banovacs were minted in Pakrac before the mint was later moved to Zagreb. These coins were known for their quality and widespread use, becoming an important medieval currency in the region.

The coin itself carried symbols that are still remembered today. One side featured a running marten, while the other showed a double cross with two crowned heads. The image of the marten later became connected with Croatian monetary tradition.

At the time, Pakrac was not just a small settlement. It was an important medieval centre with a powerful fortress, connected to the Knights Hospitaller, one of the influential military orders of the Middle Ages. Today, visitors can discover the story of the Slavonian banovac at the Museum of the City of Pakrac and learn about the town’s unusual role in Croatian financial history. The medieval coin has also inspired modern events celebrating Pakrac’s heritage, including the annual Slavonian Banovac fair.

A small Slavonian town once minted its own money, and over seven long centuries later, its medieval coin remains a symbol of Croatia’s exceptionally varied and rich history.

World.title: Croatia Among 22 EU Countries Calling for Urgent Response to Spanish Migrant Crisis
World.content:
August the 2nd, 2026 – Croatia is among 22 EU countries loudly calling for an urgent response and a meeting of EU interior ministers in response to the recent massive Spanish migrant crisis.

Index reports that Croatia is among 22 European Union countries calling for an urgent response from EU institutions following the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in North Africa. The leaders of the 22 member states have sent a letter to the leadership of the European Union requesting an emergency video conference of interior ministers to discuss the situation and possible measures.

The request was initiated by Italy and Denmark, with the countries expressing concern over recent developments at the EU’s external border. They are calling for a coordinated European response to illegal migration and stronger protection of the Union’s external borders.

Among the countries that signed the letter is Croatia, which joined other EU members in asking for an urgent response to the Spanish migrant crisis. Croatia also wants to discuss how the EU responds to other migration challenges affecting European borders. The countries also warned about what they describe as the possible misuse of the asylum system and called for further action to prevent the instrumentalisation of migration.

The requested meeting would allow EU interior ministers to assess the situation in Ceuta and discuss measures to support Spain and strengthen cooperation between member states. The 22 countries are jointly stating that migration management requires a common European approach and that the protection of the EU’s external borders remains a shared responsibility.

World.title: Croatia Airlines Nears One Million Passengers Despite Huge Losses
World.content:
August the 2nd, 2025 – Croatia Airlines has managed to get close to one million passengers transported in the first half of 2026, despite enormous, continuous losses totalling almost 50 million euros.

Croatia Airlines carried a record 981,482 passengers during the first six months of 2026, the highest first-half passenger total in the company’s history, but the airline still posted a net loss of 49.7 million euros as rising operating costs and its fleet renewal programme continued to weigh on its finances.

Financial Findings reports that passenger numbers increased by 15% compared with the same period last year, with around 130,000 more travellers choosing the national carrier. The strongest growth came on international scheduled routes, where passenger numbers rose 18%, while domestic scheduled services recorded 6% growth. Overall, Croatia Airlines operated 12,631 flights during the first half of the year, a 2% increase year-on-year, while flight hours climbed 5% to 17,648 hours. The airline’s average passenger load factor also improved to 66.2%, up 2.7 percentage points from a year earlier.

The results outpaced growth across Croatia’s airport network as a whole. While passenger traffic at Croatian airports increased by around 3% to 5.5 million passengers during the first six months of the year, Croatia Airlines expanded five times faster, strengthening its market position.

Revenue also continued to rise. Operating revenue increased by 12%, with passenger transport accounting for 84% of total operating income. Passenger transport revenue alone was up 11% compared with the first half of 2025.

However, the higher income was offset by rapidly rising costs. Operating expenses increased 22%, producing an operating loss of 36.8 million euros, while the company’s overall net loss reached 49.7 million euros for the first half of 2026.

Croatia Airlines said several factors contributed to the weaker financial result. Fuel costs rose by 11.9 million euros, maintenance expenses increased by 4.9 million euros, and aviation service costs were up 3.4 million euros. The airline also incurred additional costs associated with introducing its new Airbus A220 fleet, including pilot and cabin crew training, operational adjustments and the temporary expense of operating multiple aircraft types simultaneously during the transition.

Fleet renewal remains the company’s biggest strategic investment. Two additional Airbus A220 aircraft joined the fleet during the first half of the year, bringing the total to nine. Croatia Airlines expects to receive another seven aircraft before the end of 2026, meaning 14 of the 15 ordered A220s should be in service by year-end. The carrier says replacing its older fleet with a single aircraft type will reduce maintenance and fuel costs, improve operational efficiency and enhance the passenger experience over the long term.

The airline also cited broader industry pressures, including geopolitical uncertainty, fuel price volatility, exchange-rate movements and continuing supply-chain disruptions affecting aircraft parts and maintenance services, all of which continue to impact airline operations across Europe.

World.title: Animal Rights Group Calls for End to Breeding at Zagreb Zoo After Lioness’ Death
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – A prominent Croatian animal rights group is calling for an end to breeding at Zagreb Zoo following the tragic death of a lioness at the jaws of a male lion just days ago.

Croatian animal welfare organisation Friends of Animals (Prijatelji životinja) has called on the City of Zagreb to end animal breeding at Zagreb Zoo following the death of lioness Tayra, who was killed by the male lion Uganda after the pair were introduced for breeding. The group says the incident should prompt a fundamental review of the zoo’s policies rather than be treated as an isolated accident.

Index reports that in an open appeal to the city, the organisation urged the zoo to stop breeding animals and to end the practice of acquiring, buying, selling, exchanging or gifting animals with other zoos. It argues that Zagreb cannot undo Tayra’s death but can prevent future generations of animals from spending their entire lives in captivity.

The group also opposes reports that the zoo may bring in another lioness to replace Tayra. According to Friends of Animals, a new lioness would likely be introduced for breeding, meaning any cubs born would also spend their lives in captivity. They stress they are not calling for the zoo to close immediately or for existing animals to be relocated, but instead want breeding and the acquisition of new animals to end.

Friends of Animals argue that every new animal born or brought into the zoo extends the cycle of captivity for decades. Instead, they want the City of Zagreb to develop a long-term plan to transform the zoo into an educational, tourist and interactive centre that no longer depends on keeping animals in enclosures.

Their proposal includes replacing live animal exhibits with modern technology such as virtual recreations of natural habitats, interactive museums, 3D projections, holograms, augmented and virtual reality experiences, and live streams from national parks, protected areas and wildlife sanctuaries. The organisation believes these alternatives could educate visitors while avoiding the ethical concerns associated with captivity.

The group says Zagreb has the opportunity to become one of the first cities to begin transforming the traditional zoo model through ethical and technological innovation. It argues that modern education no longer requires cages and that respect for animals cannot be taught while keeping them confined.

Friends of Animals has requested an official response from the City of Zagreb and says Tayra’s death should serve as a warning and a catalyst for changing the long-term direction of Zagreb Zoo.

World.title: INA Confirms Major Natural Gas Potential in the Northern Adriatic
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – Croatia’s energy company INA has confirmed a significant new natural gas discovery in the northern Adriatic.

Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that this latest discovery fully reinforces previous expectations that the offshore area still holds substantial untapped reserves. It could play a very important role in the country’s future energy supply. The announcement follows the successful completion of the first well in a new multi-year investment programme.

The newly completed Ana-4 DIR well, drilled within an existing northern Adriatic production field, reached a depth of 1,282 metres. Initial testing across three gas-bearing reservoirs produced a combined flow rate of around 160,000 cubic metres of natural gas per day, making it one of INA’s strongest-performing gas wells.

The company said the results confirm that Croatia’s offshore gas fields still contain considerable remaining reserves, despite decades of production. Preparations are now underway to connect the well to the existing production infrastructure so engineers can carry out extended testing, clean the reservoirs and gather additional data needed to certify the reserves and determine long-term production capacity.

The successful well is the first in a five-well drilling campaign that forms part of an investment cycle worth approximately €65 million. Drilling was carried out using the Labin jack-up drilling rig, operated by INA’s subsidiary CROSCO, without any reported safety or environmental incidents.

Work is already moving to the next stage of the programme. The Labin rig is being relocated to the IKA JZ-6 DIR location, where drilling of the second well will begin as INA continues its effort to increase domestic gas production from the northern Adriatic.

INA says the project is strategically important because increasing domestic production strengthens Croatia’s energy security and reduces reliance on imported natural gas. The company believes the northern Adriatic will remain a key source of Croatian gas supplies for years to come, with additional development of offshore reserves planned throughout the investment programme.

World.title: Croatia to Expand Bottle Deposit Scheme in Biggest Overhaul Yet
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – Croatia’s deposit return system is set for its biggest expansion since it was introduced, with major changes coming into force from the 1st of January, 2027.

Poslovni reports that consumers will soon be able to return far more than just plastic bottles, glass bottles and cans, as the government plans to include additional types of beverage packaging in the scheme.

Under the new rules, the 10-cent refundable deposit will also apply to multilayer carton packaging, commonly known as Tetra Pak, which is widely used for milk, dairy drinks and fruit juices. In addition, all beverage containers smaller than 200 millilitres, previously excluded from the system, will also be covered. As a result, these products will cost 10 cents more at the checkout, with shoppers receiving the money back when they return the empty packaging.

Supporters say the expansion will boost recycling rates and reduce waste, bringing Croatia’s recycling system closer to broader European circular economy goals. However, manufacturers and retailers argue they are not yet ready for such a significant change.

Industry representatives warn that Croatia currently lacks sufficient facilities to recycle multilayer carton packaging and that most shops do not have reverse-vending machines capable of accepting Tetra Pak containers. Instead, retailers would have to collect them manually, raising concerns over hygiene, storage space and additional staffing requirements.

The business sector also expects higher operating costs. Producers of milk, dairy products and juices say adapting to the expanded scheme will require new investments, while retailers will face increased handling costs. Those expenses, they warn, could ultimately be reflected in higher consumer prices beyond the 10-cent refundable deposit itself.

Business groups, including the Croatian Employers’ Association, have called for the introduction of the new rules to be postponed until the necessary infrastructure is in place. They argue that expanding the system while businesses are also preparing for new EU packaging regulations places an additional burden on the sector.

The Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition has acknowledged the request for a delay but says the industry has known about the planned changes since 2023, when the relevant regulations were adopted. Officials maintain there has been ample time to prepare and say they are working to ensure the expanded deposit return system begins operating as scheduled on 1 January 2027.

If implemented on time, the reform will mark the largest change to Croatia’s deposit return system to date, extending financial incentives for recycling well beyond traditional plastic bottles, glass bottles and cans.

World.title: Croatian Service Sector Grows, But One Industry Sees Sharp 12% Drop
World.content:
August the 1st, 2026 – The Croatian service sector has seen encouragingly strong growth, but one industry has seen a very sharp 12% drop.

The Croatian service sector continued its upward trend during May 2026, with overall activity rising significantly compared to a year earlier. However, the latest official figures also reveal stark contrasts between industries, as some sectors posted double-digit growth while others experienced notable declines.

Calendar-adjusted turnover across Croatia’s service industries increased by 5.8% year-on-year in May. Poslovni reports that when looking at the first five months of 2026, turnover was up 6.2% compared with the same period last year. Despite the strong annual performance, service activity edged down 0.3% compared to April.

The biggest annual winner was the film, video and television production sector, along with sound recording and music publishing, where turnover jumped 28.4%. Real estate activities followed with a 17.7% increase, while postal and courier services rose 16.2%.

Tourism-related businesses also recorded solid growth. Accommodation and food service activities climbed 11.2% year-on-year, with accommodation alone increasing 14%, while restaurants, cafés and other food and beverage businesses saw turnover rise 8.4%.

Compared with April, water transport recorded the strongest monthly increase, surging 14.4%. Postal and courier services were up 7.6%, while other professional, scientific and technical activities rose 7.1%. Accommodation services also posted a healthy monthly gain of 5.2%.

Not every sector shared in the growth. The steepest monthly decline was recorded in office administrative and support services, where turnover fell 11.7%. Air transport dropped 4.9%, while publishing activities slipped 3.3% compared with April.

On an annual basis, the weakest-performing sector was management consultancy, where turnover declined 9.8%. Office administrative and business support services were down 7.3%, while architectural and engineering services, together with technical testing and analysis, fell 6.2%.

Although May brought a slight month-on-month slowdown, the figures suggest Croatia’s service sector remains on a growth path overall, with performance increasingly varying between industries benefiting from strong demand and those facing more challenging market conditions.

World.title: Iraqi court recovers IQD 20 billion in corruption and money laundering cases
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq’s Rusafa Investigative Court, which specializes in integrity and money laundering cases, has recovered 20 billion Iraqi dinars (approximately $15.3 million) linked to financial corruption, administrative misconduct, and fraud, the country’s judiciary announced on Sunday.

In a statement, the judiciary’s media office said the recovered funds were tied to investigations involving financial and administrative corruption as well as financial fraud.

The court said the recovery forms part of ongoing legal efforts to pursue individuals accused of using illegal methods to obtain profits at the expense of public funds.

Authorities stressed that legal proceedings against those involved remain underway, reaffirming their commitment to combating corruption and protecting state resources.

The judiciary did not disclose additional details regarding the individuals or entities involved, nor did it specify when the alleged offenses occurred.

World.title: US Embassy in Iraq urges Americans to leave the Middle East
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The US Embassy in Baghdad and the US Consulate General in Erbil advised American citizens on Saturday to leave the Middle East as tensions in the region remained high.

The US mission said in a statement that due to heightened tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation.

The mission added that Americans presently in the Middle East should exercise extreme caution and alertness and be prepared for flight cancellations, frequent airspace closures, and possible travel difficulties.

Some regional airlines have postponed the restart of previously scheduled flights, while others have cancelled some routes.

Americans in the region are advised to consider departing or to be ready to leave if tensions escalate.

In a statement, the US Embassy in Baghdad advised that those who choose to travel to or from the region should closely monitor updates regarding airport and airline operations.

US diplomatic installations, especially those outside the Middle East, have been attacked. Iran and pro-Iran groups may attack additional US interests abroad or at areas connected with the US and Americans across the world, such as US corporations and institutions, according to the statement.

The Iranian leadership is unpredictable, as seen by recent moves to strike regions without notice, as well as to expand assaults to previously untargeted territories such as Egypt, according to the US Embassy in Iraq.

The US Embassy advised Americans to remain vigilant, as the absence of past attacks on US interests or businesses in a country does not ensure their safety.

World.title: Iraq, NATO agree to open mission office in Baghdad, expand security cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews,com) — Iraqi National Security Adviser Qasim al-Aboudi and the commander of the NATO Mission Iraq (NMI), Lt. Gen. Ramon Armada, agreed on Sunday to open a NATO mission office in Baghdad while reaffirming continued cooperation on military training, cybersecurity, and strategic security partnerships.

According to a statement from al-Aboudi’s media office, cited by the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), the two officials held talks via video conference to discuss regional security developments and NATO’s ongoing support for Iraq’s armed forces.

During the discussion, both sides stressed the importance of reducing regional tensions and resolving recurring crises through dialogue and diplomatic channels. They also reviewed mechanisms for continuing NATO assistance in the areas of military training, advisory support, intelligence sharing, and capacity building.

A key outcome of the meeting was an agreement to establish a NATO Mission office in Baghdad, further strengthening coordination between the alliance and Iraqi security institutions.

Al-Aboudi said NATO’s role in Iraq remains focused on non-combat activities, including military advisory services, training, capacity building, cybersecurity support, and cooperation in artificial intelligence. He added that Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government is pursuing a policy of engagement with friendly and neighboring countries to advance development, investment, and mutually beneficial partnerships.

For his part, Armada reaffirmed that NATO’s advisory and training mission is committed to helping develop the capabilities of Iraq’s armed forces to address future security challenges. He said the alliance remains committed to supporting Iraq in line with the priorities established by the Iraqi government.

World.title: Zaidi threatens to resign as Coordination Framework divided over response to Saudi strikes
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi reportedly threatened to resign during a recent meeting of the Coordination Framework amid deep divisions over how Iraq should respond to recent Saudi military strikes, according to a report published Sunday by Baghdad-based newspaper Al-Mada.

Citing political sources, the newspaper said the prime minister’s remarks came during a tense meeting that exposed growing disagreements among senior Shiite leaders over security policy, the role of armed factions, and Baghdad’s handling of escalating regional tensions.

According to the report, the meeting became increasingly heated after intelligence was presented alleging that the armed group Saraya Awliya al-Dam was preparing to launch an attack against Jordan from Iraqi territory. The sources said Amman had warned Baghdad it would respond to any attack originating from Iraq, further intensifying the debate.

The report claims the dispute centered on whether Iraq should adhere to the government’s official position or allow individual armed factions to respond independently to the recent Saudi strikes. While most Coordination Framework leaders reportedly backed the government’s approach, one influential figure with ties to Saraya Awliya al-Dam insisted on carrying out a unilateral response.

Al-Mada reported that armed factions have given the government until next Friday to respond to Saudi Arabia. According to the sources, they warned that if Baghdad fails to act, they may launch their own response.

The newspaper also reported that the escalating dispute prompted al-Zaidi to again raise the possibility of resigning, marking what would be the second time he has reportedly made such a threat since taking office. According to the report, he previously suggested stepping down if his anti-corruption agenda failed.

The sources further claimed that the prime minister is facing mounting political pressure, including concerns about his personal security, although no official statements have confirmed those assertions.

The report also focused on the investigation into drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, stating that seven Iraqi-Saudi security meetings, with U.S. participation in some sessions, have been held over the past two months.

According to Al-Mada’s sources, the investigations have not produced conclusive evidence proving that the attacks originated from Iraqi territory, despite Saudi accusations.

The report said several scenarios remain under discussion, including the possibility that Iraqi armed factions were responsible, that Houthi operatives present in Iraq facilitated the attacks, or alternative theories promoted by some factions alleging Israeli activity in Iraq’s southern desert regions.

According to the newspaper, the ongoing crisis led al-Zaidi to cancel a planned visit to Saudi Arabia, which Iraqi officials reportedly viewed as an opportunity to attract much-needed Saudi investment at a time when Iraq faces mounting financial pressures.

The report also said armed factions have urged the prime minister to suspend efforts to bring all weapons under state control, arguing that the recent Saudi strikes have fundamentally altered the security landscape.

Al-Mada also reported that discussions during the meeting touched on the role of Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) Chairman Faleh al-Fayyadh during the recent U.S.-Saudi strikes that targeted PMF facilities.

According to the newspaper’s sources, claims circulated that al-Zaidi had warned al-Fayyadh upon returning from Turkey that PMF sites could be targeted, and that evacuation efforts were delayed. However, other participants reportedly dismissed those claims, suggesting they reflected internal political disputes rather than established facts.

The Iraqi government has previously denied having prior knowledge of the U.S.-Saudi strikes. Government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said Baghdad neither approved nor was informed in advance of the attacks.

However, U.S. President Donald Trump later told Fox News that the strikes had been coordinated with the Iraqi government, presenting an account that differs from Baghdad’s official position.

World.title: Zaidi’s failed raid on Nujaba base exposes challenges in disarmament push
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — A failed security operation targeting a facility belonging to the Iran-aligned Harakat al-Nujaba movement has underscored the challenges facing the Iraqi government as it seeks to bring all armed groups under state control before the end of September.

According to a report published by Al-Monitor, a joint Iraqi force attempted to search a Harakat al-Nujaba compound in Baghdad’s Jurf al-Naddaf district on July 24 after receiving intelligence suggesting the site contained missiles and drones. However, the operation ended without the facility being searched after armed members of the group confronted government forces.

The report, citing Iraqi security officials, said the operation involved Baghdad Operations Command, the Federal Police, and the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) Security Directorate. Shortly after arriving at the compound, commanders affiliated with Harakat al-Nujaba reportedly ordered their fighters to prevent security personnel from entering. Armed members of the group then surrounded the government force and fired warning shots into the air, forcing the operation to halt.

According to the officials, the PMF leadership subsequently instructed its personnel to withdraw, stating they had not been informed that the target was a facility affiliated with Harakat al-Nujaba. Army units involved in the operation later received similar withdrawal orders. No casualties were reported, and neither the government nor the armed group publicly disclosed details of the incident at the time.

The incident comes as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has pledged to ensure that all weapons in Iraq are brought under state control by September 30, the scheduled end of the U.S.-led coalition’s military mission in the country.

Al-Monitor described the failed operation as the first significant field test of the government’s commitment to enforcing that pledge. While previous administrations also announced plans to limit weapons to state institutions, implementation has remained difficult due to the political and military influence of several armed factions.

Hayder al-Shakeri, a researcher with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al-Monitor that although Baghdad has increasingly relied on restructuring security institutions and applying political and financial pressure on armed groups, the Jurf al-Naddaf operation demonstrated the limits of the state’s authority when confronted directly.

“If the government cannot enforce its decisions against a single armed faction, or fails to follow through with legal and political accountability, it suggests that these groups still retain an effective veto over certain state actions,” Al-Shakeri was quoted as saying.

The report noted that not all Iran-aligned factions share the same position regarding government efforts to centralize weapons under state control.

Some groups, including Asaib Ahl al-Haq, have become increasingly integrated into Iraq’s political and economic systems, potentially reducing their willingness to engage in direct confrontation. Others—including Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada—continue to oppose any move that would place their military capabilities under full government authority.

Political analyst Muhannad al-Ghazi told Al-Monitor that these factions view their weapons through an ideological lens, making voluntary disarmament highly unlikely. He argued that targeting isolated weapons caches without addressing broader military infrastructure would have only a limited impact.

The reported confrontation occurred amid heightened regional tensions following Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s recent visit to Washington, where Iraq and the United States announced a strategic economic partnership.

According to Al-Monitor, several Iran-backed factions criticized the visit, warning against what they described as replacing “military occupation” with “economic occupation” through expanded U.S. investment in Iraq.

The report also linked the incident to broader regional developments, including recent drone attacks and cross-border military operations that have intensified pressure on Baghdad’s efforts to assert control over its territory.

Al-Monitor concluded that the government’s September 30 target for fully disarming armed factions appears increasingly difficult to achieve given current realities.

Instead, analysts cited by the publication believe Baghdad may focus on more gradual measures, including relocating some weapons, closing selected facilities, and increasing political and financial pressure on groups willing to cooperate, while avoiding direct confrontation with the most heavily armed factions.

The report suggested that the ultimate success of Iraq’s disarmament strategy may depend not only on domestic enforcement but also on broader regional dynamics, particularly relations between the United States and Iran.

World.title: Jordan threatens to strike Iranian militias in Iraq if they launched attacks
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Amman has publicly warned Iraq that it will launch military operations against Iran-backed militias if they attack Jordan.

The warning comes after a rapid increase in regional violence, including recent interceptions of Iranian ballistic missiles and drones over Jordanian airspace, which targeted US installations.

An official Jordanian source told Al-Arabiya News that Jordan provided Iraq with precise intelligence indicating that pro-Iran militants are planning to strike Jordanian territory.

Jordan has publicly said that it expects the Iraqi government to take quick and effective measures to curb these armed groups.

Jordanian sources identify front organizations such as Awliya al-Dam as key players in these border-threatening actions.

The warning represents a strong change in Jordan’s defensive stance in the face of rising tensions between the United States and Iran.

Jordan harbors critical Western military installations, such as the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, which have become active targets for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and its allies in the region.

Jordan emphasized that, while it aims to avoid regional escalation, it considers national sovereignty and border security to be inviolable priorities.

World.title: Iraq, Turkey sign deal to transport 750,000 barrels of Iraqi oil to Ceyhan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq and Turkey have formally inked a one-year short-term deal to continue operations through the critical Iraq-Turkey oil pipeline.

The agreement, reached in Ankara following discussions between Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar and Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair, guarantees the ongoing transportation of at least 750,000 barrels of Iraqi crude oil per day to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.

Turkey’s state-owned crude oil and natural gas pipeline corporation (BOTAS) signed an agreement with Iraq’s State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) and the North Oil Company (NOC).

The new deal is now valid for 12 months until both countries develop a new, long-term legislative framework.

The previous agreement, which was reached in 1973, officially expired last Monday.

The short extension of the deal is crucial for Iraq’s revenue from oil exports, as Baghdad seeks alternative export routes to mitigate risks linked to the Strait of Hormuz.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi stated that both countries are developing a more comprehensive bilateral framework. This initiative is likely to include cross-border collaboration in the water, electricity, and oil sectors.

The pipeline has a maximum capacity of 1.5 million barrels per day. However, due to legal issues between Baghdad, Erbil, and Ankara, it is currently operating at a capacity ranging between 170,000 and 200,000 barrels per day.

Al-Zaidi described the deal as an important milestone that will protect Iraq’s economy from rising regional crises. Following his high-level diplomatic visit to Ankara, the agreement reestablishes energy transit stability between the two countries.

World.title: Chevron CFO bullish on Iraq after West Qurna 2, Nassiriya agreements
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Chevron boasts “significant potential” to expand its activities in Iraq over the next decade, according to Chief Financial Officer Eimear Bonner, highlighting the US oil company’s increasing trust in the country’s energy sector after recent deals with Baghdad.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Bonner said that Iraq remained one of Chevron’s top priority markets for future production expansion after the signing of preliminary agreements to pursue negotiations on the massive West Qurna 2 and Nassiriya oil fields.

She added that Chevron has been encouraged by its interaction with Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi and Iraq’s Ministry of Oil while discussions continue and that the corporation is also collaborating with Baghdad on diverse crude export routes to boost Iraq’s long-term energy security.

The statements bolster rising trust among foreign energy corporations after Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States earlier this month, during which Iraq inked more than $60 billion in investment deals covering energy, infrastructure, banking, and technology.

World.title: 'Threw slipper, carried a knife': What we know about the attack on Pappu Yadav
World.content:

NEW DELHI: A press conference by Independent MP Pappu Yadav was disrupted in Delhi on Sunday after a confrontation broke out between his supporters and a group of men. Yadavâs media convenor alleged the MP was targeted with a knife in what he described as an attempt to replicate the Atiq Ahmed incident.The incident occurred while Yadav was seated and speaking to the media. According to his media convenor, three or four men suddenly approached the MP and an altercation broke out. He alleged that one of the men first removed a slipper and hurled it before another attacker pulled out a knife."The attackers first took off a slipper and hurled it. When the knife was drawn to attack, our supporters and associates tried to restrain the assailant. I stepped forward and positioned myself between the attacker and Pappu Yadav, and I was beaten severely as a result," the convenor said.He alleged he was beaten so badly by two or three individuals that he lost consciousness. "My associates carried me away from the spot. I have no further information," he said.A supporter of Yadav who was present said he instinctively put his hand in front of the MP as the knife was swung, causing the blade to graze his finger.The situation descended into a melee, with people falling and piling on top of one another.The convenor also alleged that Delhi Police personnel present did not intervene to protect Yadav and instead focused on taking the alleged attackers away. "I tried to help Pappu Yadav escape the scene. The police seemed to be shielding the goons... Not a single policeman stepped forward to help Pappu Yadav escape. When the assault was taking place, they focused solely on saving the goons and whisked them away from the scene. We don't know where they took them," he alleged."These people had come to stage a 'Prayagraj Part Two' â they came to replicate the Atiq Ahmed incident today," the convenor said, referring to the 2023 killing of gangster-turned-politician Atiq Ahmed and his brother in Prayagraj while they were in police custody.The convenor said he had met the DCP earlier in the day and submitted a formal complaint warning that the MP was arriving and had been receiving constant threats on social media. "Despite knowing all this, they deployed only three or four police personnel here, and even they were merely protecting the goons," he alleged.He further alleged that several people had been positioned behind the media cameras before the incident. "There were people hiding behind the cameras, three or four of them. Suddenly, someone pulled out a knife, another a slipper... The MP was the target, no one else," he said.According to people present at the scene, the confrontation began after some men allegedly accused Yadav of insulting Sanatan Dharma. The men argued with him before one of them removed a slipper and attempted to throw it. Yadav's supporters then intervened, leading to a scuffle.Yadav and his supporters have alleged the men were carrying knives and had intentions to kill him. The Delhi Police have not yet issued an official statement on the incident.Yadav himself alleged in a later statementthat the confrontation was an attempt on his life and linked it to threats against his family.âI came here because last night, they went to my childrenâs home. Now, you are trying to intimidate my children too; that wonât happen,â Yadav said. âI was with the press, and a conversation was underway. Amid that, there was an attempt to kill me.âHe alleged that some of those involved were calling for him to be killed, adding, âSome âBabaâ was saying, âBurn him alive,â while others were saying, âKill him.â If people hadnât been here, I would have been finished.âYadav also connected the confrontation to the ongoing controversy over alleged discrepancies involving offerings at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.âI havenât said anything. I only asked Champat Rai or Giri Ji, where did the 200 kg of silver go? Where did the gold go?â he said.On security concerns, Yadav said he had repeatedly sought protection. âThe Delhi Police is quite capable. I have been demanding security for a long time now. What crime have I committed?â he said.The confrontation comes days after Yadav was involved in a political controversy over a protest by opposition MPs concerning alleged theft of offerings made at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya. Yadav, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, Samajwadi Party MP Awadhesh Prasad and other opposition parliamentarians staged a demonstration in Parliament premises in which they enacted a skit depicting the alleged theft of temple offerings.Yadav wore saffron during the protest and portrayed a temple priest who allegedly took offerings from a donation box. The demonstration drew criticism from seers and others, who accused the MPs of insulting Sanatan Dharma.

World.title: Assam floods: 82 dead, 1.78 lakh affected as relief efforts intensify - key points
World.content:
The Centre has approved Rs 379.35 crore under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) for Assamâs flood response

Relief and rescue under way

Villagers rescue over 1,000 people in Sivasagar

CM reviews flood-hit districts and compensation plans

IIT-Guwahati to be engaged for Brahmaputra erosion solution

Agriculture rehabilitation begins

Aid pours in from NGOs, celebrities and political organisations

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Centre sanctions Rs 379 crore for flood relief

Assam continued to grapple with the aftermath of devastating floods on Sunday, with the death toll remaining at 82 and nearly 1.78 lakh people still affected across seven districts. Although floodwaters have begun to recede in some areas, thousands remain displaced, agricultural land is submerged, and the state government has intensified relief, rehabilitation and long-term mitigation efforts.According to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA), the flood situation has improved slightly, with the number of affected people declining from over 1.92 lakh to 1.78 lakh. However, 349 villages across Golaghat, Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Bajali, Dhemaji and Sonitpur districts remain affected.Charaideo is the worst-hit district, with more than 75,000 people affected, followed by over 58,000 in Sivasagar. Nearly 15,060 hectares of crop area remain submerged, while thousands of livestock have been affected or washed away.A total of 44 relief camps are currently sheltering around 15,000 displaced people, while another 17 relief distribution centres are providing assistance to more than 5,500 residents.The state government has directed district administrations to expedite the identification of affected families so that financial assistance can begin from August 3.One of the most remarkable rescue stories emerged from the Nepali Khuti area in Sivasagar district, where local villagers used six country-made boats to rescue more than 1,000 people from five villages after floodwaters rose rapidly on July 19.Residents said families were trapped on rooftops, elevated platforms and trees as water levels surged. The volunteer rescuers continued operations through the night despite having little food or water, ferrying stranded villagers to safer areas.Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma began a tour of the worst-hit districts on Sunday to oversee relief operations and prepare for a comprehensive damage assessment exercise scheduled to begin on August 9.The government has also directed officials to ensure uninterrupted distribution of relief kits, assess damage to educational institutions before schools reopen on August 10, and prepare restoration plans for damaged Namghars (Vaishnavite prayer centres).During his visit to erosion-hit areas of Dibrugarh district, including Chabua, Balijan, Pukhurijan, Dinjan and Rahmoria, Sarma announced that the state government will engage experts from IIT-Guwahati to develop a long-term solution to the Brahmaputra riverâs erosion problem.Calling riverbank erosion one of Assamâs biggest geographical challenges, the chief minister said the state loses valuable land every year and that modern technology would be used to strengthen vulnerable riverbanks. The proposed IIT initiative will complement the governmentâs planned Rs 90 crore erosion mitigation project.Agriculture minister Pijush Hazarika visited Charaideo district on Sunday to review post-flood rehabilitation measures and launched community paddy nurseries and seedling distribution programmes for flood-affected farmers.The government said quality seedlings and other assistance would be provided to ensure cultivation resumes without delay during the current agricultural season.Support for flood-hit communities has continued to grow across Assam.Actor Randeep Hooda joined a relief drive organised by Global Sikhs in Sivasagar district, distributing essential supplies and serving food through langar for affected families. He warned that prolonged waterlogging and mud-filled homes could trigger disease outbreaks and urged people across the country to contribute to relief efforts.The Lok Janshakti Party (Ramvilas) has also launched a large-scale relief operation in Sivasagar, distributing food and essential supplies and announcing plans to feed up to 15,000 people daily for 10 days, along with setting up medical camps.The Centre has approved Rs 379.35 crore under the State Disaster Response Fund (SDRF) for Assamâs flood response. Sarma thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah for extending assistance and for deploying Inter-Ministerial Central Teams to support relief and rehabilitation planning.Reliance Foundation has also contributed Rs 21 crore to the Chief Ministerâs Relief Fund for flood relief and rehabilitation efforts.While water levels have started falling in parts of the state, the crisis is far from over. Thousands remain displaced, farmland continues to lie under water, and many families face the difficult task of rebuilding homes and livelihoods. Alongside immediate relief operations, the government is now focusing on compensation, agricultural recovery and long-term measures to address the recurring twin challenges of floods and Brahmaputra erosion.

World.title: ‘Ban on Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League a move against democracy’: Taslima Nasreen
World.content:
Sheikh Hasina; Taslima Nasreen

Nasreen backs Uniform Civil Code , calls it necessary for women's equality

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

(With ANI inputs)

NEW DELHI: Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen on Sunday criticised the ban on former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasinaâs Awami League party, calling it a "move against democracyâ and expressing uncertainty over Hasinaâs return to the country.âNo political party should be banned. The manner in which Sheikh Hasina was forced to leave the country is questionable. It was not right to ban the Awami League. It was a move against democracy. I want the ban to be lifted as soon as possible,â Nasreen told reporters at a press conference in Kolkata.Sheikh Hasina has been living in Delhi since August 5, 2024, after resigning as prime minister following weeks of student-led protests. The interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after the fall of the Awami League administration, banned the party in May 2025 under anti-terrorism laws.Meanwhile, Nasreen alleged that several Awami League workers had been tortured and killed during Sheikh Hasinaâs exile and expressed uncertainty over whether the former prime minister would be able to return to Bangladesh.âMany Awami League workers were tortured and murdered. Sheikh Hasina wants to return, but I do not know whether that will be possible.But no one wants me to go back,â she said.Nasreen also criticised Jamaat-e-Islami, now Bangladesh's principal opposition party, accusing it of opposing womenâs equality and seeking the imposition of Sharia law.âNow we have Jamaat-e-Islami as an opposition party. It is against womenâs equality, and they want Sharia rule. If that happens, no minority will survive. Bangladesh is moving towards darkness. No one is trying to civilise Bangladesh. The government is only trying to remain in power,â she added.The 63-year-old author further claimed that âhatred against Hindusâ was being spread in some madrasas and mosques in Bangladesh.âIn many madrasas and mosques, hatred is being taught against Hindus,â Nasreen remarked.Turning to the issue of the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), Nasreen said she had been advocating for such a law for the past 40 years and described it as essential in any âcivilised countryâ.âI have been fighting for the UCC for the past 40 years. This is much needed in any civilised country,â she remarked.She claimed that religious laws continued to affect womenâs rights in Bangladesh, alleging that Hindu women in the country lacked adequate legal protections, including the right to divorce.âIn Bangladesh, Hindu girls have no rights; they do not even have the right to divorce. Due to religious laws, women are suffering. Hindus are being tortured in Bangladesh. During the Yunus regime, Hindus were tortured even more,â she alleged.In July, the BJP-led West Bengal government constituted a nine-member expert committee headed by retired Supreme Court judge Justice Ranjana Prakash Desai to examine and finalise a draft UCC for the state. The state government plans to introduce the legislation during the upcoming August Assembly session.Nasreen, who has lived in exile since 1994, when she was forced to leave Bangladesh due to the threat from Islamic radicals over her work, returned to Kolkata nearly two decades. She was forced to leave the city in 2007 following protests over her writings and memoir Dwikhandito (Split into Two), published in 2003.

World.title: Can BJP crack Punjab? Inside its strategy to challenge AAP and Congress in 2027
World.content:
NEW DELHI: When it comes to

âs election playbook, there is always a method to the madness.

, which votes early next year, appears to be following the same script.

Sample these headlines:

PM Modi to visit Punjab on February 1 7 AAP MPs from Punjab merge with BJP BJP appoints Kewal Singh Dhillon as Punjab unit president Ravneet Singh Bittu resigns from Union Council of Ministers PM Modi inaugurates, lays foundation stone of several projects in Punjab Corruption is rampant in Punjab: PM Modi targets AAP government

All these headlines, when looked at in isolation, appear to be one-off political developments separated in time.

But one look at them together in the context of a wider long-term objective, they appear not just connected but also planned with a purpose.

This is a perfect example of the BJP election playbook in action.

The BJP, which over the years played second fiddle to the Akalis in Punjab, contested the 2022 elections alone after snapping ties with the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD). However, it could win only 2 seats with a vote share of 6.6%.

Even the 2024 Lok Sabha elections were a huge disappointment. The BJP polled 18.65% of votes but could not win any seat. However, the BJP appears determined not to let the past numbers dictate its future strategy.

And that explains the aggression with which the party has gone for the kill in Punjab.

Punjab, which over the years alternated between the Congress and the Akalis, broke the duopoly in 2022 when it overwhelmingly voted for Arvind Kejriwalâs AAP.





And that perhaps gives BJP its biggest hope as it marshals its resources. Now, letâs analyze all these headlines as a part of one story to understand how the BJP is gearing up to add another state to its ever-expanding kitty.

The Ravidassia outreach

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Punjab on February 1 this year, the BJPâs election playbook was already in action. The visit was part of a well thought-out and planned outreach that could increase the partyâs base and presence in the state.

The occasion was the 649th Birth Anniversary of Sant Guru Ravidas Ji. The Ravidassia community form an important electoral bloc of Punjabâs Scheduled Caste population, especially in the Doaba region.

A slew of announcements were made, including renaming of Adampur Airport after Guru Ravidas and the launch of the Shri Guru Ravidas Ji Maharaj Express between Jalandhar and Varanasi. It was the start of a planned outreach.

That outreach has continued with the Punjab BJP launching the statewide implementation of the 'Samrasta Sankalp Abhiyan' from July 29, the auspicious occasion of Guru Purnima, to commemorate the 650th birth anniversary year of Guru Ravidas Maharaj.

Punjab BJP chief Kewal Singh Dhillon said the nationwide campaign will continue till February 20 (Magha Purnima) under the guidance of the BJP national leadership and aims to spread Guru Ravidas's timeless message of equality, dignity, social harmony and social justice across Punjab.

Targeted political acquisition

The BJP, enriched by its experience from victories in states like West Bengal and Odisha, perhaps knows the importance of organisational strength in winning states. So in Punjab, after breaking its alliance with the Akalis, the BJP has been on an overdrive to build a strong local leadership. After the 2022 elections, several prominent Congress leaders had joined the BJP.

And now in the run up to the 2027 electoral battle, seven AAP members of Rajya Sabha from the state are already a part of the party.

And this acquisition includes Raghav Chaddha, once the most trusted associate of AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal. Chadha has a good understanding of the electoral thinking of AAP that rules Punjab now and can help the BJP capitalise on its weaknesses. As the elections approach, we could see Raghav Chaddha play a greater role in crafting and implementing BJPâs Punjab campaign.

The âDhillonâ signal

When the BJP replaced one Congress export Sunil Jakhar with another Kewal Singh Dhillon as its state chief, the change was aimed to send across a message. Dhillon, who is a seasoned politician and a prominent industrialist, became the first Jat

to head the BJP in the state. The purpose was clear: outreach among Sikh voters to help increase the acceptability of the party after its Akali alliance ended.

The BJP would hope that Dhillon could help the party expand its rural footprint. Besides Dhillon's political base is in Barnala, which falls in the Sangrur-Malwa region. This region is considered a stronghold of Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann and the Aam Aadmi Party.

Ravneet Singh Bittu and Punjab focus

Ravneet Singh Bittu, who joined the BJP in March 2024 ahead of the general elections after ending his long association with the Congress, seems to have an important role in the saffron partyâs blueprint for Punjab.

During the 2024 campaign, Bittu was projected as an important Sikh face for the BJP by none other than Amit Shah. For those who remember, the entire BJP had rallied in support of Bittu after Rahul Gandhi had referred to him as âtraitorâ.

The BJP made Bittu a minister in the Modi government and a member of Rajya Sabha despite his Lok Sabha election loss from Ludhiana in 2024 to showcase his importance. But after his RS tenure ended in June this year, he quit as minister amid hints that he will play a key role in BJPâs Punjab plans.

According to reports, in June, Bittu had expressed his desire to work for Punjab in the Vidhan Sabha after spending nearly 17 years in Parliament. Bittu had then said that the BJP made him the minister even though he had lost the 2024 parliamentary elections.

"People of Punjab are fed up (with other parties). People are very much aware of development and progress taking place in other (BJP-ruled) states and they want prosperity in Punjab as well," Bittu had then said.

Ravneet Singh Bittu is the grandson of former Punjab chief minister Beant Singh, who was assassinated in 1995. During his political career in the Congress, he was elected MP thrice and also served as the grand-old-party's leader in the Lok Sabha and as its whip in the Lower House.

PM Modiâs 'double-engine' promise

When Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Punjab for the second time on July 17, his focus was on development, youth and farmers. He pitched the BJPâs 'double-engine' model, arguing that a government of the same party at the Centre and in the state could bring investment, jobs and faster growth to Punjab.

âOnly the BJP can bring real change in Punjab. Only the BJP will make Punjab developed. Only the BJP will make Punjab self-reliant,â PM Modi said, adding that the state needed new investment, employment opportunities and greater global reach for products made in Punjab.

He also accused the AAP government of stalling development and merely rebranding central schemes. Citing BJP-ruled Delhi and Haryana, Modi argued that Punjab too needed a 'double-engine' government, while claiming that farmers in the state were being denied the support available elsewhere.

Rivals under fire

And while one part of PM Modiâs Punjab campaign was outreach, the other part was his fierce attack on the rivals in the state. Targeting the AAP government in Punjab over law and order and several other issues, PM Modi dubbed the ruling dispensation as a "Kattar Beiman" which neither has clean intentions, nor honesty.

PM Modi then targeted the Congress, which has been in news more for factionalism than poll readiness.

Taking a dig at infighting in the state unit over the chief minister's chair, the PM said "They are not fighting for people, they are fighting among themselves."

Also under attack was the SAD, the BJPâs former ally. Taking a dig at the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD), the Prime Minister said it is not concerned about the welfare of the public as it is caught up with its own affairs.

And finally, while the studentsâ protests against the NEET-UG paper leak forced Centre on the backfoot, the BJP is now using the same ammunition to target the Bhagwant Mann government over alleged paper leaks in Punjab.

Can BJP upset the AAP-Congress applecart in Punjab?

The BJP clearly has a plan for Punjab. It is bringing in leaders, strengthening its state organisation, reaching out to new social groups and sharpening its attack on both the AAP and the Congress. In the coming months, this push is likely to become more visible through political outreach, policy announcements and an aggressive campaign around governance, development and law and order.

But activity alone does not guarantee electoral success. The BJP may have increased its vote share and political visibility, but it still has to expand beyond its traditional urban base, build trust in rural Punjab and convert imported leaders into an effective ground organisation.

So, can it upset the AAP-Congress contest? It is still too early to say. The BJP will leave no stone unturned to make Punjab the 23rd state in its kitty. The real test will be whether its carefully assembled strategy can finally translate into seats.
