World.title: Sliding housing prices gave the Reserve Bank a surprise helping hand
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalProperty prices Sliding housing prices gave the Reserve Bank a surprise helping hand Shane Wright August 3, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s the helping hand that surprised even the Reserve Bank. The bank always knew that its three rate hikes - in February, March and May - would slow the property market. While governor Michele Bullock will say up hill and down dale that the bank does not target asset prices, the RBA’s interest rate rises were all aimed at taking steam out of the economy. And, as the Reserve Bank knows, climbing house prices make people feel wealthier and happier, leaving them more likely to open their digital wallets. Michele Bullock will take any assistance she can get to help cool inflation. Louie Douvis The so-called wealth effect also works in reverse. Falling property prices are more likely than not to make consumers a little wary when it comes to spending a dollar, adding to any deflationary pressures in the economy.



Property prices, particularly those in Sydney where residents don’t get out of bed unless they’ve got a $900,000 mortgage strapped to their back, were already responding to the RBA’s rate hikes through March and April. But it is clear that the May budget, and Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ array of changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax, is amplifying those higher interest rates. Related Article Exclusive

Property market High-priced homes have broken the intergenerational bargain This wasn’t on the Reserve’s radar when it started jacking up interest rates in February. While the government was considering a range of tax changes, it was a long way off from a settled position. And even that was upended by the events of February 28 when the US and Israel began their war against Iran. Economists often bemoan that the RBA and the government of the day are often in conflict. There were plenty upset that the May budget contained a forecast deficit of $31.5 billion, larger than the just completed financial year.



Yet, it is apparent – especially if you spend your time tracking the social media posts of real estate agents – that the government’s tax changes have contributed to the nationwide slowdown in prices and auction activity. If people aren’t buying and selling homes, their demand for everything from real estate agents to removalists to new furniture also falls. Last week’s better-than-expected inflation figures revealed some deep falls in prices for goods associated with the housing sector. Furniture prices in Sydney, for instance, fell by 4.6 per cent. Household textiles fell by 2.1 per cent. Household appliances were cheaper, both for large ones (minus 1.9 per cent) and small (minus 0.7 per cent). Even glassware and tableware prices tumbled by 5.5 per cent. Some of those falls are likely due to the stronger Australian dollar which pushes down the price of imported goods. But a slowing property market means people are less likely to want or need new furniture or plates or refrigerators. It also puts pressure on lenders to offer better deals – aka, cheaper prices or improved services – to win customers from a diminishing pool.



Chalmers and the rest of the government will never admit that their policies were aimed at cutting property prices. And the Reserve Bank is loath to concede that a drop in house values is a positive in its ongoing fight against inflation. Not that we have hit an affordability nirvana quite yet. Sydney’s median house value is still above $1.5 million. Also in the $1 million club are Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth and Canberra. Melbourne is not part of the $1 million club - something for which prospective home buyers should be glad. Even the drop in values revealed by Cotality today takes the national dwelling value back to where it was in March. So, we’re not quite back to the 50 per cent price crash of the 1890s. But the interaction of tighter monetary policy and fewer tax incentives for investors in the property market is clearly helping in the battle to get inflation down. World.content:

In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Adelaide surged into the top four for the first time this year by dishing out a 72-point belting of an outclassed Essendon.

A West Coast player went to ground in obvious pain after a gut punch from a Richmond opponent at the MCG.

Surgery for Swan after suffering a sickening lower leg injury. Young Bomber Angus Clarke was taken to hospital after suffering a concussion and neck injury in a collision with a teammate as Adelaide surged into the top four for the first time this year by dishing out a 72-point belting of Essendon at Marvel Stadium. Following a disquieting home defeat to Collingwood last week, the Crows were all business against the struggling Bombers, absorbing a first quarter challenge before growing their margin at every change to move ahead of Brisbane and Melbourne on percentage. Essendon’s Angus Clarke reels after getting a knock. AFL Photos Clarke, 19, has faced a spate of injuries this year and seemed to have shrugged off one when he hyperextended a knee early on. But he then clashed inadvertently with Isaac Kako, resulting in a concussion and an apparent neck problem that interim coach Dean Solomon said was serious enough to send him to hospital.



“His year’s been really interrupted with injury, the foot initially, gets back in the side for two or three, gets a head knock,” Solomon said. “There is concussion there but also a bit of soreness in the neck. “So they’re going to take him to hospital now to check further and make sure there’s no real damage there. It’s frustrating for him because he’s a really good young man and he’s hungry to be a good player ... he just can’t get continuity in his game.” Adelaide’s senior assistant coach Murray Davis is a contender to take over as Essendon coach, and he did his chances no harm by ensuring that Solomon would oversee another heavy defeat. Crows coach Matthew Nicks said Davis would be welcome to stay at the Crows for the remainder of the year even if he was chosen for the Essendon job ahead of candidates including James Hird. Adelaide’s Izak Rankine. Getty Images “I think that’s up to Murray, and the reason it’s up to Murray is I trust him completely,” Nicks said.



“If he wants to be with us we’d love him to stay with us and work right through. He deserves that. He’s been incredible for what he’s done for us the last couple [of] seasons. So we’d love him to stay on, but we also wish him all the best if that is the opportunity that shows up.” The Crows may also have unearthed a useful role player for the pointy end of the season, with 21-year-old debutant Oscar Ryan finding plenty of the ball and kicking a memorable first goal in the third term. Skipper Jordan Dawson shrugged off an attempted tag by Mason Redman to be the prime midfield mover for the Crows, who were sweating on the seriousness of yet another hamstring complaint - this time for young defender James Borlase. Riley Thilthorpe kicked five goals for Adelaide, while Callum Ah Chee was a lively presence up forward in only his fifth appearance of the year after joining the Crows from Brisbane. Two-metre Peter Wright presented a strong marking target for Essendon with six majors, while Zach Merrett also worked hard. Kako may find himself under the spotlight of the match review panel after a tackle that dumped Adelaide defender Josh Worrell’s head into the Docklands turf.



Before the game, Crows senior coach Matthew Nicks had conceded there was some merit in how former Pies coach Mick Malthouse had critiqued his team’s poor display against Collingwood as “horribly soft”. “Mick’s comments were warranted, I could feel what Micky Malthouse was talking about, he’s a very experienced head, he knows what he sees in footy,” Nicks told Fox Footy. “We rate ourselves highly in that toughness area but we did drop away in that second half, so what he said was warranted. Little was proven either way against the Bombers, but the improved ladder position will help. “We look at results yesterday and we don’t shy away from the fact that opportunity is now there,” Nicks said post-match. “If you win all three games then it’s ours. That’s easier said than done. “We’ve just got to continue to win now, our destiny is in our hands. In a way we’ve earned the position we’re in, we’ve now got three weeks to nail that, starting next weekend.”



Demons grind out win on Gold Coast Ed Jackson Melbourne have survived a major scare to defeat Gold Coast by nine points at People First Stadium and keep their AFL top four hopes on track. In a see-sawing match with multiple lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) win on Sunday. Jacob van Rooyen and Harrison Petty each kicked three goals for the visitors, who were clinical with their shots on goal throughout.



Max Gawn was dominant for the Demons with 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hitouts and nine clearances while Trent Rivers and Jake Bowey led the disposals for the Demons with 29 touches apiece. Kysaiah Pickett of the Demons shows plenty of dash, finding space ahead of Matt Rowell. Getty Images Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast were unable to prevent slumping to their 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca’s first match against his former club. Petracca, whose impact on the Suns was under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the defeat to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances. Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, who fought hard but couldn’t hold off the fast-finishing Demons to end their losing run.



Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break. View post on X Bailey Humphrey’s goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break. And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks. The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.



A nasty looking fall early in the fourth quarter forced Blake Howes from the field clutching his left wrist but it didn’t deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points. Suns defender Sam Collins (ribs) failed to return after sustaining a hit to his side in a marking contest with Ed Langdon in the second quarter. AAP



Tiger in the gun for behind-the-play blow Marc McGowan Richmond took a major step towards dodging a second wooden spoon in three years with a second win this season over a wayward West Coast as Tigers defender Luke Trainor faces match review scrutiny for a gut punch. Adem Yze’s men had lost eight matches in a row by an average of almost 50 points, and were on the bottom, behind Essendon on percentage, with a miserable 2-17 win-loss record before Sunday’s 11-point victory.



Richmond took advantage of the Eagles’ yips in front of goal at the MCG to climb above the Bombers and within one win of 16th-placed West Coast, who had kicked 3.17 at one stage before losing 12.12 (84) to 9.19 (73). The result eases pressure on coach Yze, who has presided over only 10 victories in 66 matches in what is a full-blown rebuild at Tigerland. “We’re rebuilding, so when you rebuild, you need games into younger players,” Yze said. “We get a win today, but we still need Jonty Faull, Harry Armstrong and Tom Sims [to get back from injury] … we’ve still got guys we need to gel together. But at the same time, if we can scratch out some wins while we’re going through what we’re going through with unavailability – it’s terrific. “We know what we’ve got within our four walls … we’ve dealt with more than what other teams have dealt with.



“But when you see Sammy [Lalor] do what he does today; he’s [only] scratching the surface. When those lads start to grow together; it’ll be really exciting.” Footy with feeling: Richmond’s Sam Lalor after kicking the sealer. Getty Images Yze re-signed until the end of 2028 in November last year, and chief executive Shane Dunne said last month he had the club’s backing. There were only 12 points between the sides at three-quarter-time, but goals to Richmond premiership veterans Tom Lynch (20 disposals, 2.4) and Toby Nankervis blew the margin out before they withstood a late fightback. The Eagles, who have been competitive most weeks despite their lack of success, have plenty to rue, with Jake Waterman’s 2.6 day – on top of putting another kick out on the full – headlining their woeful goalkicking.



Elliot Yeo had a chance to slice the difference to six points with a set shot inside the last two minutes, but sprayed it to the left, only for No.1 draft pick Lalor to seal the contest with his third major after winning a test of strength. View post on X West Coast were trying to beat Richmond at the MCG for the first time since 2015, but the 33,737 crowd instead were able to celebrate a rare Tigers triumph this season. Tim Taranto led Richmond’s charge with 32 disposals and a game-high 11 clearances, while Harley Reid was outstanding in a losing cause with 34 touches, 20 contested possessions and nine clearances. Mid-season draftee Marcus Herbert (34 disposals) was also prolific for the Eagles. Yze said he had not seen Trainor’s behind-the-play gut punch to West Coast’s Jack Williams in the second quarter. They were engaged in a standing wrestle before Trainor struck the Eagle with a clenched left fist.



The second-year Tiger, playing his 30th career game, instantly jogged away while Williams went to ground in obvious pain and went to the bench soon after. Richmond captain Toby Nankervis and Nathan Broad celebrated a rare win in 2026. Getty Images “I’m not too sure how hard the impact was, but if he’s gone and done something wrong, we’ll look at it,” Yze said. “I think there have been a few fines over the last few occasions when things like this have happened, so hopefully, we can get that type of result. “We don’t want to be losing players through stupidity [when we have so many injuries], so hopefully, it wasn’t too bad. We’ve educated our players, and they understand what’s right and wrong.”



It is the type of incident the AFL aimed to stamp out when it announced tribunal changes in February, revealing that incidents where a player strikes another in the chest or stomach were more likely to be graded medium impact and result in suspension. Match review officer Michael Christian has typically graded these incidents as low impact, which led to fines rather than bans. Richmond’s lengthy injury list includes key defensive options Noah Balta, Josh Gibcus and Campbell Gray, while prized draftee Sam Cumming (ankle) was the latest addition on Sunday. Surgery for ‘devastated’ Swan after leg injury Peter Ryan



Sydney Swans defender Will Edwards had surgery on Sunday after suffering a sickening lower leg injury against the Saints on Saturday. Will Edwards was taken from the ground with a broken leg. AFL Photos Edwards appeared to dislocate his ankle and was carted from the field having received pain medication during the Swans’ 19-point win at Marvel Stadium. Coach Dean Cox described the injury as “devastating” for the 23-year-old, who made his debut this season following a series of leg fractures and infections. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 If the Crows fade away yet again, could this Essendon contender step up?



The club is expected to provide more information about the injury and his prognosis after the operation. Midfielder James Rowbottom will also have surgery to repair a broken hand sustained during the match against St Kilda. For the Saints, Jack Silvagni (dislocated shoulder) and Tom De Koning (hip pointer) are in doubt for next Sunday night’s match against their former team, Carlton.

World.title: New Zealand First Kiwi Kids Grant plans to pay parents for having children
World.content:
New Zealand First wants more people to have babies - and would pay them to do it.

The party also confirmed former Defence Minister Ron Mark was returning to the party, and will stand in the election.

At a public meeting in Masterton, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said New Zealand was facing a "population precipice," and the rate of New Zealand citizens having children had fallen dramatically.

"We need more Kiwis having more children, and one way to do that is to substantially lower the main barrier most are facing, that is the cost," he said.

The party's Kiwi Kids Grant would seek to arrest that fall, by paying parents $5000 a year for the first three years, and for up to three children.

Peters announced the grant at an NZ First public meeting. RNZ/Giles Dexter

To qualify, one parent would need to be a New Zealand citizen.

"New Zealand needs to get our birthrate increasing before it's too late," Peters said.

Peters said the tax-free payment would be administered through the Inland Revenue Department.

The policy, which the party had costed at $400 million a year by the time it was fully up and running, would be funded through operating baselines.

Peters admitted the policy could cost more "because it might be such a roaring success".

Addressing the crowd in Masterton, he said the issue of a declining birth rate was found around the Western world.

"Other countries have implemented fundamental changes of policy to reverse this decline, and we need to make serious changes here to back home in New Zealand before it is too late," he said.

"Masking this massive problem by increasing migration is just papering off the cracks, and will be disastrous for our future. Immigration should be based on people you need, not people who need you.

Afterwards, he denied the policy was playing into 'replacement theory,' saying the policy was about helping people have children because the costs were too high.

ACT leader David Seymour said he could see what New Zealand First was trying to do, but many countries had tried to pay people to have children without results.

"It doesn't seem to have worked where it has been tried in other countries. And bear in mind, if you have one income and you earn $100,000, the earned income tax credit and Working for Families are giving you about the same amount already."

Ron Mark. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

World.title: Te Araroa shaken by strong magnitude 5.7 earthquake
World.content:
A strong magnitude 5.7 earthquake has struck near Te Araroa on the East Coast on Sunday evening.

The quake comes just a day after a magnitude 5.2 earthquake struck near Te Anau in the South Island, and follows several weeks of heightened seismic activity across the country.

GeoNet said the quake hit at 8.35pm, centred 10km south-west of Te Araroa at a depth of 39km.

The shaking was classified as "strong".

Felt reports showed more than 5240 felt the shaking by 9pm.

There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.

Some social media users said it was a sharp jolt or rumble that had shaken them and the furniture in their houses.

One Gisborne local emailed RNZ, writing that the quake "rattled the house with a strong shudder".

Two weaker magnitude 3 shakes were recorded at 8.40pm and 9.07pm, near the same location.

On Saturday, a Te Anau quake struck 35km north-west of the town at a depth of 102km.

That followed a magnitude 5.9 earthquake north of Te Anau on 25 July, which prompted a brief tsunami warning and evacuation notice for parts of the West Coast before it was cancelled.

On Friday night, a magnitude 4.6 earthquake also shook the lower North Island and upper South Island after striking offshore north-west of Porirua.

Following Saturday's Te Anau quake, GeoNet scientist Jonathan Hanson said New Zealand had been living up to its "Shaky Isles" reputation.

While it had been a busy few weeks for earthquakes, Hanson said the recent activity was not unusual overall, with New Zealand typically recording between 15 and 20 magnitude 5 earthquakes each year.

World.title: Support for data centres goes back 40 years
World.content:
Concerns are growing about the proliferation of data centres, and could curtail New Zealand's potential to become a regional hub serving Australia and the Pacific.

A paper by Fitch Solutions company BMI focuses on New Zealand's small but rapidly expanding growth due to strong cloud adoption, data sovereignty requirements and growing international connectivity.

"New Zealand's regulatory and policy environment remains one of its key competitive advantages, underpinned by political stability and a highly renewable power system," it says.

"That said, this supportive backdrop is increasingly being balanced by rising scrutiny of the sector's impact on the grid.

"Tighter scrutiny of grid usage, power contribution requirements and local opposition to large-scale projects may slow execution timelines for the biggest developments."

The cost of development

The BMI report notes there was concern the current framework did not require data centre operators to contribute proportionately to the grid infrastructure, though it was happening in practice.

"The coexistence of active investment promotion and emerging grid-contribution requirements highlights the tension between attracting globally mobile digital infrastructure investment and maintaining social licence domestically," the BMI report says.

However, information provided to RNZ from the National Grid operator Transpower on the Transmission Pricing Methodology (TPM) did set out a number of requirements.

"Under the TPM the beneficiary pays the cost of connecting to the grid - this ensures that costs are allocated to parties benefiting from those assets rather than spreading them across all consumers," Transpower said in response to RNZ questions.

"So any new large loads (like data centres) pay their own costs of connection to the grid, and they should also bring new generation with them to cover their own demand.

"Before any new large load connects to the grid, our priority is to ensure the system remains stable and has the capacity to safely manage the new connection so large projects like data centres need careful assessment before they can connect."

Still, the Green Party was calling for a moratorium on data centre development, despite the existence of the TPM as well as standard practice.

By the numbers

New Zealand had 62 data centres at the start of the third quarter ending September, with most located in Auckland, though Wellington, Christchurch, and Hamilton were gaining importance, according to the BMI report.

It says local cloud spending was forecast to rise to $3.11b, with long-term growth supported by government "cloud first" policies, as well as AWS and Microsoft's hyperscale data centres, which delivered regional services.

"Growth is increasingly driven by co-location providers such as CDC, Datacom, NEXTDC, and TenPeaks, and New Zealand's renewable-heavy power mix, and submarine cable investments strengthen its appeal, despite rising scrutiny over grid impacts."

Historical context

Data centres have been a central feature of the New Zealand technology landscape since 1967, when the country adopted the decimal currency system, which initiated the roll-out of computer banking systems and established Databank, a shared electronic data processing service for major banks.

Databank managing director Gordon Hogg pitched New Zealand as a "data fortress" at the second annual meeting of the Nuclear Free Zone conference, in 1985, which was revisited by the New Zealand Nuclear-Free Peacemaking Association in 1987.

An article published in The Dominion, on 2 November 1987. Supplied

The demand for data centres had since continued at pace, along with the technology built into them, including closed-loop water-cooling systems, introduced by CDC, and powered by 100 percent renewable energy, which were a standard feature of modern developments.

"New Zealand's data centre market will remain Auckland-centric in the near term, but regional diversification is likely to accelerate as Christchurch, Wellington, Hamilton and Southland attract incremental enterprise, government and hyperscale-related demand," the BMI report says.

Growth was seen as favouring co-location operators over self-build hyperscaler campuses, especially as AWS and Microsoft leaned more toward leased capacity.

Expansion outlook

The BMI report suggests New Zealand's renewable-heavy grid, efficient facilities and expanding submarine cable network should strengthen its position as a regional digital infrastructure node and support efforts to capture Australian-based demand.

"Our Power team expects the country's electricity sector to continue decarbonising, with thermal generation falling to 0 percent from 2031 onward," it says.

"This transition will be driven primarily by hydropower, which we forecast will account for 51 percent of the total generation mix by 2035."

New Zealand's power network was already considered to be among the most energy-efficient in the world, according to BMI.

"This energy transition will be further supported by an expected $24b of investment in the electricity system over the next 30 years, with a strong focus on renewable generation."

It says the development of Southland's Datagrid campus was central to the government's ambition to position New Zealand as a regional digital infrastructure hub.

World.title: Curing NZ's health system: First halt the deterioration, primary care leader says
World.content:
Top priority for the health system should be stopping deterioration, not promising a quick fix, says Dr Bryan Betty on his final day as chair of General Practice NZ.

His move from the role to the board of Health NZ was announced in April, after holding the position since 2023.

It is a path that's been taken before - his predecessor, Jeff Lowe, had also left to join the health agency's board.

Board members are appointed by the minister, a fact which GPNZ says reflects how important primary care expertise is to the overall sector across governments.

Betty told RNZ, in an interview the day before beginning the new role, it was the right time for a change.

"I think there's some big challenges for the health system going forward at this point," he said. "The decisions that are made now is where we'll be in five, seven years' time, 10 years' time."

The health system is under pressure. IT systems fail, leaving patient records inaccessible and forcing staff to revert to pen and paper.

Wait times for GPs, specialist appointments and at emergency departments have ballooned, leaving people without easily accessible healthcare, compounding health issues and putting pressure on dwindling staff and resources.

Last month, a man died after a nine hour wait in Waikato ED.

Experts blame years of underinvestment, and Betty criticised the previous centralisation reforms - where the DHBs were collapsed into one central agency - for being rolled out too fast.

Betty carrying out a throat-swab for a patient (file photo). RNZ/Tom Furley

The current government has announced a return to regional decision-making in recent months.

"This devolution into a regional approach is probably the place we need to be," Betty said. "I think the structural reforms that occurred with the collapsing of all the DHBs [into one central agency] was really problematic. It probably happened too quickly and it was too much for the system to necessarily cope with."

Covid-19 had arrived on top of that, "so the whole thing became pretty complex."

Now, the system was battling the effects of years of underfunding, he said - particularly in primary care.

But, "$120 million did go into general practice this year, which is actually one of the biggest injections of funding into general practice," he said. "And I think we have to say that's a positive."

In the meantime, there were places around the country where patient care was being compromised by the lack of access to care.

Betty said he was worried by the increasing use of telehealth, and of seeing whichever doctor was available, rather than seeing the same GP over time.

"Long-term chronic conditions get missed," he said. "Diagnosing a disease or a condition and managing that over time is not a one-off issue - and so in general practice, it's a series of interactions over time that you build a picture of the patient."

And increasingly, GPs were able to manage conditions formerly handled by hospitals.

"We have seen a lot of services move out of hospitals, things like Mirena insertions, pipelles, gynaeological procedures, iron infusions. A whole range of them are now done exclusively in general practice, whereas previously they were hospital based. There's going to be a lot more of that over the next few years."

Meanwhile, ED doctors were having to manage conditions normally seen by GPs.

"I was speaking to an ED consultant up in Auckland a couple of years ago about this," Betty said. "And she said for the first time, she's having to go away and train on how to initiate antihypertensives because patients can't get into the general practice, they're presenting to ED with high blood pressure."

Major diseases like rheumatic fever, which had been eliminated elsewhere in the world, were still prevalent in New Zealand, and an increasing number of people were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes before they turned 20 - predominantly among the Māori and Pasifika populations.

Housing played a big part in reducing health inequities, Betty said. This was something he saw among his patients in Porirua, who he would continue to see alongside his board role.

World.title: Disability support cuts criticised as child poverty report highlights growing hardship
World.content:
An advocate for children with disabilities says families are skipping food to pay for essential items.

A Ministry of Social Development report revealed that child poverty is getting worse and that an estimated 210,600 children - roughly the population of Wellington City - were living in households below the poverty line.

Official statistics suggest that more than a quarter of disabled children live in poverty and that children in disabled households are 4.5 times as likely to be experiencing severe material hardship compared with children in non-disabled households.

The head of the group, Children with Disability New Zealand, Glen McMillan, said the true number of disabled children living in poverty was likely much higher and that many poorer families feared asking for help because of potential discrimination.

McMillan, who is himself disabled as a result of a childhood accident, said cuts to disability support were pushing vulnerable families deeper into poverty.

"In a lot of cases, the support is absolutely needed. They don't have a choice. If there's no funding for support, then the funding has got to come from somewhere," he said.

"For example, a child may need nappies. They may be 12 years old, and they still need the nappies... Either they [families] give up the food, or they give up the hygiene, one or the other."

Many disabled children were on special diets that added to the financial burden, he said.

"They may not be able to digest or eat normal food. So, they're on a diet. That diet might cost $90 a week, and they might get a subsidy. If you take away $45 of that subsidy, then it's still going to cost $95, $90 a week. So, the extra $45 will need to come out of the household income."

McMillan said many disabled people saw the Disability Support Services (DSS) Bill as a withdrawal of support, and instead, wanted the benefit abatement rate to be increased.

"People that are on a benefit have an abatement rate. They can only earn so much before part of their benefit is removed. I think they [the government] need to increase the abatement rate to allow people to earn a little bit more because the cost of living is going up."

The Disability Issues Minister, Louise Upston, said one of the purposes of the DSS Bill was to make it easier for disabled people to understand what support was available and to continue to improve support.

"Without the DSS Bill, DSS policies - including funding policies - would remain operating without a legislative framework," she said.

Upston said the Bill did not change current eligibility and access settings, nor did it increase family responsibility.

World.title: Ron Mark returns to NZ First for election
World.content:
New Zealand First has confirmed former MP Ron Mark will stand again at this year's election.

And the former defence minister says if he returns to Parliament, he wants the defence job once again.

Mark, who served as an MP from 1996 to 2008, and again from 2014 to 2020, served as defence minister in the Labour-led coalition. He has also been the minister for veterans' affairs and the minister for state-owned enterprises.

He told RNZ he decided to run again after conversations with his partner and late mother-in-law, as well as a big conversation inside his own head.

Mark said he "absolutely" wanted to be defence minister again, and that would "without a doubt" be on the table for any coalition negotiations.

The role is currently held by National's Chris Penk.

Mark said Penk was a "damn good man," but "you can't win and be a nice guy".

"You've got to break half a dozen eggs to make an omlette, and we're in the shit, defence wise. We're losing people hand over fist," Mark said.

Penk's office declined to comment.

Mark said if he became minister again, he would "look after" military people, and hinted he would take a look at the current defence leadership.

"You don't put yourself in an employment court by being insensible with your wording, but the Minister of Defence gets to sign the warrants, and the Minister of Defence gets to pick who they want to run the organisation, so therefore the Ministry of Defence is quite justified in looking at the track record over the last six years and making their own mind up as to who should be running the show or not."

Mark also served two stints as Carterton's mayor.

New Zealand First says Mark will run in the Wairarapa electorate.

"With a lifetime of service in the military, local government, Parliament and internationally, Ron Mark brings proven leadership and a deep commitment to serving the people of New Zealand," the party said in a statement.

Current MP Andy Foster, who is based in the Wairarapa electorate, will instead contest the Remutaka electorate.

Foster, who said it was Mark that got him involved in New Zealand First in the first place, said he would not have stood aside for anyone other than Mark.

"I was aware that Ron was thinking about it, and I knew that if Ron stood, I was going to be happy with it. If it had been anybody else, I probably wouldn't have been so happy. But because it's Ron, and I have the relationship I have with Ron, I'm happy with that. So it's not a problem."

NZ First has revealed a number of returning candidates and political defections in recent months.

Former National MP Alfred Ngaro was confirmed to be joining the party in May. He's joined by another former National MP, Harete Hipango-Brownlie.

Former Whanganui Mayor Michael Laws is standing as a candidate too. He will contest the Waitaki electorate, currently held by National's Miles Anderson.

World.title: NRLW: Warriors fall short in tussle with Titans
World.content:
The Warriors wāhine clawed their way back into the contest only to fall agonisingly short in a 18-16 defeat to the Gold Coast Titans in Wagga Wagga.

The second loss of the NRL-W season for the Kiwi side came down to a dramatic finish in the Magic Round clash.

The Warriors remain the top four for now, with undefeated Broncos topping the table. Gold Coast cemented third place with the win.

Down 18-0 with 16 minutes remaining, the Warriors unlocked their attacking flair, much of it down to Mele Hufanga on the left side.

The comeback began with the Kiwi Ferns star who charged onto a ball form former Broncos teammate Gayle Brougton to score her first try as a Warrior.

Hufanga's try was followed by Ivana Lauitiiti who was next in the scoring action, before Stacey Waaka came through pulling in an incredibly high kick to score in the corner.

Pushing for a late try, the Warriors were stopped by the clock, held back by relentless Titans defence.

Earlier Gold Coast hit the front with Ivana Lolesio outpacing the Kiwi defenders to chase down the grubber kick for their first try.

Back rower Evania Isa'ako busting through scored before the break with 24-year-old Indie Bostok scoring just after halftime.

Next round the Warriors host the Knights in Hamilton.

World.title: Live: Aussie cyclist 'proud not to spew' after gruelling gold-medal run
World.content:
(Getty)

Australian Leigh Hoffman has won three golds and a silver medal in this packed program.

He was the second last rider in that men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal, and he looked ready to vomit up there.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years time.

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

World.title: 'Rubbish' costs Rabbitohs as Hynes chases NRL record, Eels beat Tigers
World.content:
South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has said "rubbish" from his team continues to cost them chances to win games, as the Rabbitohs were beaten by the Cronulla Sharks.

The Rabbitohs started Sunday's top-eight battle brightly, scoring first and then playing against 12 men when Cronulla's Teig Wilton was sin-binned for a high shot on Jack Wighton.

But the Sharks would bounce back with 18 unanswered points before half-time, before kicking on in the second half for a 32-16 win.

Souths were their own worst enemy at times, missing more than 50 tackles as well as conceding six penalties and three six-again restarts.

The loss leaves the Rabbitohs seventh on the NRL ladder with 10 wins and nine losses, just one win ahead of 10th place Manly in the tight race for the top-eight.

After Sunday's 16-point loss to Cronulla, Bennett told reporters Souths' repeated errors were costing them the chance of competing with the best team in the league.

"Our Achilles heel is when we don't execute and then we pay a bit of a price for it," Bennett said.

"We can run deep (in the premiership) any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets in our game.

"If we can get that right, we can hold our own with most teams in the competition."

Meanwhile, Sharks halfback Nicho Hynes set a new club record by successfully kicking his 32nd consecutive goal.

Entering the day with a streak of 26, Hynes was perfect from his six attempts on Sunday to extend his run and close within three of the all-time record.

Canterbury Bulldogs great Hazem El Masri holds the record when he converted 35 consecutive goals in 2003.

In the final match on Sunday, Parramatta broke the hearts of Wests Tigers fans with a late try to Isaiah Iongi, snatching a 16-13 win.

The Eels led 12-0 at half-time before suffering a shocking second half, camped in their own end thanks to repeated errors, while two defence lapses allowed the Tigers to level the score.

Tigers halfback Adam Doueihi, who returned to the side after refusing to play last week, scored the try to level the scores, and kicked the Tigers ahead with a 72nd-minute field goal.

But a late try to Iongi in the 76th minute sealed an unconvincing win for the blue and gold.

Relive all of Sunday's NRL action in the blog below.

World.title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
World.content:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

World.title: Eagles star in tears after loss, Crows into top four after downing Dons
World.content:
Melbourne captain Max Gawn was inspirational in his team's nine-point win over Gold Coast. (Getty Images)

Melbourne has cemented its top six status ahead of next weekend's clash with ladder leaders Fremantle, defeating Gold Coast by nine points at Carrara Stadium.

In a contest featuring several lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) victory.

After a four-goal display against Geelong last week, Harrison Petty kicked three majors including a crucial after-the-siren effort at the end of the third quarter, while Jacob van Rooyen also kicked three for the visitors.

Melbourne captain Max Gawn was huge for the Demons, notching 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hit-outs and nine clearances.

After last weekend's loss to the Cats, Demons coach Steven King was thrilled by his team's ability to find a way to victory ahead of the clash with the Dockers.

"We've already played them once earlier this year, and we got taught a lesson," King said.

"This time we'll be at the MCG and we love playing there but I'm sure they'll come over as a full dress rehearsal for what's in front of them as a footy club.

"It's a privilege to play in big games that count, and we're lucky we grabbed our opportunity today and can still be relevant in this competition for what's ahead."

Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast was unable to prevent slumping to its 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca's first match against his former club.

Petracca, whose impact at the Suns had been under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the loss to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances.

Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, with coach Damien Hardwick lamenting a similar display to previous defeats.

"It's just frustrating because a lot of those things are absolutely within our control, and it's the stuff that we need to eradicate," Hardwick said.

Gold Coast slumped to its 10th straight loss, a feat unthinkable at the start of the season. (Getty Images)

"I've got to coach harder and tougher because otherwise we don't move forward.

"So we've learned a lot of lessons like that this year, unfortunately, but not getting the result we're after."

Both teams had injury worries with Sam Collins (ribs) and Blake Howes (wrist) sent to hospital for X-rays after coming off in separate incidents.

Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break.

Bailey Humphrey's goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break.

And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks.

The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.

Howes' nasty looking fall early in the last term didn't deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points.

While the Demons host the Dockers next weekend, the Suns will aim to snap their losing run in Canberra against GWS.

World.title: After javelin gold, Aussie star heads straight back to hospital work
World.content:
Sydney doctor Mackenzie Little has finally become a golden girl with the javelin as she led one last parade of Commonwealth Games field event medallists in the green and gold.

The remarkable 29-year-old Little, a doctor at Northern Beaches Hospital, can barely even call herself a part-time athlete these days, such is her busy medical life, but she still proved too good for her opponents as she finally lifted a major international title.

She nailed victory with her first throw and then revealed she will be jetting straight back to work on Tuesday as an ear, nose and throat registrar.

On a night when pole vaulter Kurtis Marschall completed Australia's golden track-and-field program by soaring to a Games-record 5.85 metres and a third-straight title, Little's achievement felt even more astonishing.

"I'm so I'm relieved and excited — this is so fantastic. Nailing the first throw is maybe something to do with how my training's been a bit quality over quantity in the last couple of years," she said.

"I wish I could say, you know, that I'm really, really training my butt off, but I'm just having to fit things in around my job. I'm having to make the most of sometimes challenging situations, not having all the time in the world.

"I perform surgeries and see outpatients in clinics and take care of patients who are in the ward sick in hospital. Then in the evenings, I'll get to training, but I've had to change my training locations this year to stay within 30 minutes of the hospital. When you're on call, you need to — overnight and in the evenings — be within 30 minutes of the hospital in case of emergencies.

"I'm gonna go and fly home straight away and get back to work."

On a tricky night for throwers in the Scotstoun Stadium on the last evening of track and field competition, Little believed her technique of throwing low and hard to cut through the wind helped her to a season best 61.88m with an opener that no-one else threatened.

New Zealand silver medallist Tori Moorby hurled 60.08m in the third round to grab the silver, while Kenya's Irene Jepkemboi took the bronze.

Kurtis Marschall reacts after securing his third Commonwealth Games gold medal in the pole vault. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Marschall, winner at both the Gold Coast and Birmingham Commonwealth Games, finished the night in style by becoming only the third Australian ever to win three titles in a row in the same event, and ending with a leap that surpassed his hero Steve Hooker's 5.80m in Melbourne 20 years ago.

Entering the competition late, the hot favourite from Adelaide held his nerve to defeat South African silver medallist Kyle Rademeyer and England's bronze winner Owen Heard (both 5.70m).

It was the latest big achievement for the 29-year-old, who earlier in the season handed a once-in-a-blue-moon defeat to the sport's modern-day legend, Armand 'Mondo' Duplantis.

"I just wanted to solidify myself in the record books, like I already did with the gold medal, but I definitely wanted to jump that 5.85 and take it off Steve," Marschall said.

Brooke Buschkuehl in action and on her way to bronze in the long jump. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Melbourne's Brooke Buschkuehl, the indefatigable 33-year-old mum, also made it a hat-trick of medals, but again missed out on the one she really wanted as she added a bronze in the long jump to go with her two silvers from Gold Coast and Birmingham.

Promising Wollongong teenager Delta Amidzovski, the 19-year-old world junior long jump champion, finished fourth, just five centimetres off a podium place.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Quick hits: Sprinter's surprise, a bored prince and a stunning upset
World.content:
An Australian sprinter receives a surprise visit, Jamaica celebrates in style after beating the Diamonds and Prince George looks bored at the cycling.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Surprise guests shock Aussie sprinter

Chloe Mannix-Power (right) had some fans she was not expecting to see in the stands. (Reuters: Phil Noble)

Chloe Mannix-Power somewhat controversially missed out on an individual 100-metre berth at these Games, but hit the track for the first time in the women's 4x100m heats.

In the moments after she and teammates Ebony Lane, Monique Hanlon and Georgia Harris made it through to the women's 4x100m final, Mannix-Power looked up into the stands and received quite a shock.

"I thought [my parents] were at home watching on the lounge, but no they're up in the top of the grandstand cheering me on," she said.

"My parents love a surprise moment, they've done it before, so to be honest I kind of had a little feeling they would be up there, but they never tell me they're here until the end of the race."

Mannix-Power later helped Australia finish fourth in the final.

2. Prince George bored?

Prince William, Princess Catherine and their three children took in a few of the sports on day nine.

Prince George, however, seemed as though he wanted to be anywhere else when they visited the velodrome.

Prince George watches on at the velodrome. (AP: Andrew Milligan)

Earlier, the royals watched on as the Diamonds lost 46-45 to Jamaica in a major upset in the netball semifinals.

The Prince and Princess of Wales took to Instagram to thank the athletes for putting on a show.

The Prince and Princess of Wales and their family watching the netball at the Hydro in Glasgow. (Getty Images)

"Incredible atmosphere at the Commonwealth Games today," a post from their official Instagram account read.

"Watching world-class talent compete and seeing the power of sport to bring people together is truly special.

"Thank you to everyone involved for such a wonderful day."

3. 'Absolute scenes'

Jamaica celebrates its win over the Diamonds. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

Not only did the Royals take in Jamaica's shock victory, but they also witnessed some of the wildest celebrations seen at the Commonwealth Games.

After Sophie Dwyer missed the shot that would have sent the semifinal to extra time, the entire Jamaican squad celebrated like they never had before.

We lost count of how many social media videos featured the caption: "Absolute scenes."

Loading Instagram content

For the Jamaicans, this was personal.

They were still hurting from their loss to the Diamonds in the 2022 Commonwealth Games final in Birmingham.

"We're carrying a bit of vengeance from the last Commonwealth Games," Jamaica captain Shamera Sterling-Humphrey said.

"We've graduated from bronze medals. We didn't want bronze this year."

Jamaica faces New Zealand in the final, while the Diamonds meet England in the bronze medal play-off.

4. Montag admits to being 'selfish'

Elizabeth McMillen led Jemima Montag for most of the race, but did not win gold. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

It was an Australian sweep of the medals in the women's 10,000m race walk, but the fight for the gold medal between teammates was a fierce one.

Australian Elizabeth McMillen and Jemima Montag broke clear from the pack early and led for the entire race.

McMillen was at the front, with Montag her shadow just behind.

Montag's strategy was to use McMillen as protection from the wind, a tactic which worked to perfection.

McMillen's lead for the better part of 23 laps of the 25-lap race, before Montag ducked out from behind her and put on the burners in a decisive attack to claim gold.

It was a move she had no regrets over.

"In a race you have to be selfish. Unfortunately it's an individual sport, not a team," Montag said.

"If it was cycling or something with drafting, where you do change the lead around then absolutely.

"But as much as I would love to, sometimes you have to forget it's a teammate that you care about and just remember it's another competitor and it's another body that in front of you and to ultimately be selfish."

McMillen was not particularly happy, but understood.

"What can you do? That's racing for you," McMillen said.

"I did look back a few times thinking, 'Are you going to help out here?', but no. I was the rabbit today, so what are you going to do?"

5. Indian boxer explains celebration

Arundhati Choudhary celebrates in her unique way. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

India boxer Arundhati Choudhary is a beacon of positivity inside and outside the ring.

Choudhary, who won gold in the women's 70-kilogram category in Glasgow, takes inspiration from a Hindu deity, Lord Rama.

This is why she opts for a bow and arrow celebration.

"In India we have Lord Rama, who killed negativity with his bow," Choudhary explained.

"Last year I was suffering from surgery and my family was also suffering from many problems.

"So I just throw the bow and arrow and shoot all the negativity out."

World.title: 'Pattern of missteps': Football bodies launch stunning Infantino rebuke
World.content:
Successfully stopping Gianni Infantino's FIFA plan to sell World Cup profits to private investors was the first half of a high-stakes game in global soccer politics.

The second half kicked off overnight with what seemed a clear aim of ending Infantino's decade-long presidency.

"No option should be off the table," said European soccer body UEFA, whose president Aleksander Čeferin has led the fight against Infantino in a seismic week for FIFA.

"The current FIFA leadership has not only lost UEFA's confidence but also that of many other members of the football family."

Aleksander Čeferin (left) has been a vocal critic of Gianni Infantino's latest quest to privatise part of FIFA. (Getty Images: Nicolò Campo/LightRocket)

After that comment, the governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) called for accountability, saying: "A [World Cup] proposal of this magnitude does not reach that stage by accident. It is a symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first. This recent unilateral and egregious act of poor governance and leadership follows a pattern of missteps and similar behaviour. A full review of this leadership must now take place."

Mr Infantino had proposed creating a $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) company to run the World Cup with private investors but drew backlash that grew every day since Tuesday's announcement.

The FIFA president was forced to scrap the plan early Saturday after his senior adviser who sat on a White House panel resigned and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined Europe and North America in opposing it.

UEFA's blistering statement

UEFA, the governing body of European soccer, issued its blistering statement hours after FIFA announced it was withdrawing its private equity plan.

"We cannot keep going on like this with secret schemes on fast-track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game," UEFA said.

"We must identify those responsible and hold them to account.

"It is right that, in the coming days and weeks, UEFA will work with its associations and in close cooperation with other confederations to reflect on how this happened and devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again."

Lise Klaveness (right) looks on as Gianni Infantino takes a selfie with a fan during the World Cup. (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Norwegian soccer federation president Lise Klaveness, an elected member of the UEFA executive committee, said steps must be taken to protect the integrity of the sport.

"The entire framework of international football cooperation was unnecessarily put at risk in pursuit of individual interests rather than the best interests of the game," Mr Klaveness said.

"This has been visible to many for a long time, including those of us elected to positions intended to safeguard checks and balances and provide ongoing oversight. We have to recognise that these mechanisms have not worked well enough."

Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa (right) also criticised the way the privatisation plan had been rolled out. (Getty Images: Kevin C. Cox)

The president of the AFC, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, said, "The future of global football must always be shaped through proper consultation, collective dialogue and respect for the established governance structures of our game."

Mr Infantino's audacious bid fell apart after UEFA's 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the AFC also said they opposed the plan.

CONCACAF's statement added that FIFA leaders have "a duty of service over power. Where that duty is not upheld, accountability cannot be optional".

FIFA's internal revolt

There was also an internal revolt.

Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

Hours later, FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour issued a statement to the Associated Press, saying FIFA staff were deceived by Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and that the project must not continue.

Kevin Lamour says the FIFA plan is a project of "one person". (Getty Images: Joosep Martinson)

"It is the project of one person," wrote Mr Lamour, a longtime colleague of Mr Infantino at both FIFA and UEFA.

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Infantino had proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $US20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor", described by FIFA, is a New York-based investment firm launched by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

This is not Infantino's first big plan to flop

A tumultuous week in international soccer is at least the third time Mr Infantino has rocked it with an ambitious plan many in the sport saw as reckless.

But the fallout from FIFA's Joshua Kushner-backed plan is the first time UEFA has acted quickly to create momentum for removing the man who was its former long-time employee.

In 2018, Mr Infantino pushed a secretive offer of $US25 billion from Japan's SoftBank to create new competitions, which posed a long-term risk to continental events for clubs and national teams.

Vladimir Putin awarded an Order of Friendship to Gianni Infantino after the 2018 World Cup in Russia. (Getty Images: Mikhail Metzel/TASS)

In 2021, Mr Infantino proposed playing World Cups every two years instead of four — an idea that also angered the International Olympic Committee where he is an elected member.

Both plans created big rifts in the sport and were eventually dropped by FIFA.

Despite the turmoil, Mr Infantino was re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

The third time is shaping up to be different.

November 18 is the deadline for candidates to enter the next presidential contest, exactly four months ahead of the vote in Rabat, Morocco, where FIFA has its African headquarters.

FIFA statutes allow Mr Infantino one more four-year term in office. The failed spin-off venture seemed like a way to create a commissioner-like role for Mr Infantino beyond 2031, likely paying much more than his current annual salary and a bonus deal of more than $US6 million.

Gianni Infantino with Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and Jordan's Crown Prince Hussein at the FIFA Arab Cup 2025. (Getty Images: Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto)

It would take 106 votes to ensure a majority in a contested election. Continents surely do not vote uniformly en bloc, but most of Europe's 55, plus Asia's 46 and CONCACAF's 35 FIFA members would be a solid base.

The Qatar FA issued a statement in support of Infantino on Saturday.

Its president, Sheikh Hamad bin Khalifa bin Ahmed Al Thani, said: "We welcome FIFA President Gianni Infantino's decision to withdraw the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal in the interest of the global football community.

"While the proposal had merit, we applaud the wisdom behind prioritising unity among Member Associations. The Qatar Football Association fully supports president Infantino's efforts to continue growing and strengthening the game globally."

Tech.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming.

The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.

I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it.

Our HyperX Omen 15 review unit is a $1,199 configuration sold through Walmart with an eight-core Intel Core 5 210H “Raptor Lake” chip, RTX 5050 discreet GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. There are pricier Omen 15 configs out there with RTX 5070 GPUs and OLED screens, but that’s like spending Acura money on a Honda Civic. On the lower end, HP still has a Victus 15 config with the RTX 5050 for $900, but it has 8GB of RAM — that’s not really tenable, especially for playing the latest games.

The good news is that the Omen 15 with an RTX 5050 is pretty serviceable for playing games at its 1920 x 1200 native resolution. Last-gen games like Control can get a smooth 70 to 80fps on High preset while using DLSS. Cyberpunk 2077 can run on the Ultra preset (no ray tracing) with DLSS set to Quality and get 60 to 70fps— sometimes dipping down to 40 while driving with lots of stuff onscreen. Standard frame generation boosts it to 95 to 105fps, and 70s to low 80s in a car. Multi Frame Gen, which you don’t get on last-gen GPUs, can push that ever further if you don’t mind more “fake frames.”

Newer games are a more Medium to Low affair. For example, Helldivers 2 runs comfortably at just above 60fps on its Medium preset with DLSS set to Quality — though it dips into the 40s when the bug guts hit the fan. But Battlefield 6 was lower, down in the 50fps range while running Medium preset with DLSS cranked to Performance. I also tested Halo: Campaign Evolved, which defaulted to its Very Low preset, where it looked like a potato. On Low settings, with DLSS set to Medium, it mustered between 50 to 60fps, but with frequent drops into the 40s with lots of enemies onscreen.

On the right, an ethernet jack and one USB-A. On the left, a 3.5mm audio jack, one USB-A, and the power connector. On the rear, HDMI 2.1 and one USB-C. Seriously, where’s the rest?

While playing all these games, the fans kicked up to a decent volume, but they weren’t obnoxiously loud, and the chassis stayed reasonably cool. The hottest point, a small spot under the chassis, rose to 113 degrees Fahrenheit / 45 Celsius. But the main areas that normally make contact with your hands or lap didn’t get too warm — pretty good thermals for a somewhat compact gaming laptop.

So the RTX 5050 GPU and its 8GB of VRAM can get by with the latest graphically intense games, so long as you’re not expecting a visual powerhouse. But what about living with the rest of the laptop?

Much of the Omen 15’s price has gone to its specs. That means there are some rough edges showing in the usual areas. The trackpad has a responsive mechanical click, but if you pick up the laptop by either of its front corners the chassis flexes and causes an accidental click. This is common in mostly plastic laptops, but still annoying.

The keyboard has decent enough tactility when typing. But even though I know gamers love a number pad, it makes this 15-inch laptop feel cramped. I don’t enjoy typing on it like I have other HP laptops. The speakers? A little muddy-sounding — especially for music. And the ports? It has HDMI 2.1 and gigabit ethernet, which is great, but only one USB-C to go with its two USB-A ports. And all of them are a modest 10Gbps — not particularly speedy compared to USB4 or Thunderbolt 4. Gaming laptops are supposed to have ports aplenty, but this is just ports apassable.

Previous Next











1 / 7 The screen does a decent job controlling glare.

Aside from its gaming performance, the Omen 15’s other strength is its screen. The 1920 x 1200 IPS panel isn’t particularly special, but at 400 nits it’s decently bright and it has nice contrast and colors. It’s good for games, and fine for productivity work and light content creation. I did a bit of Lightroom Classic editing on the Omen 15, and my 50-megapixel RAW files were workable at a modest clip. (It helped that I was editing a batch of under 50 images, and not, like, 2,000.) The bigger problem with trying to do creative things was the Omen’s paltry 512GB of storage. It fills up quickly when games like Battlefield 6 take up 142GB. There’s a second M.2 slot for another drive, just as there’s a second RAM slot, which is great for future upgrades — but boy will that cost you right now. You can hold out for RAM and SSD prices to come back down to Earth, but if that takes as long as it’s expected to, the Omen 15 might feel pretty outdated by then.

The Omen was also fine for my everyday work: Chrome tabs, four virtual desktops, Signal, Slack, music streaming, etc. While the 1080p webcam is a little grainy and slightly low in saturation, it looks fine on video calls. The main barrier to getting work done on the Omen 15 is that its battery never lasted me more than five and a half hours. That’s far from the worst for gaming laptops, but keep that chunky power adapter with its barrel plug nearby.

That HyperX lid logo still doesn’t look great to me, but I’m getting used to ignoring it.

The HyperX Omen 15 is a decent gaming laptop. It’s just not the value the Victus 15 used to be. But neither is anything else. Absent a really good sale, you’re going to pay over $1,000 for anything with the RTX 5050, and usually a lot more. But buying into even the bottom rung of the 50-series gets you all of Nvidia’s latest features, like Multi Frame Gen and whatever DLSS 5 eventually shapes up to be. Last-gen 40-series or AMD GPUs aren’t bad options, but Multi Frame Gen can help keep frame rates playable for longer.

It’s still worth looking for those sales, though. HP, Best Buy, and Walmart often have deals on most of HP’s product line. Even now, there’s an Omen 16 with an RTX 5060 GPU and slightly larger (but dimmer) screen for just $100 more than the Omen 15.

RAMageddon makes buying a new gaming laptop daunting. If you need to buy now and you don’t want to go open-box or secondhand, you just have to come to terms with the fact that you’re going to be paying higher prices than equivalent models from a year or two ago — even in the “entry level.” Considering the circumstances, the Omen 15 is an okay value at $1,200 for getting into laptop gaming.
